## Infrastructure [#infrastructure](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html)
With the SlurmDBD, we are able to collect data from multiple
clusters in a single location.
This does impose some constraints on the user naming and IDs.
Accounting is maintained by user name (not user ID), but a
given user name should refer to the same person across all
of the computers.
Authentication relies upon user ID numbers, so those must
be uniform across all computers communicating with each
SlurmDBD, at least for users requiring authentication.
In particular, the configured SlurmUser must have the
same name and ID across all clusters.
If you plan to have administrators of user accounts, limits,
etc. they must also have consistent names and IDs across all
clusters.
If you plan to restrict access to accounting records (e.g.

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise practical guide to submitting Slurm batch jobs (sbatch), with examples and useful tips.

1) Basic idea
- Create a batch script (a plain shell script) with Slurm directives in header lines starting with #SBATCH.
- Submit it with: sbatch my_script.sh
- sbatch prints a job ID on success. Check status with squeue -u youruser or squeue -j <jobid>.

2) Minimal batch script (CPU job)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my_cpu_job
#SBATCH --output=job.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job.%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00

# load modules, prepare env
module load python
srun python train.py   # or run your commands directly

3) GPU job example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my_gpu_job
#SBATCH --output=gpu_job.%j.out
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1

Here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial covering the most common tasks, commands, and best practices you’ll need to run jobs on an HPC cluster.

1) Core concepts
- Controller (slurmctld) schedules jobs; compute nodes run jobs.
- Job = an allocation of resources (nodes/CPUs/GPUs/memory) for some time.
- Batch job = script submitted with sbatch. Interactive allocation = salloc / srun.
- Partitions are schedulable groups of nodes (like queues).
- TRES = tracked resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs, licenses, etc).

2) Submitting batch jobs (sbatch)
- Basic workflow: write a shell script with SBATCH directives, then run sbatch script.sh.
- Minimal example:
  #!/bin/sh
  #SBATCH --job-name=myjob
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=4
  #SBATCH --mem=16G
  #SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out

  srun my_program arg1 arg2
- Important SBATCH options:
  --time=HH:MM:SS (or D-HH:MM:SS)
  --nodes=N
  --ntasks / --ntasks-per-node
  --cpus-per-task (for multithreaded tasks)
  --mem (total for job) vs --mem-per-cpu
  --partition=name
  --account=acct
  --qos=name
  --gres=gpu:1 (request GPUs)
  --output, --error (filename patterns support %j (jobid), %a (array index))
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345:12346 to run after jobs succeed.

3) Interactive & allocations (salloc, srun)
- salloc requests an allocation and gives you an interactive shell on the allocation:
  salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=01:00:00 --gres=gpu:1
- Use srun to launch tasks inside an allocation or to run tasks from a batch script:
  srun --ntasks=4 ./mpi_program
- For quick test shells you can also use srun --pty bash

4) Job arrays
- Useful for parameter sweeps; a single submission creates many jobs:
  #SBATCH --array=1-100%10    (100 tasks, at most 10 running concurrently)
- Inside the script use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (or %a in file names) to pick parameters or ranges.

5) Requesting GPUs and conditional considerations
- Request with --gres=gpu:count (or --gres=gpu:V100:1 if specific type allowed).
- When aiming to submit only if idle GPUs exist, check sinfo for idle GPU node counts first (idle nodes count must be >0).

6) Inspecting jobs and cluster state
- squeue shows current queued/running jobs. Useful options:
  squeue -u $USER
  squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.20j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.9l %.6D %R"  (custom format)
- sinfo shows partitions and node availability (allocated/idle/down counts):
  sinfo
  sinfo -N -l   (node-level)
- scontrol show job <jobid> prints detailed job fields (reasons, TRES, resources, dependencies).
- sstat -j <jobid> shows runtime resource usage for running jobs.
- sacct for historical/completed jobs and accounting (start/end/exitcode).

7) Cancelling, holding, requeuing (admin/user)
- Cancel: scancel <jobid> (or scancel -u username, scancel -p partition)
- Hold/release: scontrol hold <jobid>; scontrol release <jobid>
- Requeue: scontrol requeue <jobid> or scancel --signal? (admins normally use scontrol_requeue)

8) Common troubleshooting steps
- Job is PENDING: check REASON column in squeue. Common reasons: Resources, Priority, PartitionDown, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOSMaxWalltime, User/QOS limits.
- If squeue doesn’t show a reason or you need more detail, run:
  scontrol show job <jobid>
- If job disappears from squeue and you expect history, check sacct to see completion/exit codes and runtime.
- For preemption/priority issues, sprio and sdiag can help diagnose scheduling behavior.

9) Useful environment variables available inside jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_NNODES, SLURM_NODELIST, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE

10) Monitoring & accounting
- sacct for completed jobs (filters by user; by default do not add extra state filters unless requested).
- sreport for usage reports (CPU-hours/GPU-hours) by user/account/partition.
- scontrol show config and scontrol ping for controller health (admins).

11) Best practices
- Always request realistic walltime; overestimating wastes queue priority, underestimating can kill jobs.
- Request memory explicitly (--mem or --mem-per-cpu); avoid relying on defaults.
- Test new code interactively (salloc/srun) on small inputs before a large sbatch run.
- Use job arrays for many similar/independent tasks instead of many separate sbatch calls.
- Redirect stdout/stderr to files; include %j or %a to avoid collisions.
- Check node/partition status (sinfo) before heavy submissions.
- For repeatable workflows, checkpoint and make jobs restartable.
- Be mindful of site-specific policies (accounts, QOS, node constraints).

- Submit batch: sbatch script.sh
- Interactive allocation: salloc [options]
- Run in allocation or step: srun [options] command
- Show queue: squeue (squeue -u $USER)
- Show nodes/partitions: sinfo
- Job details: scontrol show job <id>
- Resource usage (running): sstat -j <id>
- Historic accounting: sacct
- Cancel job: scancel <id>
- Job arrays: sbatch --array=1-100 script.sh
- Request GPU: --gres=gpu:1

- The official Slurm docs are the canonical reference (sbatch, srun, salloc, squeue, sinfo, sacct pages).
- Your cluster’s local documentation / help pages for site-specific partitions, accounts, and GPU types.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Sure — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial that covers the common concepts, commands, examples, and troubleshooting tips you’ll need to run jobs on an HPC cluster.

1) Quick architecture & concepts
- slurmctld: cluster controller / scheduler.
- slurmd: node daemon that runs tasks.
- slurmdbd: optional accounting DB service.
- Nodes: physical/virtual machines that run jobs.
- Partitions: named sets of nodes (like queues).
- Job: a submitted workload (batch or interactive).
- Job step: one parallel piece inside a job (srun creates steps).
- Allocation vs. job vs. step: sbatch/salloc allocate resources and create jobs; srun runs tasks/steps inside an allocation.

2) Key commands
- sbatch script.sh — submit a batch job (non-interactive).
- srun … — run a job step (interactive or inside an allocation).
- salloc … — request an interactive allocation (gives a shell with resources).
- squeue — view queued/running jobs.
- sinfo — view partitions and node status.
- sacct — historical accounting for completed jobs.
- scontrol show job <id> — detailed job information.
- scancel <jobid> — cancel a job.

3) Basic sbatch script (typical)
Example (replace with cluster-appropriate values):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1         # request 1 GPU (if available)

module load python/3.9
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- #SBATCH lines are directives interpreted by sbatch.
- --nodes, --ntasks, --cpus-per-task, and --mem define resources. ntasks often maps to MPI ranks; cpus-per-task to threads (OpenMP).
- --gres=gpu:N requests GPUs (cluster-specific GPU names may vary).
- %j in --output expands to job ID.

4) sbatch vs srun vs salloc (short)
- sbatch: submit a batch script, job runs later under scheduler.
- srun: within an allocation it launches tasks; srun can also launch immediate parallel jobs (but most batch scripts use sbatch + srun).
- salloc: get an interactive allocation (then use srun or run commands directly).

5) Useful sbatch options / features
- Job arrays: --array=1-100 to run many similar tasks (use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID).
- Dependencies: --dependency=afterok:12345 to start after job 12345 finishes successfully.
- QOS/account: --qos=..., --account=... (cluster policy controlled).
- Email notifications: --mail-user=you@org --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL
- Time format: HH:MM:SS or D-HH:MM:SS (cluster may accept different formats).

6) Environment variables available in jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (when arrays), SLURM_JOB_NAME.
Use these in scripts to adapt behavior per job/array index.

7) MPI and multi-node jobs
- Request nodes and tasks: e.g., --nodes=4 --ntasks-per-node=8 (or --ntasks=32).
- Launch MPI with srun mpirun-wrapper: srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_app or srun ./my_mpi_app (cluster MPI config-dependent).
- Avoid mixing mpirun and srun unless your cluster docs recommend it.

8) GPUs and containers
- GPUs: request with --gres=gpu:N or cluster-specific gres keys. Check sinfo for GPU partitions/nodes.
- Containers: Singularity / Apptainer often used. Example: singularity exec image.sif python train.py inside job script.

9) Monitoring & debugging
- squeue -u $USER to see your jobs.
- scontrol show job <id> for detailed config and reason for pending state.
- sstat -j <jobid> for realtime resource usage (running jobs).
- sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed for accounting of finished jobs.
- Examine job-<id>.out / job-<id>.err files written by --output/--error.
- Pending reasons (from squeue REASON column): Resources, Priority, Dependency, QOS, PartitionTimeLimit, etc. Use scontrol show job <id> for extra detail if needed.

10) Common pitfalls & best practices
- Over-requesting memory or GPUs reduces scheduler fit; request realistic resources.
- For multi-threaded codes, match cpus-per-task to number of threads (export OMP_NUM_THREADS accordingly).
- Prefer specifying --mem-per-cpu when you want memory scaled by CPU.
- Use job arrays for many similar short tasks (more efficient than many single-job submissions).
- Keep runtime estimates realistic; long requests can push you to the back of the queue.
- Save checkpoints frequently for long runs; enable restart logic.

11) Troubleshooting quick checklist
- Job stuck PENDING: check REASON in squeue; if “Resources” you may need to wait or request fewer resources/another partition; if “Dependency” or “QOS” check job options.
- Job fails quickly with ExitCode != 0: check stderr file and node/step info with scontrol show job.
- No GPUs available: use sinfo to inspect GPU node states and partitions.
- Account/QOS limits: contact admins or use sacctmgr_list (admins) to inspect limits.

12) Where to go next (advanced topics)
- Fairshare and priorities: sprio, sshare.
- Reservations: scontrol show reservation / scontrol create reservation (admin).
- Scheduler tuning & diagnostics: sdiag, sprio_weights, slurmctld logs (admin).
- Accounting reports: sreport for CPU/GPU-hour reports.

If you want:
- a one-page cheat sheet of the most-used commands,
- a ready-to-submit example for MPI or GPU training (I can generate one),
- or cluster-specific advice (e.g., exact partition names, gres values) — tell me what cluster resource names or workload type you have and I’ll tailor examples.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Sure — here’s a compact Slurm tutorial covering the common commands, a sample batch script, how to run interactively, monitoring & debugging, job arrays/dependencies, GPU requests, and some best practices.

Quick overview of core commands
- sbatch: submit a batch script (non-interactive).
- srun: launch tasks (used inside jobs or to create job steps / interactive runs).
- salloc: allocate resources interactively (gives you a shell/allocation).
- squeue: view current queue and job states.
- sinfo: view partitions and node states/capacity.
- sacct: query historical/accounting information for completed jobs.
- scontrol: view/change detailed Slurm entity state (jobs, nodes, partitions).
- scancel: cancel jobs.

Minimal batch script example (save as job.sh and run sbatch job.sh)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my-job
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1               # request 1 GPU
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00            # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --output=job.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job.%j.err

module load python/3.10
# run with srun so Slurm tracks task(s)
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- sbatch returns immediately with a job ID; the job may wait in queue until resources are available.
- Use --mem (total per node) or --mem-per-cpu; use --cpus-per-task for multi-threaded tasks (OpenMP etc).
- For multi-node MPI jobs request --ntasks and use srun -n $SLURM_NTASKS mpirun/your-mpi-app.

Interactive usage
- Get an interactive allocation (then run commands inside it):
  salloc --partition=interactive --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=01:00:00
  srun --pty bash -i
- Or single-command interactive:
  srun --partition=interactive --gres=gpu:1 --pty bash

Checking queue & nodes
- squeue -u $USER         # your jobs
- squeue -j JOBID         # info for a job
- squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R"  # custom columns (example)
- sinfo                   # partition/node counts and states (alloc/idle/down)
- sinfo -N -l             # per-node details

Diagnose pending jobs
- squeue shows reason column (REASON or RE) for pending jobs (PD state).
- For more detail: scontrol show job JOBID — shows constraints/feasible nodes and reason text.

Historical/accounting queries
- sacct -j JOBID                     # post-run accounting for that job
- sacct -u username --starttime=2024-01-01  # user history from date
- sacct output can be formatted (--format=JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,ExitCode,...)

Live job stats & debugging
- sstat -j JOBID                      # live resource usage for running jobs (CPU%, RSS, I/O)
- Check output/error files (--output/--error) for job logs.
- scontrol show job JOBID             # full job config + allocation info
- scontrol show node nodename         # node-level state and reason (if down/drained)
- If a job fails quickly, use sacct -j JOBID --format=Elapsed,ExitCode,State to inspect exit code.

Job arrays & dependencies
- Arrays: in SBATCH header or sbatch: #SBATCH --array=1-100%10
  Use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in script to index work.
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 script.sh
  Common types: afterok, afterany, aftercorr, singleton, after.

GPU requests
- Request GPUs with --gres=gpu:N (example: --gres=gpu:2).
- To make conditional submit decisions (e.g., "only submit if GPU nodes idle"), you must check sinfo first to ensure idle GPU nodes exist. (For cluster ops: use sinfo to verify idle GPU nodes before submission.)

Common states you’ll see in squeue
- R: running
- PD: pending (waiting); REASON column explains why
- CG: completing
- S: suspended
- F: failed

Cancel/hold/requeue
- Cancel a job: scancel JOBID
- Hold a job: scontrol hold JOBID
- Release hold: scontrol release JOBID
(These are cluster-changing actions — use your admin tools or ask your operator if you need help.)

Best practices / tips
- Request realistic time limits: overestimating wastes scheduling; underestimating leads to timeouts.
- Test on small jobs first (short walltime, small data) before scaling up.
- Pin CPUs and set OMP_NUM_THREADS consistent with --cpus-per-task for threaded apps.
- Use job arrays for embarrassingly parallel tasks rather than many independent sbatch submissions.
- Capture both stdout/stderr to files (--output, --error) and include job ID in filenames e.g., job.%j.out.
- Check sinfo before large submissions to see partition/node availability.
- Use salloc/srun for interactive debugging and quick experiments.
- For reproducibility, log the environment (module list, git commit, python env list) from the job script.

Quick cheat-sheet (examples)
- Submit: sbatch job.sh
- Check your queue: squeue -u $USER
- Show detailed job: scontrol show job JOBID
- Cancel: scancel JOBID
- Interactive allocate: salloc --time=01:00:00
- Interactive run: srun --gres=gpu:1 --pty bash
- List partitions/nodes: sinfo -s
- Historical job info: sacct -j JOBID --format=JobID,JobName,User,State,ExitCode,Elapsed

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Short answer: write clear, minimal SBATCH directives that exactly request the resources you need, prepare the environment (modules, conda, etc.), run your job with srun (or the launcher your site prefers), capture useful environment/logging information, and make the script reproducible and testable. Below are a checklist, explanations of common options, a few short templates, and practical tips.

Checklist (what every batch script should do)
- Start with a shebang (#!/bin/bash) and safe shell options (e.g., set -euo pipefail).
- Set SBATCH directives for job-name, output, error, partition, time, nodes/ntasks/cpus-per-task, memory and GPUs (gres) as appropriate.
- Load modules / activate environments explicitly.
- cd to the intended working directory or use absolute paths.
- Stage input data and outputs (or reference shared filesystem paths).
- Use srun for the actual program (srun integrates with Slurm and sets task ranks).
- Print minimal runtime diagnostics (date, hostname, env, nproc, free -h, nvidia-smi for GPUs).
- Log stdout/stderr to files with useful names (include %j jobid or %x job name).
- Keep walltime reasonable and add safety margins; use checkpointing if long runs.
- Include cleanup/exit handling where needed (trap on TERM).

Common SBATCH options and what they mean
- --job-name=NAME : human-readable job name.
- --output=FILE, --error=FILE : files for stdout/stderr; use %j (jobid) or %x (jobname).
- --partition=PART : which partition/queue.
- --time=HH:MM:SS : walltime limit (always set).
- --nodes=N : number of nodes.
- --ntasks=NT : number of tasks total (MPI ranks).
- --cpus-per-task=M : threads per task (for OpenMP).
- --mem=MEM or --mem-per-cpu= : RAM reservation.
- --gres=gpu:K or gpu:V100:K : request GPUs.
- --exclusive : node exclusive allocation.
- --account=NAME / --qos= : accounting/QoS tags if your cluster requires them.
- --array=0-99%10 : job arrays; %10 caps concurrent tasks to 10.
- --dependency=afterok:12345 : run after another job finishes successfully.
- --mail-type=FAIL,END,BEGIN --mail-user=you@org : email notifications.

Basic single-node CPU template
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x_%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G

set -euo pipefail
date
echo "Job: $SLURM_JOB_ID $SLURM_JOB_NAME"
module purge
module load python/3.10
cd /home/$USER/myproject
echo "Loaded modules:"; module list

srun python train.py --epochs 10 --data /scratch/$USER/data

GPU single-node template
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu_train
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=6
#SBATCH --mem=32G

set -euo pipefail
date; hostname
module purge
module load cuda/12.0 cudnn
source ~/envs/myenv/bin/activate
nvidia-smi
srun --cpu_bind=cores python train_gpu.py --batch 64

Job array example (many similar short tasks)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=array_job
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --array=0-99%20
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G

set -euo pipefail
TASK_ID=$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
echo "Running array task $TASK_ID"
srun python process_chunk.py --chunk $TASK_ID

Good practices and tips
- Test small first: run with --time=00:05:00 and small inputs, and check logs.
- Prefer srun for MPI and parallel programs; many sites require srun rather than mpirun for correct Slurm integration.
- Distinguish ntasks vs cpus-per-task: ntasks is number of MPI ranks; cpus-per-task is threads each rank uses.
- Use --mem-per-cpu when you want memory tied to CPU count; use --mem when you want node-level memory.
- Include module list and environment information in logs for reproducibility.
- Use %j and %x in filenames so a single directory can hold many job outputs without collision.
- For GPU jobs, call nvidia-smi at start to record device allocation and status.
- Avoid hardcoding paths on ephemeral node-local scratch; copy used files in at start and copy results out at end.
- Use checkpointing (save model periodically) for long runs and consider job requeue or array/resubmit strategies for resilience.
- For debugging: run interactively (salloc or srun --pty bash) or request a short debug partition if available.
- Be explicit about licenses, accounts, QOS if cluster enforces them.

Debugging and cost control
- Always set --time; Slurm will kill jobs that exceed it.
- Keep an eye on memory: OOMs often kill jobs silently. Check sacct or job exit code for oom-kill indicators.
- Use sacct -j JOBID --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed to inspect exit info after completion.
- Use sprio / sdiag if your jobs are stuck pending to see priority/backfill issues (ask admins if unexplained).

If you want, I can:
- Review one of your existing batch scripts and suggest improvements (paste it here).
- Produce a template tailored to your workload (MPI across N nodes, Data-parallel GPU, array with x tasks). Which would you like?

Short answer: write a batch script with #SBATCH directives that request resources, then run sbatch myscript.sh.

What to put in the batch script (minimal example)
- Shebang and SBATCH directives (one per resource/option). Example:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob           # job name
#SBATCH --partition=gpu            # partition
#SBATCH --nodes=1                  # nodes
#SBATCH --ntasks=1                 # MPI ranks
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4          # threads per task
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1               # request 1 GPU
#SBATCH --mem=16G                  # memory
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00            # HH:MM:SS walltime
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out      # stdout file (%j expands to jobid)
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err       # stderr file
# Commands to run:
module load python
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes and useful options
- Submit: sbatch myscript.sh. sbatch prints the assigned job ID on success.
- Time format: HH:MM:SS (or D-HH:MM:SS).
- Memory: suffix with K/M/G (e.g., 16000M or 16G).
- GPUs: use --gres=gpu:N or cluster-specific names (ask admins if unsure).
- Job arrays: #SBATCH --array=0-9 or --array=0-99%10 and use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script.
- Request particular node(s): --nodelist=node01 or -w node[01-03].
- Interactive/allocations: use salloc or srun for interactive jobs (not sbatch).
- Default output: if not set, Slurm writes slurm-<jobid>.out.
- Check status: squeue -u $USER. For finished jobs use sacct.
- Cancel: scancel <jobid>.

Cluster-specific tips
- Check partition/node availability before requesting GPUs (sinfo). Some clusters require specific gres names or accounts—if unsure, check your cluster docs or ask admins.
- If you want me to submit a script for you, tell me the exact script path and submission parameters; I will hand that over to the operator to run.

Sure — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use whether you’re a user submitting jobs or learning the basics. If you want a deep dive into any section (batch scripts, GPUs, debugging, admin topics), tell me which and I’ll expand.

1) What Slurm is (very short)
- Slurm is a workload manager for scheduling batch and interactive jobs on HPC clusters. Key components: slurmctld (controller/scheduler), slurmd (node daemons), and optionally slurmdbd (accounting).

2) Common Slurm concepts
- Partition: a named group of nodes (like a queue).
- Job: a submitted workload (batch or interactive).
- Job states: PENDING (PD), RUNNING (R), COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.
- Resources: nodes, CPUs, memory, GPUs, licenses, QOS, accounts.
- Job array: many similar jobs with a single submission (indexed tasks).

3) Important commands (quick reference)
- sbatch <script.sh> — submit a batch job
- srun [options] — run a command under Slurm (interactive or within scripts)
- salloc [options] — allocate an interactive allocation
- scancel <jobid> — cancel job(s)
- squeue [filters] — view queued/running jobs (squeue -u $USER)
- sinfo — see partition/node availability
- sacct -j <jobid> — view historical accounting for completed jobs
- scontrol show job <jobid> — show detailed job info
- sstat -j <jobid> — runtime stats for running jobs

4) Minimal sbatch script (example)
- Example header lines you put at top of script (each is a separate line):
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=myjob
  #SBATCH --partition=gpu
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
  #SBATCH --mem=32G
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  #SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
  #SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
- Then your commands:
  module load python/3.10
  srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- --gres=gpu:1 requests one GPU. Different clusters may use different gres names (gpu, gpu:V100, etc.).
- Use %j in output filenames to include the job ID.

5) Interactive jobs
- salloc --partition=gpu --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
- srun --pty bash   (or srun --mpi=pmix --pty bash)
- Or srun --x11 to forward display

6) Job arrays
- #SBATCH --array=1-100%10 runs 100 tasks but only 10 concurrently.
- Use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the job to index input files.

7) Dependencies and chaining
- sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> second_job.sh
- Dependency types: after, afterok, afternotok, singleton, etc.

8) Monitoring & debugging
- squeue -j <jobid> or squeue -u $USER
- If a job is PENDING, squeue often shows a reason column: e.g., Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, PartitionDown, Dependency.
- For more details: scontrol show job <jobid> (includes reason in more detail).
- Check slurm-%j.out and .err for your program output.
- For runtime metrics while running: sstat -j <jobid>

9) Best practices
- Submit a small quick test job first (30s–1m) to ensure the environment modules, paths, and data are correct.
- Request conservative resources, then scale up. Over-requesting harms scheduling and may increase wait time.
- Specify a realistic walltime; shorter requests often start sooner.
- Put module loads and environment setup in the script (do not rely on interactive env).
- Use checkpoints or save intermediate outputs to shared storage to avoid losing long runs.
- Use job arrays for parallel parameter sweeps rather than many small independent sbatch files.

10) GPU-specific tips
- Use --gres=gpu:N to request GPUs.
- Use nvidia-smi or gpustat inside a running job to verify GPU assignment.
- For conditional GPU submissions (if you asked to submit only when idle GPUs exist), admins/operators should check sinfo to verify idle GPU nodes first.

11) Accounting & history
- sacct -u $USER --starttime=2024-01-01 shows past usage (CPU/GPU hours, exit codes).
- sreport can generate summaries (CPU-hours/GPU-hours) across accounts/time windows.

12) Common trouble reasons
- "Resources" — requested resources not available right now.
- "ReqNodeNotAvail" — specific node constraints unmet.
- "Priority" — higher-priority jobs scheduled first.
- "Dependency" — job is waiting for another job to finish.
- "PartitionDown/Drained" — partition or nodes unavailable.

13) Where to learn more

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise guide to submitting jobs with Slurm.

Basic concepts
- Batch jobs: submit a shell script with sbatch. The script contains resource requests and the commands to run.
- Interactive jobs: use salloc or srun --pty for an interactive allocation.
- Monitor: squeue (running/pending), sacct (historical/accounting), scancel (cancel).

Minimal batch script (example)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00

module load python
srun python my_script.py

Notes:
- #!/bin/bash must be first line.
- #SBATCH lines set job options inside the script.
- slurm-%j.out will contain stdout/stderr; %j expands to the job ID.
- srun is used inside the job to launch tasks; for single-process jobs srun is optional but recommended.

Common sbatch options (cli or #SBATCH)
- --partition=PARTITION (or #SBATCH --partition=...)
- --gres=gpu:1 (for GPUs)
- --cpus-per-task=N
- --mem=8G (per node, unless your cluster interprets otherwise)
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --job-name=NAME
- --output=FILE, --error=FILE (or --output=FILE to capture both)
- --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@example.com
- --array=1-100 or --array=1-100%10 (job arrays; use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside script)
- --dependency=afterok:12345 (run after job 12345 completes successfully)

Example submit command (from shell)
sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=32G --time=04:00:00 --job-name=train --output=train.%j.log train.sh

Quick one-liner submission
sbatch --wrap="python train.py --epochs 10" --time=00:30:00 --cpus-per-task=2

Interactive session
- Request an interactive allocation: salloc --partition=interactive --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
- Then run srun --pty bash or run commands in that allocation.

Monitoring and debugging
- squeue -u $USER to see your queued/running jobs
- squeue -j <jobid> or scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed state/pending reason
- sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed for historical results
- scancel <jobid> to cancel

GPU-submission caveat
- If you asked for an interactive conditional GPU submission, only nodes shown as idle in sinfo are eligible. (This is cluster policy detail; check sinfo if needed.)

Best practices / tips
- Explicitly set --time; jobs that exceed time are killed.
- Request only the resources you need to improve scheduling.
- Use job arrays for parameter sweeps instead of many separate jobs.
- Capture stderr/stdout to files for post-mortem.
- Load modules / activate conda inside the script; the script runs in the submit directory by default.
- Check cluster docs or admins for account/QOS limits, partition names, and GPU accounting.

If you want, tell me:
- whether you need a CPU or GPU job,
- how many CPUs/GPU/memory and expected runtime,
and I can draft a ready-to-submit sbatch script for you.

1) Key commands (what they do)
- sbatch: submit a batch script (non-interactive).
- srun: launch tasks/steps (can be used inside a batch job or from an allocation).
- salloc: get an allocation for interactive work (then use srun or a shell).
- squeue: view current queue (running/pending jobs).
- sacct: view historical/accounting records for completed/failed jobs.
- scontrol show job <id>: show detailed job info.
- scancel <id>: cancel a job.

2) Basic sbatch batch script (example)
- Save as job.sh and submit with: sbatch job.sh
Example contents (put these lines near top of your script):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out        # %j expands to jobid
#SBATCH --error=job-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1               # request 1 GPU
# any module loads or env setup
module load python
# run your program; prefer srun for parallel/mpi-aware launch
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- #SBATCH directives are parsed by sbatch; you can also pass these options on sbatch command line (e.g., sbatch --time=01:00:00 job.sh).
- Use meaningful --job-name and set --output/--error so logs are captured.

3) Interactive allocation and running
- Request an interactive allocation:
  salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00 --cpus-per-task=4
- Inside the allocation, start an interactive shell or processes:
  srun --pty bash   (starts a shell on allocated nodes)
  srun -n4 ./mpi_program   (runs 4 MPI tasks)

4) Job arrays (parameter sweeps)
- Use --array to submit many similar tasks with one job:
#SBATCH --array=1-100%20    # run indices 1..100, max 20 concurrently
Access index with $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script:
python run_case.py --case $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

5) Job dependencies
- Submit job B after job A succeeds:
  jid=$(sbatch jobA.sh | awk '{print $4}')    # capture job id from sbatch output
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:$jid jobB.sh
- Common dependency types: afterok, afterany, aftercorr, after, singleton, expand.

6) Common resource request options
- --nodes=N            number of nodes
- --ntasks=T           total tasks (MPI ranks)
- --cpus-per-task=C    CPUs/threads per task (for multithreaded tasks)
- --mem=16G or --mem-per-cpu=4G
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --partition=name
- --qos=name
- --account=name
- --gres=gpu:1         GPUs (or gpu:V100:2 to request type)
- --job-name, --output, --error, --mail-type, --mail-user

7) Checking and debugging jobs
- squeue -u $USER shows your queued and running jobs (REASON column for pending).
- scontrol show job <jobid> gives detailed fields, including dependency and resources.
- sacct -j <jobid> -o JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed shows historical outcome.
- sstat -j <jobid> can show runtime resource usage for running jobs (cpu%, rss).
- If a job is pending, first check squeue’s REASON. For detailed reasons, scontrol show job <id> may show required resources or node constraints.
- Common pending reasons: Resources, ReqNodeNotAvail, Priority, QOSDenied, Dependency.

8) Good practices / tips
- Test at small scale first (short time, 1 CPU) before large runs.
- Request realistic CPU/GPU/memory — over-requesting wastes queue slots and increases wait time.
- Always capture stdout/stderr with --output/--error (use %j for job id).
- Use modules or environment setup in the script (module load ...).
- Prefer srun for launching parallel tasks inside Slurm jobs (it sets up ranks and allocates tasks).

- Use job arrays for embarrassingly parallel parameter sweeps (easier than many sbatch calls).

- sacct for historical usage (states, exit codes, elapsed, consumed resources).
- sreport for aggregate usage reports (CPU/GPU-hours by user/account/partition).
- scontrol_license to inspect tracked licenses.

10) Where to learn more
- Official Slurm docs: https://slurm.schedmd.com/ (sbatch, srun, salloc pages are very helpful).
- Your cluster’s user guide — it often contains site-specific partitions, nodes, and best practices.

If you want, I can:

- Walk through interpreting a pending job (if you give me a job ID; I’ll run squeue and explain).

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a “good” Slurm batch script is clear, reproducible, requests just the resources you actually need, and launches your job in a way the scheduler expects (usually via srun). Below are concise guidelines, a compact template, several common examples, and a checklist to help you write robust, portable scripts.

Short guidelines
- Put scheduler directives in #SBATCH header lines (or pass equivalent flags to sbatch).
- Request accurate resources: nodes, ntasks, cpus-per-task, mem, time, gres (gpus), QOS/account/account.
- Use srun to launch work (preferred over plain mpirun unless your MPI vendor requires mpirun).
- Set environment (modules/conda/singularity) explicitly so the run is reproducible.
- Redirect stdout/stderr to job-specific files (use %j / %x for jobid/jobname).
- Use set -e and traps for safer failure handling and to enable cleanup.
- For arrays use --array and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID; throttle massive arrays with %limit.
- Keep the walltime conservative but not excessive — underestimating causes kill; overestimating wastes queue time.

Minimal template (fill values)
# SBATCH lines:
#SBATCH --job-name=job-name
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out       # %x=jobname %j=jobid
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu               # or cpu/short/long etc.
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                  # if GPU needed
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

# Shell setup and safety
set -euo pipefail
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST started at $(date)"

# Load modules / activate env
module purge
module load gcc/10 python/3.10 cuda/12.1
source /path/to/conda.sh && conda activate myenv

# Export threading settings when using OpenMP or BLAS
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=${OMP_NUM_THREADS}

# Run the workload with srun
srun --mpi=pmix_v3 my_program --arg value

# Optional cleanup
echo "Job finished at $(date)"

Example 1 — single-node multi-threaded job
#SBATCH --job-name=py-train
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00

set -e
module load python/3.10
source activate myenv
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
srun python train.py --batch 128

Example 2 — MPI multi-node job (use srun)
#SBATCH --job-name=mpi-job
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=8
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00

module load mpi/openmpi
srun --mpi=pmix_v3 ./my_mpi_executable -arg

Notes: ntasks = total ranks. ntasks-per-node × nodes = total ntasks. Use cpus-per-task for per-rank threads.

Example 3 — GPU training (single node, 4 GPUs)
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-train
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:4
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00

module load cuda/12.1 cudnn
source activate pytorch
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
srun python train_gpu.py --gpus 4

Example 4 — job array (parameter sweep)
#SBATCH --job-name=array
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G

param_file=params.txt
PARAM=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" $param_file)
srun python run_param.py --param "$PARAM"

Best-practice checklist
- Request actual resources: measure small runs first, then scale your requests.
- Prefer srun for execution; it integrates with the job allocation.
- Use #SBATCH --output and --error with %j/%x for unique logs.
- Set environment variables controlling thread counts (OMP_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS).
- Use --cpus-per-task for threaded codes and --ntasks for MPI ranks.
- For GPUs, request --gres=gpu:N and ensure your framework sees the GPUs (check CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES).
- Use --time realistically (underestimate => kill; too long => long queue wait).
- Use modules or container images for reproducibility (Singularity/Apptainer).
- Add --mem or --mem-per-cpu to avoid node OOM kills. Be explicit — default may be low.
- Add small checkpoints/logging so you can resume or diagnose failures.
- For long workflows, consider --dependency options to chain jobs or --array with % limit.

Robustness and failure handling
- set -euo pipefail to stop on errors.
- trap '... cleanup ...' EXIT to copy logs or free temporary storage.
- Consider --requeue if you want the scheduler to requeue on preemption (cluster must allow).
- For very long work, use application-level checkpointing.

Debugging tips
- Test interactively first: salloc --nodes=1 --time=00:30:00 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1
- Use small test scripts and sbatch --test-only to check directive parsing (sbatch --test-only script.sh).
- Inspect queue with squeue -j <jobid> or squeue -u $USER.

results.agent_response:
Here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial covering the common workflows, commands, examples, and quick diagnostics you’ll use day-to-day.

Basic concepts
- Controller (slurmctld) schedules jobs; compute nodes run them.
- Jobs are either batch (sbatch), interactive (salloc + srun), or run tasks inside allocations (srun).
- Key resources: partition (queue), nodes, CPUs, memory, GPUs (gres), time limit, accounts/QOS.
- Job metadata/env: SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, SLURM_NODELIST, etc.

Common commands
- sbatch script.sh — submit a batch job.
- srun [opts] --pty bash — run a job step or start interactive shell inside an allocation.
- salloc [opts] — allocate resources for interactive use (then use srun inside).
- squeue — show active queue (RUNNING, PENDING), use -u user, -p partition, -j jobid filters.
- sinfo — show partition/node availability and states.
- scancel JOBID — cancel a job (or scancel --user=username).
- sacct — query historical/completed job accounting.
- scontrol show job JOBID — detailed job info; scontrol show config for controller settings.
- sstat JOBID — runtime resource stats for a running job.
- sreport / sshare — accounting and fairshare reports.
- scontrol_reservation_show / squeue --reservation=name — reservation info.

Minimal batch script example
(put in script.sh)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err

module load python
srun python myscript.py

Submit:
$ sbatch script.sh
Capture job id:
$ jid=$(sbatch --parsable script.sh)

GPU example
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00

Interactive GPU session
$ salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00:00
then inside allocation:
$ srun --pty bash

Job arrays (many similar tasks)
#SBATCH --array=1-100%20
Use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside your script to index work. %20 limits concurrent tasks to 20.

Dependencies
- Run job B after job A succeeds:
$ sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 jobB.sh

Checking queue & details
- Show your jobs:
$ squeue -u $USER
- Show one job (brief):
$ squeue -j 12345 -o "%.18i %.9P %.30j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R"
- If more detail needed:
$ scontrol show job 12345
- If squeue doesn’t show a finished job, query history:
$ sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed

Diagnosing pending jobs
1) squeue -l or include REASON column to see why it’s pending.
2) For a detailed reason: scontrol show job JOBID
3) Common reasons: Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOSLimit, Dependency.

Resource/partition status
$ sinfo
Shows partitions and NODES(A/I/D) counts. Use sinfo -o or sinfo -l for more detail.

Runtime stats for running jobs
$ sstat -j JOBID
(useful for CPU%, memory, I/O while job runs)

Cancel and hold
- Cancel a job: scancel 12345
- Hold a job: scontrol hold 12345
- Release: scontrol release 12345

Accounting and history
- sacct --user=username --starttime=YYYY-MM-DD — historical jobs with ExitCode, time, memory.
- sreport — GPU/CPU-hour usage reports by account/user/partition.

Best practices
- Test at small scale first (short time, small resources).
- Request realistic time limits; over-requesting wastes queue fairness and may delay start.
- Prefer --mem-per-cpu when memory scales with CPU; use --mem for whole-node requests.
- Use job arrays for many similar independent tasks to avoid many small sbatch submissions.
- Collect stdout/stderr to files with --output/--error (include %j jobid).
- Use modules or container runtimes (Singularity/Apptainer) to fix environments.
- Check sinfo before submitting to pick appropriate partition and verify idle nodes.
- Use --parsable to get machine-readable job id for scripting.
- Add checkpointing or periodic saves for long jobs.
- Respect QOS/account and account association (--account=...). If preemption is possible, use --no-requeue or checkpoint.

Examples of useful flags
- --partition, -p
- --time, -t (format D-HH:MM:SS or minutes)
- --nodes, -N
- --ntasks, -n
- --cpus-per-task, -c
- --mem (or --mem-per-cpu)
- --gres=gpu:1
- --job-name, -J
- --output, -o and --error, -e
- --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@domain
- --dependency=afterok:ID,afterany:ID
- --array=1-100%10
- --account=acctname
- --qos=name

Quick troubleshooting checklist
- Job pending long? Check squeue REASON → scontrol show job for details.
- Job failed quickly? Inspect slurm-%j.err and stdout, and sacct for ExitCode.
- Job not found in squeue? Use sacct to find past jobs.
- Nodes down/drained? sinfo and sinfo -R (reasons) show node problems.
- Low priority? Use sprio to view priority factors and sshare to see fairshare.

Where to read more
- slurm.schedmd.com documentation (sbatch, srun, salloc, squeue, sinfo, sacct pages).
- Local cluster user guide / policies (accounts, partitions, QOS, storage quotas).

If you want, I can:
- Create a starter sbatch script tailored to your code (tell me #CPUs, memory, GPUs, partition, time).
- Walk through interpreting a specific squeue or scontrol show job output if you paste it.
- Show how to set up job arrays or dependency chains for a workflow.

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, safe sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It includes defensive shell settings, explicit resource directives, robust logging, signal/exit handling, and common best-practices (temporary work dir, environment loading, array support, and using srun for task launch).

Example safe sbatch template
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob                 # job name
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out          # %x = job-name, %j = jobid
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                  # partition/queue
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                     # request GPUs (if needed)
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --chdir=$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR        # ensure running from submit dir
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL             # optional notifications
#SBATCH --array=0-9%5                    # optional array (throttle with %)

# ---- strict shell / logging / temp dir ----
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

# immediate timestamped logging
echo "[$(date --iso-8601=seconds)] Starting job $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME)"
echo "Nodes: $SLURM_NODELIST  Tasks: $SLURM_NTASKS  CPUs/task: $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"

TMPDIR=${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/${USER}/${SLURM_JOB_ID}
mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"
export TMPDIR

# ---- cleanup + signal handling ----
cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "[$(date --iso-8601=seconds)] Cleaning up, exit code=$rc"
  # example: kill background children if any
  pkill -P $$ || true
  # remove ephemeral files if you created them
  # rm -rf "$TMPDIR"
}
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

# ---- environment setup ----
module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/12.0    # adapt to your site modules
# or: source /path/to/venv/bin/activate

# optionally for array jobs
TASK_ID=${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID:-0}
echo "Array task id: $TASK_ID"

# ---- run your workload under srun ----
# use srun for MPI/parallel correctness, preserves Slurm accounting
srun --cpu-bind=cores my_program --input inputs/idx_${TASK_ID}.json

echo "[$(date --iso-8601=seconds)] Job $SLURM_JOB_ID finished"

Key points and rationale (short)
- SBATCH directives: declare time/memory/cpus/gres/partition up front so scheduler can place the job correctly. Use --chdir or cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR to avoid surprises.
- Strict shell flags (set -euo pipefail): fail fast on errors and undefined vars. IFS helps avoid word-splitting bugs.
- Trap + cleanup: ensures background children and temp files are handled when the job is terminated or on exit.
- Logging: write timestamps, job ID, node list, and SLURM env vars to output to make postmortem debugging easier.
- Use srun to launch tasks (MPI/parallel) rather than plain mpirun where possible — srun is Slurm-aware.
- Temporary files: use per-job TMPDIR to avoid collisions and ensure cleanup.
- Arrays: use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to index work safely.
- Resource requests: be explicit (cpus-per-task, mem, gres). Don’t assume defaults.

Optional extras
- Redirect combined stdout/stderr to a single file with exec > >(tee -a "$LOG") 2>&1 if you want live/local copy plus persistent log.
- Checkpointing hooks (trap and save state) for long-running jobs.
- Validate inputs early and fail with clear messages rather than letting long runs continue.

- the language/tool you run (Python, MPI, Singularity), and whether you need GPUs or arrays — I’ll produce a tailored script ready for sbatch.

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a “good” Slurm batch script is clear about resource requests, reproducible, robust to failures/signals, and easy to test/debug. Below are concise guidelines, an annotated example template you can adapt, and a short checklist of best practices.

High-level rules
- Request only the resources you actually need: partition, nodes, ntasks, cpus-per-task, gres (GPUs), time, memory. Over-requesting wastes cluster capacity; under-requesting causes failures.
- Make intent explicit with #SBATCH headers (or equivalent sbatch cmdline flags). Prefer in-script directives so the job is self-contained.
- Set up a reproducible runtime environment (modules, conda/env activation, container) and record versions (git commit, pip freeze).
- Use srun for parallel/accelerated work when possible (srun knows Slurm’s allocation and topology). Use mpirun only if your MPI implementation requires it — prefer srun for MPI on modern clusters.
- Add simple failure handling and debugging aids (set -euo pipefail, traps to handle TERM signals).
- Test locally / with a tiny allocation before large runs. Use job arrays for parameter sweeps.

Annotated example template
(Adapt fields like partition, time, gres, mem, nodes for your cluster.)

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my_analysis             # job name
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out                 # %x = job name, %j = job id
#SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err                  # separate stderr file (optional)
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                    # partition/queue
#SBATCH --nodes=1                          # number of nodes
#SBATCH --ntasks=1                         # number of MPI ranks/tasks
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8                  # threads per task (OpenMP / threads)
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                       # GPUs per node (use cluster convention)
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00                    # walltime (HH:MM:SS)
#SBATCH --mem=32G                          # memory (or use --mem-per-cpu)
#SBATCH --mail-type=FAIL,END               # optional notifications
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

# Fail fast and make debugging easier
set -euo pipefail
trap 'echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID received SIGTERM or ended"; exit 1' TERM

# Optional: log some Slurm environment variables for debugging
echo "Job: $SLURM_JOB_ID, Name: $SLURM_JOB_NAME"
echo "Nodes: $SLURM_NODELIST, NTASKS: $SLURM_NTASKS, CPUS_PER_TASK: $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"

# Switch to working directory (or use --workdir)
cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR

# Load modules or activate environments
module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/11.8
source /path/to/venv/bin/activate

# Export thread controls for hybrid codes
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=$OMP_NUM_THREADS

# Use SLURM_TMPDIR for temporary scratch if available
mkdir -p $SLURM_TMPDIR/myjob && cd $SLURM_TMPDIR/myjob

# Run the work — prefer srun
srun --mpi=pmix bash -c 'python train.py --config configs/foo.yaml'

# Optional: copy outputs back to $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR
cp -r $SLURM_TMPDIR/myjob/* $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR/

Key explanations and tips
- Job naming and outputs: use --output with %x/%j so logs are easy to find and unique. Consider --open-mode=append if you rerun.
- Time limits: request slightly more than expected runtime. If you don’t know, run a short debug job and profile. Large overestimates can hurt scheduling fairness.
- CPUs vs tasks:
  - Pure MPI: set --ntasks=N and --cpus-per-task=1 (or >1 for multi-threaded MPI).
  - Threaded/OpenMP: set --ntasks=1 and --cpus-per-task=threads.
  - Hybrid: set both accordingly (ntasks = MPI ranks per node * nodes).
- GPUs: use the cluster’s convention (usually --gres=gpu:COUNT). Avoid assuming driver visibility; use nvidia-smi to check.
- Memory: prefer --mem-per-cpu when memory scales with threads, or --mem for whole-job memory.
- Containers: use Singularity/Apptainer for reproducibility. For GPU containers use the runtime flag (e.g., singularity exec --nv).
- Job arrays: use #SBATCH --array=1-100 to sweep many parameter sets. Inside the script, use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to index parameters/files.
- Dependencies: chain jobs with --dependency=afterok:<jobid> for workflows.
- Resource accounting: request QoS/account if your cluster requires it.
- Testing/debugging: use small resources and small datasets first. For interactive debugging, use salloc/srun --pty or the cluster’s interactive partition.
- Cleanup and exit codes: ensure non-zero exit codes are propagated. Use set -e and check return codes when using conditional sequences.
- Signal handling: trap TERM to checkpoint or clean temporary files when possible. Slurm sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL.

Useful commands to monitor and diagnose jobs
- squeue -j $JOBID or squeue -u $USER to view active jobs and reasons.
- sacct -j $JOBID --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS,TotalCPU to see final usage.
- scontrol show job $JOBID for detailed job config and reason for pending state.
- sinfo to inspect partitions and node states.

Small checklist before submitting
- [ ] Does the #SBATCH header accurately reflect resources?
- [ ] Are modules/containers pinned to versions or a recorded environment snapshot included?
- [ ] Is output/error redirected to sensible files (with jobid)?
- [ ] Are thread/MPI env vars set (OMP_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS)?
- [ ] Is there a small test submission that runs and produces expected results?
- [ ] Are temporary files placed on $SLURM_TMPDIR and cleaned/copied back?

If you want, I can:
- Provide a more specific template tuned to MPI, GPU deep learning, or a Python data pipeline.
- Review a draft of your script and suggest improvements (paste it here).

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial you can use to get started, submit jobs, and debug common problems. I’ll cover core concepts, common commands, example job scripts (batch and interactive), job arrays & dependencies, resource/GPU guidance, and quick troubleshooting tips.

Core concepts
- slurmctld: the controller (scheduler) that accepts and runs jobs.
- Node / partition: nodes are compute machines; partitions are named queues (groups of nodes) you submit to.
- Job: a unit of work you submit (sbatch) or run interactively (srun/salloc).
- TRES/gres: trackable resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs). GPUs are requested via gres (e.g., --gres=gpu:1).
- QOS, accounts, fairshare: policies that control priority and limits.
- Job states: PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.

Quick commands (most useful)
- sbatch <script.sh> — submit a batch job.
- srun ... — run a command inside an allocation (interactive or inside job).
- salloc ... — allocate resources interactively (gives a shell).
- squeue [-u user] [-p partition] — view queued/running jobs.
- sinfo — view partitions and node states.
- sacct — query finished job accounting/history.
- scontrol show job <id> — show detailed job info.
- scancel <jobid> — cancel a job.
- sstat -j <jobid> — (running jobs) live stats (CPU, memory).
- scontrol show node <nodename> — node details.

Simple sbatch script (example)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
# If you need GPUs:
# #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1

module load python/3.10
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- %j expands to the job ID in output filenames.
- Use module load (or your site’s environment management) to set environment.
- Put srun before the main command in scripts to ensure correct allocation/smp behavior.

Interactive / debug sessions
- Quick interactive shell on a partition:
  srun --partition=debug --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=2 --time=00:30:00 --pty bash
- Or request an allocation and then run commands:
  salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=8 --time=01:00:00
  Then run srun or the commands you need in the allocation shell.

Job arrays
- For many similar tasks (e.g., parameter sweeps):
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
# inside script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
- %10 limits concurrent tasks to 10.

Job dependencies
- Submit job B after A completes successfully:
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobidA> jobB.sh
- other options: afterany, aftercorr, singleton, etc.

Checking job status & reasons
- squeue -j <jobid> or squeue -u $USER shows pending reasons (if reported).
- If squeue doesn’t show a reason or you need more detail: scontrol show job <jobid>.
- Common pending reasons: Resources, Priority, PartitionTimeLimit, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOSMaxJobsPerUser.

GPU-specific tips
- Request GPUs explicitly: --gres=gpu:1 (or gpu:tesla:2 if your cluster uses types).
- Use sinfo to find GPU partitions: sinfo -o "%P %G %D %C" or ask your admin for partition names.
- When checking availability for conditional submissions, only count nodes listed as idle for GPU allocation (allocated/mixed/down/drained are not available).
- Inside job, GPU devices are typically visible via nvidia-smi; environment variables like CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES may be set.

Accounting & historical data
- sacct -j <jobid> or sacct -u <user> to view completed jobs (exit codes, elapsed, resource usage).
- sreport and sshare for usage/fairshare summaries (admin-level).

Common troubleshooting checklist
- Job stuck PENDING:
  - Run squeue to see the reason. If not present, scontrol show job <id>.
  - Check partition limits, QOS, account charges/limits.
  - Check node states with sinfo; if nodes are drained/down they reduce capacity.
- Job fails quickly with non-zero exit:
  - Inspect job-%j.err and job-%j.out.
  - Verify modules, paths, environment variables in the batch script.
  - Use small test jobs with shorter time and less memory to reproduce.
- Job out-of-memory:
  - Increase --mem or request more CPUs-per-task if memory is per-core.
  - Use ulimit or check container limits if running inside one.
- Node-specific hardware failures:
  - scontrol show node <name> and sinfo -R to see reasons/drain messages.
- No GPU seen inside job:
  - Confirm --gres is requested in sbatch/srun.
  - Check nvidia-smi; confirm module/drivers loaded.

Best practices
- Start small: request minimal resources and short walltime for testing.
- Make output and error files explicit so logs are preserved.
- Use job arrays for parameter sweeps rather than many individual sbatch calls.
- Use dependencies to serialize multi-stage workflows.
- Keep reproducible environment: modules, container images (Singularity/Apptainer).
- Ask your cluster admins for site-specific queues, limits, and recommended partitions.

Useful environment variables inside jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NAME, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
- SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE, SLURM_NODELIST

Where to learn more
- Your cluster’s user guide / FAQ (site-specific policies and partitions).
- Official Slurm docs (scheduling, sbatch, srun, scontrol): see slurm.schedmd.com
- For command syntax and reason codes: use lookup_slurm_docs or man pages (man sbatch, man squeue).

If you’d like, I can:
- Create a job script tailored to your application (give partition, CPUs, memory, GPUs, time).
- Walk through diagnosing a specific stuck or failed job (give job ID).
- Show example sbatch + sbatch dependency + array combined script.

Which of the above would you like next?

results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, safe sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It shows defensive shell settings, clean setup/teardown, recommended SBATCH directives, sensible environment handling (threading, modules, venv), and how to launch your workload with srun. Comments explain why each block is useful.

Example safe sbatch script pattern
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=example_job             # short name
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out                 # %x=name, %j=jobid
#SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                    # change to your partition
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                       # request GPUs if needed
#SBATCH --account=your_account             # optional
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL               # optional notifications
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

# ----------------- defensive shell setup -----------------
set -euo pipefail        # fail fast on errors / undefined variables / pipeline failures
IFS=$'\n\t'              # safer word-splitting

# Helpful env shorthands provided by Slurm:
# $SLURM_JOB_ID, $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, $SLURM_NTASKS, $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR, ...
echo "Starting job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $(hostname) at $(date)"
echo "Nodes: $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST  Tasks: $SLURM_NTASKS  CPUs/task: $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"

# ----------------- temporary workspace & cleanup -----------------
TMPDIR=${TMPDIR:-/scratch/${USER}/${SLURM_JOB_ID}}
mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"
chmod 700 "$TMPDIR"

cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "Cleanup: return code $rc"
  # copy back artifacts if running on remote scratch (safe example)
  # rsync -av "$TMPDIR"/results/ "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"/results/ || true
  rm -rf "$TMPDIR"
}
trap cleanup EXIT

# ----------------- environment / modules / venv -----------------
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"    # run where user submitted
module purge
module load python/3.10   # example; use your site's modules

# Set threaded-library affinities to match allocated CPUs
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}
export NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}

# Activate virtualenv / conda if needed
# source /path/to/venv/bin/activate

# ----------------- optional GPU check -----------------
if command -v nvidia-smi &>/dev/null; then
  echo "GPUs visible on node:"
  nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,memory.total --format=csv,noheader
fi

# ----------------- run your job (use srun for Slurm-managed launch) -----------------
# - Prefer srun for launching parallel work so Slurm can track processes.
# - Use --cpu-bind or --distribution if needed for affinity.
srun --cpu-bind=cores my_program --arg1 val1

# For MPI-style jobs, use: srun --mpi=pmix ./a.out
# For single-process jobs that internally multi-thread, just run the command (srun is still fine).

# ----------------- finish -----------------
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID finished at $(date)"

Best-practice notes (short)
- Put all SBATCH directives at the top (before any non-comment line); sbatch stops parsing after the first non-comment.
- Use set -euo pipefail and trap cleanup to avoid leaving junk and to capture failures.
- Prefer srun (not mpirun) unless you have a special MPI runtime requirement; srun integrates with Slurm for accounting and node-local launch.
- Set OMP_NUM_THREADS / MKL_NUM_THREADS to SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK to avoid oversubscription.
- Don’t hard-code absolute paths to cluster-specific commands; use module system or documented environment modules.
- Be cautious with credentials and environment variables (don’t write secrets to shared TMPDIR).
- For array jobs include #SBATCH --array=1-100%10 and use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to isolate per-task work directories.
- For GPU conditional logic: if you need to submit only when idle GPUs exist, query sinfo first (operator-side requirement for conditional submits).

If you want, I can produce:
- a version tailored for multi-node MPI (showing srun --mpi and NMPI layout),
- a GPU-training template that includes torch/cuda checks and checkpoint safe-save/restore,
- or an array-job template that safely creates per-task tempdirs and collects results. Which one would you like?

Here’s a concise, practical guide to the basic Slurm batch-submission workflow and the most-used options.

1) Prepare a batch script
- Create a shell script (e.g., myjob.sh) starting with a shebang (#!/bin/bash).
- Add SBATCH directives (lines beginning with #SBATCH) to request resources and set job metadata. Common directives:
  - --job-name=NAME
  - --partition=PARTITION
  - --nodes=N
  - --ntasks=NTASKS
  - --cpus-per-task=CPUS
  - --mem=16G (or --mem-per-cpu=4G)
  - --time=HH:MM:SS
  - --output=slurm-%j.out / --error=err-%j.out
  - --account=ACCOUNT, --qos=QOS
  - --gres=gpu:1  (or cluster may support --gpus=)
  - --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@site.edu
- After the SBATCH lines, put the commands to run (module loads, srun, mpirun, python, etc.). Use srun for launching MPI/parallel tasks where possible.

Example minimal script:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=hello
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out

module load python
srun python train.py

2) Submit the job
- sbatch myjob.sh
- sbatch prints the assigned job ID and exits; the job may remain pending until resources free up.
- Command-line options override scripts: sbatch --time=02:00:00 myjob.sh

3) Monitor the job
- squeue -u $USER (shows PENDING / RUNNING jobs)
- squeue -j <jobid> or scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed info (allocations, reason for pending)
- sstat -j <jobid> for live stats of running jobs (if supported)
- sacct -j <jobid> for accounting info after completion

4) Common job operations
- Cancel: scancel <jobid>
- Hold / release / requeue: scontrol hold/release/requeue <jobid> (admin actions)
- Job arrays: #SBATCH --array=1-100 and access index via $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> myjob.sh

5) Interactive testing and debugging
- salloc --partition=short --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=00:30:00   (gives an interactive allocation)
- sbatch small test scripts before scaling to many nodes
- Use small time limits and check slurm-<jobid>.out to iterate quickly

6) Useful tips / gotchas
- Always request a realistic time limit; short limits help scheduling and faster turnaround.
- Time format is HH:MM:SS (some clusters accept days).
- Output file defaults to slurm-<jobid>.out unless overridden.
- Prefer srun to launch tasks inside batch scripts (it integrates with Slurm’s job step management).
- GPU and other resource flags can be cluster-dependent (gres or --gpus). Check local cluster docs.
- If a job is pending, check the REASON column in squeue; scontrol show job <id> gives more detail.
- Use sacct for historical accounting (finished jobs), squeue for current queue.

- Provide a tailored example script for your application (MPI, GPU PyTorch, multi-task), or
- Show common sbatch examples for arrays, dependencies, or GPU requests. Which would you like?

Below is a concise, safe sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It includes defensive shell settings, common SBATCH directives, signal trapping/cleanup, environment capture, and recommended runtime practices (use srun for commands, stage I/O to fast local scratch, etc.). Put ALL #SBATCH lines before the first non-comment line in the script.

Example safe sbatch script pattern (edit values to your site/needs):

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob                 # short name
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out            # %j = jobid
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                  # partition name
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                     # request 1 GPU (if needed)
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00                  # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL              # optional
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com       # optional
#SBATCH --export=ALL                      # or NONE and explicitly set env

# ---- defensive shell options ----
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

# ---- useful env / bookkeeping ----
echo "Job: ${SLURM_JOB_ID} on ${SLURM_JOB_NODELIST}"
echo "Started at: $(date)"
echo "Command line: $0 $*"

# ---- setup local scratch and cleanup ----
SCRATCH_DIR="${TMPDIR:-/scratch}/${USER}/job_${SLURM_JOB_ID}"
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH_DIR"
echo "Using scratch: $SCRATCH_DIR"

cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "Cleaning up. Exit code=$rc"
  # Example: copy results back, remove large temp files
  # rsync -av --remove-source-files "$SCRATCH_DIR"/ /home/${USER}/results/job_${SLURM_JOB_ID}/
  rm -rf "$SCRATCH_DIR"
  echo "Cleanup done at: $(date)"
}
trap 'cleanup' EXIT INT TERM

# ---- load modules / conda / env ----
module purge
module load cuda/12.1   # example; use your site modules
# source /path/to/conda.sh
# conda activate myenv

# ---- resource-affinity hints (optional) ----
# export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-8}
# export MKL_NUM_THREADS=${OMP_NUM_THREADS}

# ---- run work using srun (not plain mpirun unless site requires) ----
# srun will respect the allocation and integrate with Slurm accounting
srun --cpu_bind=cores my_program --input data.in --output "$SCRATCH_DIR"/out.bin

# ---- final status ----
echo "Finished at: $(date)"

Short notes / best practices
- Always keep #SBATCH directives at top (before any non-comment). Slurm stops reading #SBATCH after first non-comment line.
- Use set -euo pipefail and a trap handler to ensure cleanup runs on failure/kill.
- Use srun for commands inside the job so Slurm applies the allocation and task pinning.
- Stage large I/O to node-local fast scratch ($TMPDIR or /tmp) and copy back on exit; avoid NFS hot-spotting.
- Set OMP_NUM_THREADS / MKL_NUM_THREADS to match cpus-per-task to avoid oversubscription.
- Use --output/--error with %j for traceable logs; consider --open-mode=append if reruns should append.
- Prefer --export=NONE and explicitly pass only needed env vars to avoid leaking secrets.
- For GPU work, request gres and ensure CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is handled by your site or set via srun.
- Keep runtime limits slightly higher than expected to avoid premature timeout; monitor and tune.

results.prompt: Explain basic Slurm submission steps
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise, practical overview of the basic Slurm batch-submission workflow and the common options you’ll use.

1) Create a batch script
- Start with a shell shebang: #!/bin/bash
- Put all Slurm options as #SBATCH directives at the top (before the first non-comment line) or pass them on the sbatch command line.
- Typical directives to include:
  - Partition: #SBATCH -p gpu
  - Job name: #SBATCH -J myjob
  - Time limit: #SBATCH -t 02:00:00  (HH:MM:SS)
  - Nodes/tasks/CPUs:
    - #SBATCH -N 1            (nodes)
    - #SBATCH --ntasks=1     (tasks, MPI ranks)
    - #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
  - Memory: #SBATCH --mem=16G  or per-cpu #SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=4G
  - GPUs: #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1  (or #SBATCH --gpus=1 on newer Slurm)
  - Output files: #SBATCH -o myjob.%j.out  #SBATCH -e myjob.%j.err
  - Account/QOS: #SBATCH -A myacct  #SBATCH --qos=high
  - Job arrays: #SBATCH --array=1-10%2
  - Dependencies (when submitting): sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 script.sh
- After directives, load modules, set up env, copy data if necessary, then launch your app (prefer srun for process launch under Slurm).
Example minimal script:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J myjob
#SBATCH -p gpu
#SBATCH -N 1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH -t 02:00:00
#SBATCH -o myjob.%j.out

module load python/3.10
srun python train.py --epochs 10

2) Submit the job
- Submit: sbatch myscript.sh
- sbatch will print: Submitted batch job <JOBID>

3) Monitor job state
- squeue -u $USER (shows RUNNING/PENDING etc.)
- squeue -j <JOBID> or scontrol show job <JOBID> (detailed)
- sstat -j <jobid> (live resource usage for running jobs)
- sacct -j <JOBID> (after completion for accounting/exit codes)

4) Inspect reasons for pending jobs
- squeue shows a PENDING reason column; for a specific job you can also run scontrol show job <JOBID> to see detailed pending reason.

5) Cancel / modify
- Cancel: scancel <JOBID>
- Some job attributes (like time limit or account) can be changed by admins with scontrol update; normal users can’t arbitrarily change most attributes after submission.

6) Job arrays & environment variables
- Use #SBATCH --array=1-100 and inside the script reference $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
- Useful env vars: $SLURM_JOB_ID, $SLURM_NTASKS, $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

7) Debugging & good practices
- Test interactively on a small interactive allocation (salloc or srun --pty) or run a very short job first.
- Request realistic time and memory; under-requesting causes OOM/timeouts, over-requesting increases wait time and wastes quota.
- Capture stdout/stderr to files with jobid substitution (%j) for debugging.
- Use srun to launch MPI or parallel tasks so Slurm manages placement.
- For reproducibility, record module list and environment in the output.
- Stage large data to node-local or parallel filesystem before running if I/O is heavy; clean up temporary files.
- Use job arrays to run many similar tasks efficiently (and throttle with %N).

8) Useful commands quick cheat-sheet
- Submit: sbatch script.sh
- Show queue: squeue -u $USER
- Show job: scontrol show job <JOBID>
- Live stats: sstat -j <JOBID>
- Accounting/historical: sacct -j <JOBID>
- Cancel: scancel <JOBID>

If you want, I can:
- Show an example script tailored to your application (MPI / GPU / multi-threaded).
- Explain differences between ntasks, cpus-per-task, and tasks-per-node.
- Walk through creating and submitting a job array or a GPU-conditional submit. Which would you like?
