results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference — concepts, common commands, job script examples, troubleshooting tips, and best practices.

1) What Slurm is (brief)
- Slurm is a workload manager/scheduler for clusters. It allocates resources (nodes/CPUs/GPUs/memory), runs jobs, and enforces limits (time, QOS, partitions, accounts).

2) Key concepts & terminology
- Job: a batch or interactive workload submitted to Slurm.
- Node: a compute server.
- Partition: a named set of nodes (like a queue).
- QOS / account: policies and limits for users/groups.
- Allocation types: batch (sbatch), interactive allocation (salloc), and immediate runs (srun).
- Job array: many similar jobs managed as a single submission.
- Scheduler states: PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, NODE_FAIL, etc.

3) Common read-only commands (view cluster state)
- sinfo — view partition/node status (allocated/idle/down counts).
- squeue — view queued/running jobs (jobid, user, state, time, nodes).
- sacct — historical accounting (completed/failed jobs).
- scontrol show job <jobid> — detailed job info.
- scontrol show node <nodename> — detailed node info.
- sdiag / sprio / sshare — scheduler diagnostics, priority/fairshare.

4) Common mutating commands (submit/control jobs)
- sbatch <script.sh> — submit a batch script.
- srun [options] <command> — run a command in an allocation (or submit an interactive job if used inside salloc).
- salloc — get an interactive allocation, then use srun inside it.
- scancel <jobid> — cancel a job.
- scontrol hold/release/requeue — control job state (admins).

5) Typical sbatch header example
Use directives at top of script (they map to sbatch options):

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out        # %j = jobid
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00              # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                 # request 1 GPU
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10             # job array, max 10 concurrent

# load modules, run
module load python/3.10
srun python train.py --config cfg${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}.yaml

6) Important sbatch/srun options (common)
- --partition=NAME
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --nodes=N and --ntasks / --ntasks-per-node
- --cpus-per-task (for multi-threaded tasks)
- --mem or --mem-per-cpu
- --gres=gpu:N (request GPUs)
- --job-name, --output, --error
- --array=IDX or START-END%MAXCONC (job arrays)
- --dependency=afterok:<jobid> (chain jobs)

7) Job arrays
- Submit once with --array=1-100; inside script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID.
- Useful for parameter sweeps; reduces scheduler overhead.

8) Dependencies
- --dependency=afterok:12345 (run only if job 12345 succeeds)
- Other types: afterany, aftercorr, after, singleton

9) Interactive work
- salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
- srun --pty bash  (or srun --x11 for GUI, or use srun to launch commands inside allocation)

10) Checking why a job is pending or stuck
- squeue -j <jobid> (see PENDING reason column)
- If squeue lacks detail, use scontrol show job <jobid> for full pending reason and constraints
- Common PENDING reasons: Resources, Priority, Dependency, Partition/QOS limits, ReqNodeNotAvail

11) Inspecting completed/failed jobs
- sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,ElapsedRaw
- Check slurm-%j.out and slurm-%j.err for stdout/stderr paths from your job script.

12) Resource accounting & limits
- sshare — view fairshare and usage.
- sacctmgr show user/account — account limits and associations (admin-only).
- QOS can impose max runtime, max jobs, preemption behavior.

13) Node/partition health
- sinfo — quick view of partitions and node counts (allocated/idle/down).
- sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons — list nodes in drain/down with reasons.
- scontrol show node <node> — detailed node condition (e.g., real memory, CPUs, features, reason).

14) Troubleshooting checklist
- For pending jobs: squeue (reason) → scontrol show job (details) → sinfo (are nodes free?) → check QOS/account limits.
- For failed jobs: sacct to see ExitCode → check stdout/stderr and job script for resource insufficiency or module errors.
- For running job issues: sstat <jobid> for live job resource usage (if supported).
- For scheduler problems: sdiag and sprio to inspect backfill and priorities (admin).

15) Best practices
- Do small test runs locally or with tiny resources before large runs.
- Request resources accurately (under-requesting causes failures; over-requesting wastes scheduling capacity).
- Use checkpoints and write intermediate output to persistent storage.
- Use job arrays for many similar runs.
- Use modules or containers (Singularity/Apptainer) for consistent environments.
- Capture stdout/stderr with descriptive file names (include %j).
- Don’t run large interactive workloads on login nodes — use salloc.
- Monitor quotas and fairshare; discuss change requests with admins.

16) Performance & scaling tips
- Use --cpus-per-task for multi-threaded programs (OpenMP).
- Use mpirun or srun for MPI jobs (prefer srun or MPI compiled with Slurm).
- Pack tasks per node intentionally: use --ntasks-per-node and task binding options (--cpu-bind).
- For GPU jobs, match CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES/OMP_NUM_THREADS to requested resources.

17) Where to learn more (official docs)
- Slurm official docs and man pages (man sbatch, srun, squeue, sinfo, sacct, scontrol).
- slurm.schedmd.com — reference and admin guides.
- Your cluster’s user guide / wiki for local policies (partitions, QOS, scratch, reservation rules).

If you want, I can:
- Walk through building a job script for a specific workflow (MPI, GPU, or multi-threaded).
- Explain a specific command or output (e.g., interpret your squeue line).
- Provide a checklist for debugging a particular job ID (if you give the job ID).

results.agent_response:
#!/bin/bash
#
# Safe, minimal sbatch job script pattern — edit the SBATCH values and the run steps below.
#
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob                 # short name
#SBATCH --output=%x.%j.out               # %x=jobname, %j=jobid
#SBATCH --error=%x.%j.err
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00                  # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                  # or cpu partition name
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G                        # or --mem-per-cpu=4G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                     # only if you need GPUs
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL             # optional
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com      # optional
#SBATCH --export=ALL                     # export environment (or list vars)

set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

# ---- Prepare job-local tmpdir and cleanup ----
# Use a unique tmpdir (local fast storage if available)
TMPDIR=${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/${USER}_${SLURM_JOB_ID}
mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"
cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "Job exiting with status $rc at $(date)"
  # copy logs/artifacts back to $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR or $SCRATCH here if needed
  # tar -czf "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR/${SLURM_JOB_NAME}_${SLURM_JOB_ID}.tgz" "$TMPDIR" || true
  rm -rf "$TMPDIR"
}
trap 'cleanup' EXIT
trap 'echo "Received SIGTERM, attempting graceful shutdown"; kill -- -$$' TERM INT

# ---- Diagnostics: useful info for debugging ----
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME) started on $(hostname) at $(date)"
echo "Partition: $SLURM_JOB_PARTITION; Nodes: $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
echo "Working directory: $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
echo "TMPDIR: $TMPDIR"
echo "Environment:"
env | sort

# ---- Environment tuning ----
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-4}   # thread libraries respect this
ulimit -c 0                                        # disable core dumps (optional)

# Load modules / activate envs
module purge
module load cuda/12.0 python/3.10   # example; use your site's modules
source ~/venvs/myenv/bin/activate

# Move to submission directory (good practice)
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"

# ---- Run the actual work with srun (preferred for proper Slurm accounting) ----
# Use srun so Slurm can track tasks and propagate signals correctly.
srun --cpu-bind=cores my_executable --threads "$OMP_NUM_THREADS" \
     --input data/input.dat --output results/out.${SLURM_JOB_ID}.dat

# Optionally run postprocessing (also via srun if it needs allocation)
# srun python postprocess.py results/out.${SLURM_JOB_ID}.dat

echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID finished at $(date)"

Notes / best practices:
- Put all #SBATCH directives at the top of the file before any executable lines; sbatch stops parsing directives at the first non-comment, non-whitespace line.
- Use set -euo pipefail and traps to ensure cleanup runs and failures are noticed.
- Use a job-local TMPDIR (fast local disk) and remove it in cleanup; copy outputs back to persistent storage before removing.
- Prefer srun to launch processes inside the allocation so Slurm can manage/kill them properly and account for resources.
- Set OMP_NUM_THREADS from SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK and tune thread affinity (e.g., --cpu-bind) for hybrid MPI/OpenMP jobs.
- Use explicit memory (--mem or --mem-per-cpu) and cpus (--cpus-per-task, --ntasks) requests to avoid OOM kills and scheduling surprises.
- Handle SIGTERM in your job so long-running programs can checkpoint or exit cleanly; trap kills process group to avoid stray children.
- Keep modules and virtualenv activation inside the script to ensure reproducible environments.
- For GPU jobs, request --gres=gpu:N and ensure your code targets the allocated devices (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set by Slurm on many systems).
- Log useful job metadata (hostname, node list, env, job id) at start for debugging.

If you want, I can adapt this template for: MPI jobs, multi-node GPU training (distributed), or for a specific cluster's module names and scratch paths. Which type would you like?

A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference: basic commands, typical sbatch examples (CPU, GPU, MPI, arrays), interactive usage, monitoring / debugging tips, and best practices.

Quick command reference
- sinfo — show partitions and node states (allocated/idle/down).
- squeue — show queued and running jobs (use -u $USER to filter).
- sbatch myjob.sh — submit a batch job script (non-interactive).
- srun — run a command inside an allocation or start tasks inside a batch job.
- salloc — request an interactive allocation (then use srun or run shell).
- scancel JOBID — cancel a job.
- scontrol show job JOBID — show detailed job configuration and reason for pending.
- sacct -j JOBID — accounting info for completed jobs.
- sstat -j JOBID — runtime stats for a running job (live resource usage).
- sinfo -R — list nodes in DRAIN/DOWN with reasons.

Minimal sbatch batch script (CPU job)
- Example file: myjob.sh
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=test
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
  #SBATCH --mem=8G
  #SBATCH --time=01:00:00
  #SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
  module load python
  python train.py

- Submit: sbatch myjob.sh
- Output file: slurm-<JOBID>.out

Requesting GPUs
- Single-node GPU example:
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1         # request 1 GPU (driver depends on cluster)
  #SBATCH --mem=32G
  #SBATCH --time=04:00:00

MPI / multi-node parallel job
- Use mpirun / srun inside the batch script:
  #SBATCH --nodes=2
  #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=32
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  module load mpi
  srun my_mpi_program   # srun launches the MPI tasks across allocation

Interactive usage
- Quick interactive allocation:
  salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00:00
  srun --pty bash -i      # get an interactive shell
- Or run a single interactive command:
  srun --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00 python -i

Job arrays (many similar tasks)
- Example (100 tasks, at most 10 concurrently):
  #SBATCH --array=1-100%10
- Inside the script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick input per-task.

Dependencies and chaining jobs
- Submit job B to run after job A completes successfully:
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid_A> jobB.sh

Monitoring and debugging
- squeue -u $USER — show your queued/running jobs
- squeue -j <JOBID> — get state and (usually) pending reason
- If squeue does not show a useful reason, run:
  scontrol show job <JOBID>   — detailed pending reason or required resources
- For running jobs:
  sstat -j <JOBID>   — live CPU/memory usage (if enabled)
  sacct -j <JOBID>   — accounting info after job finishes (exit code, elapsed)
- Common pending reasons: Resources, Priority, PartitionDown, QOS, License. Use scontrol show job to get the detailed reason string.

Common #SBATCH options (most used)
- --job-name=NAME
- --nodes=N, --ntasks=N, --ntasks-per-node=N
- --cpus-per-task=N
- --mem=SIZE or --mem-per-cpu=SIZE
- --time=DD-HH:MM:SS or HH:MM:SS
- --gres=gpu:N
- --partition=NAME
- --output=FILE and --error=FILE (or combined with --output=slurm-%j.out)
- --mail-user=you@site --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL

Environment variables available in jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, etc. Use them in scripts to adapt behavior.

Best practices
- Always test with a small, short job first (1 node, short time) to verify script and modules.
- Request realistic resources: over-requesting time or memory reduces scheduler throughput and can delay your job.
- Set --time to a sensible upper bound — shorter limits often help the job start sooner.
- Use output files named with %j (job ID) so logs don’t collide across runs.
- Capture exit codes in scripts and fail fast (set -e).
- If pending, check squeue and scontrol for the reason before contacting admins.
- For GPU jobs, confirm cluster uses gres=gpu and what GPU types are available (sinfo shows node resources).
- Keep software environment reproducible (modules, virtualenv/conda, container images if supported).

Troubleshooting tips
- Job never starts: check squeue for pending reason; check sinfo for partition/node availability.
- Job fails quickly: inspect slurm-<JOBID>.out and check the batch script for missing modules or wrong paths.
- Out-of-memory: increase --mem or detect memory leak; use sacct to see ExitCode and signal (e.g., OOM killed).
- Unexpected task placement: check --ntasks, --cpus-per-task and use srun with --cpu-bind options if needed.

Where to learn more
- The official Slurm documentation is authoritative (sacct, srun, sbatch, scontrol pages). If you want, I can fetch specific doc pages or give cluster-specific templates.

Would you like:
- a ready-to-use template for CPU, GPU, or MPI jobs tailored to your cluster defaults?
- help debugging a specific job script or a pending job ID? (If so, tell me the job ID or which template you want.)

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a good Slurm batch script is clear, reproducible, correctly requests resources, and fails fast so problems surface quickly. Below is a compact checklist, a minimal template, a richer template (MPI/GPU/array), and practical tips & common pitfalls.

Checklist (what to include)
- Shebang and safe shell flags: #!/bin/bash and set -euo pipefail.
- Clear SBATCH directives: job name, partition, time, nodes/ntasks, cpus-per-task, memory (or mem-per-cpu), gres for GPUs, output/error paths, account/QOS if required.
- Run from submit dir: cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR.
- Load environment: module/conda/virtualenv and record versions.
- Use srun to launch parallel tasks (MPI/heterogeneous).
- Export thread counts: export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK (or similar).
- Diagnostics at start: hostname, date, nodelist, env, nvidia-smi (if GPU).
- Trap termination signals to checkpoint/clean up if needed.
- Use %j in output filenames for jobid; include timestamps or $SLURM_JOB_ID for reproducibility.
- Keep logs/artifacts in a scratch area and copy back on completion.

Minimal example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --output=job.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job.%j.err

set -euo pipefail
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"

module load gcc/12 python/3.10
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
echo "Starting: $(date)"

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

./my_program --threads $OMP_NUM_THREADS > output.${SLURM_JOB_ID}.log

Advanced template (MPI or GPU, arrays, trap)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=mpi_gpu_array
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=2
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=4
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
#SBATCH --time=06:00:00
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=4G
#SBATCH --output=logs/job_%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/job_%A_%a.err
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
#SBATCH --signal=B:SIGTERM@90

set -euo pipefail
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"

module purge
module load gcc openmpi cuda/12.1
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID Array $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
date

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=$OMP_NUM_THREADS

# trap to do a quick checkpoint/cleanup on preemption
cleanup() {
  echo "Caught signal at $(date) — performing cleanup"
  # e.g., save partial results, sync to persistent storage
}
trap cleanup SIGTERM SIGINT EXIT

# For MPI: let srun launch the rank processes
srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_program --task $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

Practical tips and best practices
- Request resources you actually need: over-requesting wastes cluster capacity and may delay scheduling.
- cpus-per-task vs ntasks: For multi-threaded single-process jobs use ntasks=1 and cpus-per-task=N. For MPI use ntasks equal to ranks and set cpus-per-task for per-rank threads.
- Memory: prefer --mem-per-cpu when memory scales with CPUs; use --mem for a fixed amount per node.
- GPUs: request with --gres=gpu:N. For conditional submissions that require idle GPUs, check sinfo first (see cluster policy).
- Use srun to start parallel work; srun handles allocation and CPU/GPU binding better than plain ./binary.
- Environment reproducibility: record module list (module list 2>&1), python -m pip freeze, and git commit hash.
- Use scratch (local SSD) for heavy I/O and copy results back to persistent storage at the end.
- Logging: include both STDOUT and STDERR files, and include jobid (%j) in filenames.
- Arrays: use --array with % to limit concurrency (e.g., 1-100%10).
- Preemption handling: use --signal to get advance notice; trap SIGTERM to checkpoint.
- Test smaller first: run with smaller input or shorter time, or interactively with salloc/srun to debug.
- Fail fast: set -e and check exit codes; validate input files early in the script.
- Don’t assume interactive environment: always cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR or use absolute paths.
- Respect site policies: include --account, --qos, or other headers your cluster requires.

Common mistakes
- Forgetting cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR (runs from home or controller working dir).
- Mis-matching cpus-per-task and thread counts (oversubscription).
- Not exporting OMP_NUM_THREADS or MKL_NUM_THREADS leading to slow performance.
- Writing output to a shared filesystem without buffering or checking quotas.
- Leaving module/environment setup out (works locally but fails in batch).
- Using srun incorrectly (e.g., launching background jobs that outlive batch job).

Debugging tips
- Add diagnostic prints at top: hostname, nproc, env, lscpu, nvidia-smi.
- Run interactively with salloc or srun --pty to reproduce environment.
- Use small, fast test inputs; increase resources only after it works.
- Use the cluster’s job output + error files; include timestamps and job id.

If you want, tell me:
- the kind of workload (MPI, GPU, single-threaded, OpenMP, Python), and
- whether you need an array or checkpointing,
and I’ll produce a tailored script for your cluster and application.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Great — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference and starting guide.

1) Quick overview
- Slurm is a job scheduler: submit batch jobs (sbatch), request interactive allocations (salloc / srun), and inspect the queue (squeue, sinfo).  
- Key concepts: job, step, partition, node, task, cpus-per-task, gres (GPUs), QOS/account, job arrays, and dependencies.

2) Core commands
- sbatch myscript.sh — submit a batch job script.  
- srun [opts] command — launch tasks (inside an allocation or from salloc); also used inside sbatch scripts.  
- salloc [opts] — request an interactive allocation.  
- squeue [-u $USER] — list queued/running jobs and pending reasons.  
- sinfo — show partitions and node availability.  
- scancel JOBID — cancel a job.  
- scontrol show job JOBID — detailed job info (reasons, TRES, etc.).  
- sacct -j JOBID — historical accounting for completed jobs.

3) Minimal batch script template (sbatch)
- Put scheduler options as SBATCH directives at top of script.
Example layout:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=myjob.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=myjob.%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00          # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --ntasks=1               # total MPI ranks
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4        # threads per rank (OpenMP)
#SBATCH --mem=8G                 # per-node or per-job depending on config
# optional: GPUs
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1

# Environment setup
module load python/3.10
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

# Run
srun python train.py

Notes:
- #SBATCH lines are equivalent to sbatch command-line options (e.g., sbatch --time=01:00:00).
- Use srun to launch the program so Slurm tracks tasks and output properly.

4) Common resource options
- --partition=NAME (which partition/queue)  
- --time=HH:MM:SS (walltime limit)  
- --ntasks=N (MPI ranks)  
- --cpus-per-task=M (threads per rank, e.g., OpenMP)  
- --nodes=X (number of nodes)  
- --mem=8G or --mem-per-cpu=2G  
- --gres=gpu:1 (request GPUs)  
- --job-name and --output / --error for logging

5) Job arrays
- Submit many similar tasks efficiently:
sbatch --array=1-100%10 job.sh
- %10 limits concurrency to 10 tasks at once. Inside the script $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID holds the index.

6) Dependencies
- Chain jobs using --depend:
sbatch --depend=afterok:12345 next_job.sh
- Types: after, afterok, afternotok, afterany, aftercorr (for arrays).

7) Interactive work
- Request shell on compute node:
salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=01:00:00 --gres=gpu:1
srun --pty bash -l
Or directly:
srun --pty --nodes=1 --time=01:00:00 bash

8) MPI and hybrid jobs
- Launch MPI with srun (preferred) or mpirun if your cluster requires it:
srun -n 32 ./mpi_program
- For hybrid MPI+OpenMP: set --cpus-per-task and export OMP_NUM_THREADS accordingly.

9) GPUs
- Request with --gres=gpu:N and check sinfo for GPU partitions.  
- Many clusters populate CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES or GPU device mapping automatically; check your local cluster docs. If not, you may need to set device selection inside your job.

10) Monitoring & debugging
- squeue -u $USER -o "%.18i %.9P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R" — custom columns (example).  
- scontrol show job JOBID — detailed state, reason, TRES, and stderr/stdout paths.  
- If a job is pending, squeue will often show a reason (Resources, Priority, QOSGrpMemLimit, etc.). Use scontrol show job to see expanded reason if squeue omits it.  
- Inspect output files (stdout/stderr) and module/environment. Use read_file or check job-specific log paths.

11) Accounting & history
- sacct -j JOBID --format=JobID,JobName,User,State,ExitCode,Elapsed — get exit codes and runtime for completed jobs.  
- sreport and sshare can show usage and fairshare.

12) Common failure causes & how to investigate
- Pending because of insufficient resources: sinfo and squeue reason; lower resource request or change partition.  
- Exceeded time limit: job shows TIMEOUT in sacct; increase --time and requeue.  
- Memory kill: check OOM logs and adjust --mem.  
- Missing modules / environment: ensure modules are loaded in the job script before running programs.

13) Best practices
- Request only what you need (CPU, memory, GPUs) to improve scheduler fairness.  
- Write output and error to files with %j (job ID) to avoid collisions.  
- Use checkpoints for long jobs and make small test runs with short --time before full production runs.  
- Use job arrays for parameter sweeps or many small, similar tasks.  
- Use --nice or QOS appropriately per local policy; consult admin for accounts and limits.

14) Where to look next / docs
- Official Slurm docs (slurm.schedmd.com) for sbatch, srun, squeue, job arrays, and gres.  
- Cluster-specific user guide / module list (your HPC site) for partitions, GPU mapping, and allowed QOS/accounts.

results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, safe sbatch script pattern you can adapt. It follows sbatch rules (all #SBATCH directives before any non-comment line), uses strict shell safety flags, traps signals for graceful cleanup, avoids inheriting unexpected environment, uses srun for work, and writes per-job logs.

Script template (edit resource/request lines to your needs):

#!/bin/bash
#
# Example safe sbatch wrapper
#
# NOTE: all #SBATCH directives must appear before the first non-comment, non-whitespace line.

#SBATCH --job-name=myjob               # short name
#SBATCH --output=logs/slurm-%j.out     # %j expands to jobid
#SBATCH --error=logs/slurm-%j.err      # or combine with --output if you prefer
#SBATCH --chdir=%x                      # optional: %x not standard everywhere; consider --chdir=/path
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00                # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                   # if you need GPUs; remove if not
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL           # optional notifications
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
#SBATCH --export=NONE                  # do not inherit environment; explicitly export needed vars
#SBATCH --ntasks=1                     # change for MPI/parallel jobs
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1

# ---- shell safety and environment ----
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'
umask 022

# Ensure log dir exists inside submit dir (or set a full path)
mkdir -p "${SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR:-.}/logs"

# Export only what you need (since --export=NONE makes the job start with a minimal environment)
export PATH=/usr/local/bin:$PATH
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-4}

# Optional: limit core dumps and file sizes
ulimit -c 0        # disable core files
ulimit -v unlimited

# ---- helper/cleanup functions ----
cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "Job ${SLURM_JOB_ID:-unknown} cleaning up, exit status $rc" >&2
  # add graceful termination/flush/archival here, e.g. kill children, rsync logs
  if [ -n "${child_pid:-}" ] && ps -p "$child_pid" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "Killing child PID $child_pid" >&2
    kill -TERM "$child_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
    wait "$child_pid" || true
  fi
  # If you produce temporary files inside $TMPDIR, clean them.
  # Example: [ -n "${TMPDIR:-}" ] && rm -rf "${TMPDIR}/myjob-${SLURM_JOB_ID}" || true
}
# Always run cleanup on exit, INT, TERM
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

# ---- optional: print job environment for debugging ----
echo "JobID=${SLURM_JOB_ID} JobName=${SLURM_JOB_NAME}"
echo "SubmitDir=${SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR:-$(pwd)}"
echo "NodeList=${SLURM_NODELIST:-unknown}"
echo "CPUS_PER_TASK=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-unknown}"
echo "Starting at $(date)"

# ---- modules / environment setup ----
module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/12.1            # adjust for your cluster's module names

# create a per-job temp dir if needed
export TMPDIR="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/job-${SLURM_JOB_ID}"
mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"

# ---- run your workload ----
# Use srun for parallel/mpi tasks so Slurm sets up step-level accounting
# Example single-process or multi-threaded command:
srun --cpu_bind=cores python -u my_script.py --epochs 10 &
child_pid=$!
wait "$child_pid"
exit_code=$?

# ---- final message, exit with original exit code ----
echo "Finished at $(date) with exit code $exit_code"
exit $exit_code

Quick notes / best-practices checklist
- Put all #SBATCH directives at the top (before any non-comment code).
- Use set -euo pipefail and IFS for safer shell behavior.
- Use --export=NONE and explicitly export only required variables to avoid surprises from your login shell.
- Use srun for job steps that need Slurm bookkeeping (MPI, distributed, or multi-node).
- Create and use per-job log and tmp directories; make them under $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR or an absolute path.
- Trap TERM/INT/EXIT to perform cleanup, checkpoint, or graceful shutdown actions. Avoid orphaned children.
- Prefer absolute paths for data, binaries, and scripts; do not assume $PATH or working directory unless you set --chdir or cd explicitly.
- Keep resource requests conservative and accurate (cpus/mem/gres/time) to help scheduler fit your job.
- Test interactively (salloc/srun) with the same resource request before submitting large batch runs.
- For long-running experiments, add periodic checkpointing or save state frequently so preemption/draining doesn't lose all progress.
- Combine stdout/stderr if easier to manage (--output and --error to same file) or leave separate to keep stderr visible.

If you want, I can:
- produce a variant for job arrays,
- include MPI/mpirun examples,
- or tailor this template for GPU training (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES handling, NCCL setups). Which would you like?

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial covering the common day‑to‑day tasks, commands, examples, and troubleshooting tips.

Basic concepts
- Slurm components you’ll use: sbatch (submit batch scripts), srun (launch job steps / interactive work), salloc (allocate interactive resources), squeue (view queue), sinfo (view partitions/nodes), sacct (accounting/history), scontrol (detailed show/change).
- Job lifecycle: submit (sbatch) → pending (waiting for resources) → running → completed/failed/timed out/cancelled.
- Resources: partition, nodes, tasks, CPUs per task, memory, GPUs (gres), time limit, QOS, account.

Simple batch script (single-node CPU job)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=normal
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --output=job.%j.out

module load python
srun python train.py

- Save as job.sh and submit with: sbatch job.sh
- sbatch prints a job ID; job will be scheduled according to available resources and policies.

GPU job example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-job
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --output=gpu.%j.out

module load cuda
srun python train_gpu.py

- --gres=gpu:N requests N GPUs on allocated nodes.

MPI / multi-node example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=32
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --time=03:00:00

module load mpi
srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_app

Job arrays (many similar jobs)
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
# inside script, use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick input
- %10 limits concurrent tasks to 10.

Dependencies (run job B after A completes successfully)
sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 jobB.sh

Interactive work
- salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00 bash
  (allocates resources and gives an interactive shell)
- srun --pty --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 bash
  (create an interactive job step inside allocation)

Monitoring and querying
- squeue: current queue and running jobs
  - squeue -u $USER (your jobs)
  - squeue -j JOBID (one job)
  - squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.20j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R" (custom format)
- sinfo: partition/node availability and counts
  - sinfo -s (summary)
  - sinfo -N (per-node)
- sacct: historical accounting (completed/failed jobs)
  - sacct -u alice --starttime=2024-04-01
- scontrol show job JOBID: detailed job config and reason fields
- sstat -j JOBID: live resource stats for running job (CPU/memory I/O)

Common job file directives (summary)
- --partition / -p
- --nodes / -N
- --ntasks
- --ntasks-per-node
- --cpus-per-task
- --mem or --mem-per-cpu
- --gres (e.g., gpu:1)
- --time / -t
- --job-name
- --output / --error

Job stdout/stderr and logs
- Default output file: slurm-%j.out (depends on site). Set with --output and --error or combine with --output=job.%j.out.
- Check job output and the script’s commands; many “failure” questions are solved by reading the output file.

Common pending reasons and what to check
- Resources (ReqNodeNotAvail / Resources): requested nodes/GPUs are busy—check sinfo for idle nodes.
- Priority/Backfill/Preemption (Priority): lower priority; check sprio and sshare if you need priority changes.
- QOS/Account limits (QOSMaxJobsPerUser / QOSMaxWall): site limits; contact admin or change account/QOS.
- Partition down/drained: sinfo will show nodes down/drained; ask admin to resolve.
- Dependency not satisfied: the job has --dependency set; check dependency job status.

Debugging tips
- If a job is pending: run squeue -j JOBID (see REASON column). Use scontrol show job JOBID for more detail.
- If job fails quickly: look at job.%j.out and error file; check exit code from sacct (ExitCode).
- If resources appear free but job doesn’t start: check partition limits, QOS, reservations, and node states with sinfo and scontrol.
- For GPU submits conditional on free GPUs: inspect sinfo to confirm idle GPU nodes (allocated/drained/down nodes do not count as available).

Resubmitting & cancellation
- Cancel: scancel JOBID
- Requeue: scontrol requeue JOBID (site policy may restrict)
- To re-run failed jobs, check exit codes and logs, adjust script/resources, then sbatch again.

Useful commands cheat sheet
- Submit: sbatch script.sh
- Interactive: salloc ... or srun --pty bash
- Run a step inside a job: srun <cmd>
- See queue: squeue [-u user] [-p partition] [-j jobid]
- See partitions/nodes: sinfo [-s] [-N]
- Job details: scontrol show job JOBID
- Job history: sacct -j JOBID or sacct -u user --starttime=...
- Live stats: sstat -j JOBID
- Cancel job: scancel JOBID

Best practices
- Request realistic time limits; excessive overestimates reduce scheduling flexibility and waiting times.
- Request only the resources you need (CPUs, memory, GPUs).
- Use modules to set environment; ensure env is reproducible.
- Use job arrays for many similar tasks instead of separate sbatch commands.
- Keep scripts small and test interactively (salloc) before full submission.
- Use meaningful job names and --output patterns including %j to track outputs.

When to contact admin
- Nodes are down or drained for long periods (sinfo shows drains).
- You hit account/QOS or cluster-wide limits you don’t understand.
- Strange scheduler behavior (backfill anomalies) or scontrol errors.

If you want, I can:
- Show a step‑by‑step example for your exact workflow (MPI, TensorFlow, singularity/containers, etc.).
- Explain a particular Slurm error or pending reason if you paste squeue / scontrol output (tell me the job ID).
Which would you like?

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a reference.

1) Key concepts and workflow
- Controller schedules jobs submitted by users. A job requests resources (nodes, CPUs, memory, GPUs, time) and then runs when scheduler can allocate them.
- Common modes:
  - Batch (sbatch): submit a script to run later.
  - Interactive allocation (salloc) or interactive step (srun --pty): get an allocation and run interactively.
  - Direct job-step run (srun): run a command inside an allocation (used inside sbatch scripts or after salloc).
- Typical monitoring/diagnostic tools (read-only):
  - squeue — current queue (RUNNING/PENDING/etc).
  - sinfo — partition/node availability and states.
  - scontrol show job <id> — detailed job settings & reason.
  - sacct — historical accounting for completed jobs.
  - sstat — runtime resource usage for a running job.
  - scontrol show config / sdiag / sprio — scheduler diagnostics and priorities.

2) Minimal sbatch script header (example)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out            # %j = jobid
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --gpus=1                         # or --gpus-per-node=1 depending on config
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --account=myaccount

# run your program
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- #SBATCH lines are parsed by sbatch before the script runs. After the first non-comment line, no more #SBATCH directives are processed.
- Output filename patterns: %j (jobid), %A (array master id), %a (array index), %N (node list), etc.

3) Resource request flags (common)
- Nodes: --nodes=N
- Tasks (MPI processes): --ntasks=M
- CPUs per task (threads): --cpus-per-task=T
- Memory: --mem=16G (per node) or --mem-per-cpu=4G
- Walltime: --time=HH:MM:SS
- Partition: --partition=name
- GPUs: --gpus=COUNT or --gpus-per-node=COUNT (cluster-dependent)
- Account/QOS: --account=acct --qos=name
- Constrain nodes: -w node[01-03] or --constraint=feature

4) Job arrays and dependencies
- Job array: #SBATCH --array=1-100 or sbatch --array=1-100%10 (the %10 limits concurrent array tasks to 10).
  - Within the script, use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to vary work per index.
  - Output patterns: --output=out-%A_%a.txt (master jobid + array index).
- Dependencies:
  - Wait for job 1234 to succeed: sbatch --dependency=afterok:1234 nextjob.sh
  - Other types: afterany, afterok, aftercorr, after, singleton, etc.

5) Interactive usage
- salloc --time=01:00:00 --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gpus=1
  - then run srun --pty bash to get an interactive shell in the allocation.
- For quick one-off commands inside an allocation: srun -n1 --pty /bin/bash

6) Monitoring and debugging
- squeue -u $USER shows your queued/running jobs.
- squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %R" shows jobID, partition, name, user, state, elapsed, and REASON column.
- If squeue shows no reason or you need full details: scontrol show job <jobid> (gives pending reason, requested nodes, gres, StdErr/StdOut paths).
- For completed jobs and exit codes: sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed
- Inspect job stdout/stderr (files produced per --output/--error).
- For a running job’s resource usage: sstat -j <jobid>.<stepid>
- If nodes look unavailable: sinfo (partition/node counts) and sinfo -R (reasons for drained/down nodes).

7) Common pending reasons and quick fixes
- Resources — waiting for CPUs/gpus/memory/nodes: reduce resource requests, change partition, or wait.
- Priority — other jobs have higher priority: check sprio or squeue ordering.
- Dependency — job blocked by dependency: confirm dependency job ID and state.
- ReqNodeNotAvail — requested specific node(s) not available: remove -w or change constraint.
- PartitionDown / NodeDown / NodeDrain — partition or nodes are administratively down/drained: contact admin or pick another partition.
- QOSLimit / AssociationLimit — user/account reached quota or QOS limit: reduce resources or contact accounting/admin.
- To get exact reason for a pending job: scontrol show job <id>.

8) Best practices
- Request realistic resources and time limits; over-requesting causes longer queue times.
- Start with small tests to validate environment and dependencies.
- Use job arrays for many similar short tasks instead of many single-job submissions.
- Keep stdout/stderr organized with %j or %A_%a in filenames.
- Use checkpoints for long runs and make periodic saves.
- Use modules/conda activation in the script so job environment is reproducible.
- Capture environment with module list or conda env export if debugging failures.

9) Common commands quick reference
- Submit: sbatch myscript.sh
- Interactive allocation: salloc ...
- Run a step inside allocation: srun myprog
- Show queue: squeue -u alice  (or squeue -j 12345)
- Show partitions/nodes: sinfo
- Job details: scontrol show job 12345
- Cancel: scancel 12345
- Hold/release: scontrol hold 12345 ; scontrol release 12345
- Accounting/history: sacct -j 12345 or sacct -u username
- Scheduler diagnostics: sdiag ; sprio

10) Where to read more
- Slurm man pages: sbatch(1), srun(1), squeue(1), sinfo(1), scontrol(8), sacct(1).
- Official docs: https://slurm.schedmd.com/

If you want, I can:
- Create a ready-to-submit sbatch template for your workload (tell me CPUs, mem, gpus, nodes, time, partition).
- Walk through diagnosing a specific pending job (give me the job ID).
- Show examples for MPI, GPU TensorFlow/PyTorch launches, or containerized runs (Singularity/Apptainer).

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, practical, and “safe” sbatch script pattern you can adapt. It focuses on robustness (fail-fast), traceability (logs/IDs), cleanup, and a simple preemption/termination handler.

Example safe_sbatch.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out            # jobname-jobid.out
#SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err             # jobname-jobid.err
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00               # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
## #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1               # uncomment for GPU
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL          # optional
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com   # optional

set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

# Safety limits (avoid huge core dumps)
ulimit -c 0

# Create an isolated temp work dir, delete on exit
TMPDIR=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/job-${SLURM_JOB_ID}-XXXX")
cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "$(date -Is) - cleanup called, rc=$rc" >> "${TMPDIR}/job_cleanup.log"
  # copy important artifacts to $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR or shared storage
  cp -a "${TMPDIR}/." "${SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR:-$PWD}/job-${SLURM_JOB_ID}-artifacts" || true
  # remove tmpdir if desired
  rm -rf "${TMPDIR}"
}
trap 'cleanup' EXIT

# Graceful termination handler (SIGTERM from slurm before SIGKILL)
on_term() {
  echo "$(date -Is) - Caught SIGTERM, attempting graceful shutdown" >> "${TMPDIR}/job_cleanup.log"
  # place checkpoint/save commands here
  # if your cluster permits, you could request requeue:
  # scontrol requeue "${SLURM_JOB_ID}" || true
  exit 1
}
trap 'on_term' TERM

# Move to the submission directory (or a host-local working dir)
cd "${SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR:-$PWD}"

# Load modules / activate virtualenvs inside the job
module purge
module load python/3.10   # adjust to your environment
# source venv/bin/activate

# Runtime logging
echo "Job ${SLURM_JOB_ID} started on $(hostname) at $(date -Is)"
echo "Nodes: ${SLURM_NODELIST}, TaskID: ${SLURM_PROCID:-N/A}"

# Example: run your task (use srun for parallel tasks)
# srun --cpu-bind=cores my_mpi_or_multithreaded_program --arg val
# For a single-process script:
python train.py --output "${TMPDIR}/results" || { echo "Task failed"; exit 2; }

echo "Job ${SLURM_JOB_ID} finished at $(date -Is)"
# artifacts will be copied in cleanup()

Key points and best practices
- set -euo pipefail and IFS make scripts fail early and avoid subtle bugs from unset vars.
- Use %x (job name) and %j (job id) in output/error filenames so logs are unique and traceable.
- Create an isolated temporary directory with mktemp -d, and copy artifacts back to submit dir on exit.
- Use traps: EXIT to always run cleanup, TERM to try to checkpoint or save state when Slurm sends SIGTERM before preemption/time-limit kill.
- Use ulimit to avoid huge core files filling disks.
- Load modules / activate environments inside the script (do not assume interactive environment).
- Use srun for MPI/parallel work; for single-process jobs, run the command directly or with srun for consistent cgroup placement.
- Don’t put secrets or long-lived credentials in the script. Use secure vaults or environment variables injected at runtime if needed.
- For job arrays, use SBATCH --array=1-100%20 and read SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to index inputs/seed files.
- For GPUs, request --gres=gpu:N and ensure your code binds to the GPU via CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES if necessary.
- For long-running/critical jobs, implement periodic checkpointing and test the SIGTERM handler locally.

Short array example (task-indexed work)
#SBATCH --array=1-100%20
...
TASK_ID=${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}
input="inputs/params_${TASK_ID}.json"
srun python run_task.py --input "${input}" --out "${TMPDIR}/out-${TASK_ID}.json"

If you want, tell me what kind of workload you run (Python training, MPI, multi-thread, GPU, array jobs) and I’ll produce a tailored template with recommended resource directives and a preemption-checkpoint snippet.

results.prompt: Explain basic Slurm submission steps
results.agent_response:
Here are the basic steps and best-practices for submitting a job to Slurm.

1) Create a batch script
- Start with a shell shebang: #!/bin/bash
- Put SBATCH directives near the top (one per line) to request resources and set metadata. Common options:
  - #SBATCH --job-name=jobname
  - #SBATCH --partition=gpu|cpu (or your cluster's partition)
  - #SBATCH --nodes=1
  - #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  - #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
  - #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1         (for GPUs)
  - #SBATCH --mem=16G or --mem-per-cpu=4G
  - #SBATCH --time=02:00:00     (HH:MM:SS)
  - #SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out  (or slurm-%j.out)
  - #SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL and #SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
- Note: SBATCH directives are processed only up to the first non-comment, non-whitespace line.

2) Put setup and the work to run after the directives
- Load modules, activate virtualenv/conda, set environment variables.
- Launch tasks with srun (recommended) or appropriate MPI/launcher:
  - srun my_program arg1 arg2
  - or mpirun / mpiexec inside an srun allocation, depending on your environment.

3) Submit the job
- sbatch myscript.sh
- sbatch returns the job ID on success (e.g., “Submitted batch job 12345”).

4) Monitor the job
- squeue -u $USER or squeue -j <jobid> to see RUNNING/PENDING state and pending reason.
- scontrol show job <jobid> for full job details (resources, environment, pending reason).
- sstat -j <jobid> (for running jobs) to see live resource use.
- sacct -j <jobid> after completion for accounting (exit code, elapsed time, etc.).

5) Check job output and logs
- By default Slurm writes stdout/stderr to slurm-<jobid>.out unless you set --output/--error.
- Inspect that file for program output and errors.

6) Common management commands
- scancel <jobid> to cancel.
- sbatch --array=1-100 to create job arrays; use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in the script.
- srun / salloc for interactive allocations if you need an interactive shell.

7) Tips / best practices
- Always request a realistic --time; underestimating can lead to premature job termination, overestimating can hurt scheduling.
- Request only the resources you need (CPUs, memory, GPUs) so scheduler can pack jobs efficiently.
- Use --mem-per-cpu vs --mem depending on whether memory is per-task or per-node on your cluster.
- Capture environment and module list in job output (e.g., module list; env) to aid debugging.
- For GPUs, request --gres=gpu:N and verify with your local docs whether you also need gres-flags or constraints.
- If a job is stuck PENDING, check the “REASON” column in squeue or scontrol show job to see resource or QOS limits.

Minimal example script (content lines):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=test
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --output=test-%j.out

module load python
srun python train.py --epochs 10

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Short answer: write a batch script with SBATCH directives and run sbatch <script>. sbatch returns a job ID.

Detailed steps and examples

1) Create a batch script (bash/sh). Put resource requests in SBATCH directives near the top:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob                # job name
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                 # partition/queue
#SBATCH --nodes=1                       # number of nodes
#SBATCH --ntasks=1                      # total tasks (MPI ranks)
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8               # threads per task
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                    # request 1 GPU (if available)
#SBATCH --mem=32G                       # memory
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00                 # walltime HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out           # stdout file (%j = jobid)
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err            # stderr file
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL            # email on end/fail
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

# your commands
module load python
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- Command-line options to sbatch override #SBATCH lines. Example: sbatch --time=01:00:00 myscript.sh
- For a simple one-liner you can use: sbatch --wrap="python myscript.py"
- For interactive development use salloc or srun (interactive allocation) instead of sbatch.

Useful features
- Job arrays: add #SBATCH --array=1-10%2 and use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script.
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 myscript.sh (start when job 12345 succeeds). Other types: afterany, after, singleton, etc.
- Account/QOS: add --account=acctname or --qos=name if your cluster requires charging.

Checking status and results
- squeue -u $USER to see queued/running jobs.
- scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed job info.
- sacct -j <jobid> to see accounting/finished job results.
- Output goes to the file you set with --output (default slurm-<jobid>.out).

Cluster-specific limits
- Policies (max time, memory, partitions, accounts, allowed GPUs) vary by site. If your job is pending, squeue will often show a reason (or use scontrol show job <id> for more detail).

If you want, tell me:
- an example command you want to run or
- which partition/GPUs or resources you need,
and I can draft a ready-to-submit script for you.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Great — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference and starter guide. It covers common commands, how to write job scripts, resource-request semantics, arrays & dependencies, interactive work, monitoring/troubleshooting, and best practices.

1) Key concepts and commands
- sbatch: submit a batch job script (non-interactive).
- srun: launch a job step / run tasks (used inside a batch job or for interactive runs).
- salloc: obtain an interactive allocation (then use srun or run commands).
- squeue: view active queue (pending/running) and job states.
- sinfo: view partitions and node states (allocated/idle/down).
- scontrol show: show detailed info for jobs/nodes/partitions.
- sacct: historical/accounting info for completed jobs.
- scancel: cancel jobs.
- sstat: runtime stats for running jobs (I/O, memory, CPU).
- sreport/sshare: usage and fairshare reports (accounting).

2) Minimal sbatch job script (example)
Lines beginning with #SBATCH set job options. Save as job.sh and submit with sbatch job.sh.

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=test-job
#SBATCH --output=job.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job.%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=normal
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00

module load python
srun python train.py

Notes:
- %j expands to the Slurm job ID in filenames.
- Use srun to launch executables inside the allocated resources. If your script only runs one process, you can call the program directly too.

3) Common resource flags and semantics
- --nodes=N or -N N : number of distinct nodes.
- --ntasks=N or -n N : total MPI/rank count.
- --ntasks-per-node=N : tasks per node.
- --cpus-per-task=N : threads per task (e.g., for OpenMP or data loaders).
- --mem=8G or --mem-per-cpu=2G : memory requests.
- --time=HH:MM:SS : walltime limit.
- --partition=name : partition/queue to use.
- --gres=gpu:1 or --gres=gpu:V100:2 : generic resources (gpus).
- --qos=name : request a QOS if your site uses them.
- --mail-type=END,FAIL and --mail-user=you@... : email notifications.

4) GPU-specific notes
- Request GPUs with --gres=gpu:<count>. On some clusters you also need a GPU partition.
- For conditional/automated GPU submission, determine idle GPU nodes with sinfo first (idle GPU nodes only count as available).
- Ensure drivers/cuda modules are loaded in your job.

5) Interactive usage
- salloc --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --time=01:00:00 --partition=debug
  Once allocation is granted, run srun --pty bash to get a shell on an allocated node or run programs directly.
- srun --pty -p interactive --gres=gpu:1 bash  (short direct interactive run if allowed)

6) Job arrays and dependencies
- Array example: #SBATCH --array=1-100
  Each array task receives SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID environment variable.
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 job.sh
  Common dependency types: after, afterok, afternotok, afterany, singleton.

7) Monitoring and inspecting jobs
- squeue -u $USER shows your queued/running jobs.
- squeue -j <jobid> -o "%.18i %.20P %.40j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R" to display custom columns (format varies by site).
- sinfo shows partition/node states: NODES(A/I/D) indicates Allocated/Idle/Down counts.
- scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed job fields (reason, allocation, TRES, StdOut/Err paths).
- sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed for history and exit codes.
- sstat -j <jobid> for live resource usage (only works for running jobs).

8) Common job states and pending reasons (how to diagnose "stuck" jobs)
- PENDING: check the "REASON" column in squeue (e.g., Resources, Priority, Dependency, QOSMax, AssocGrp, BeginTime).
- If squeue shows no reason column, run scontrol show job <jobid> to see the detailed reason.
- Common reasons:
  - Resources: not enough free CPUs/GPUs/memory or no nodes matching constraints.
  - Priority: higher-priority jobs occupy resources.
  - Dependency: waiting for another job to complete.
  - BeginTime: scheduled to start in the future.
  - QOS/Account limits: association or user limits reached.
  - NodeDown/Drained: nodes suitable for the job are down/drained.
- For nodes: sinfo and sinfo -R (or sinfo_reasons) show nodes in down/drain and reasons.

9) Logs and exit codes
- Standard output and error files are controlled by --output and --error; check them first for application errors.
- sacct shows ExitCode (0 = success). If ExitCode non-zero, examine job stderr/stdout plus node logs.
- If job fails to launch (LAUNCH_FAILED, PROLOG/EPILOG failure), scontrol show job <id> will list the launch failure reason.

10) Best practices
- Request only required resources and realistic walltime; shorter jobs can start sooner.
- Use --cpus-per-task for multi-threaded code; use ntasks for MPI ranks.
- Use modules or container runtimes (Singularity) in job scripts to get reproducible environments.
- Save stdout/stderr and consider periodic checkpoints for long runs; set --requeue if appropriate.
- For parallel jobs, use srun inside the job script to launch tasks so Slurm manages placement and bindings.
- Test interactively with salloc/srun on small input before submitting large batch runs.
- For debugging pending issues, collect squeue, scontrol show job, and sinfo outputs to diagnose reasons.

11) Useful environment variables inside jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, SLURM_JOB_NAME

12) Examples (quick)
- Submit: sbatch job.sh
- Check queue: squeue -u alice
- Cancel: scancel 12345
- Submit array: sbatch --array=1-50 my_array_job.sh
- Dependency submit: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 downstream.sh

13) Troubleshooting checklist
- If pending: squeue -j <id> (check REASON) → scontrol show job <id> for details → sinfo for node availability.
- If job failed: inspect job.%j.err/out → sacct -j <id> for ExitCode → scontrol show job for prolog/epilog or launch failures.
- If resource contention: consider smaller resource requests, different partition, or ask admin about quotas/QOS.

If you want:
- A customized example job script for MPI, GPU PyTorch training, or array-parallel data processing, tell me which and I’ll produce one.
- Help diagnosing a specific job or the current cluster state, give a job ID or say what you want checked and I’ll run the relevant Slurm commands.

results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, safe sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It includes defensive shell settings, clean signal/exit handling, a per-job temporary workspace, safe launching with srun (preferred over mpirun under Slurm), and clear #SBATCH directives. Replace <...> placeholders for your site/user paths and program.

Script (template)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=<job-name>
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out           # %x = job name, %j = jobid
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                    # change as needed
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                       # GPUs per job
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
# optional job array:
# SBATCH --array=1-10%4

# --- safe shell options ---
set -euo pipefail
# uncomment for verbose trace while debugging:
# set -x
umask 0022

# --- simple logging of job metadata ---
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME) started on $(date)"
echo "Nodes: $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
echo "CPUs/task: $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, GPUs: ${SLURM_GPUS_ON_NODE:-unknown}"

# --- create and use a per-job temp dir (prefer fast local scratch if available) ---
export JOB_TMP="${TMPDIR:-/scratch/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID}"
mkdir -p "$JOB_TMP"
cd "$JOB_TMP"

# --- cleanup handler: copy results back, kill stray children, preserve exit code ---
on_exit() {
  rc=$?
  echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID exiting with status $rc at $(date)"
  # kill any child processes that may remain
  pkill -P $$ || true
  # copy results back (make this path valid for your site)
  rsync -a --remove-source-files ./results/ /home/$USER/results/$SLURM_JOB_ID/ || true
  exit $rc
}
trap on_exit EXIT

# --- load modules / activate envs ---
module purge
module load gcc/12 cuda/11.8        # example; use your site modules
# source /path/to/venv/bin/activate

# --- run the job ---
# Prefer srun so Slurm manages distribution and accounting
# Use --cpu-bind or --hint if you need CPU affinity
srun --mpi=pmix --cpu-bind=cores ./my_program --threads "$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"

# Or for array tasks: ./my_program --task-id $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

# explicit exit (on_exit trap will run)
exit 0

Key points / best practices
- #SBATCH directives: must appear before the first non-comment line in the script. Keep shebang (#!/bin/bash) as the first line.
- Use set -euo pipefail to fail fast and avoid surprises from unset variables; enable set -x temporarily while debugging.
- Use a trap/cleanup function (trap ... EXIT) to copy outputs back and kill stray children. Preserve and re-exit with the original exit code.
- Create and use a per-job temporary directory (local fast scratch if available) and rsync results back to a persistent filesystem at the end.
- Prefer srun for launching tasks under Slurm (srun gives proper allocation, binding, and accounting). If you must use mpirun, ensure it integrates with Slurm and uses SLURM_NTASKS/SLURM_NODELIST.
- For GPUs: request them with --gres=gpu:N and let Slurm set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES — do not hardcode GPU device assignments inside the job.
- Use --cpus-per-task for multi-threaded tasks and set memory (--mem or --mem-per-cpu) to avoid OOMs.
- Avoid long-running copies at job start on shared storage; stage inputs to local scratch where possible and rsync only outputs back at end.
- Make logs reproducible: include %j (jobid) and %x (jobname) in output filenames so parallel runs don’t clobber each other.
- Use job arrays for many similar short tasks (#SBATCH --array=...) and limit concurrent tasks with %N to avoid overloading the scheduler or filesystem.
- For debug/development jobs, set a short --time and smaller resource requests.
- Consider ulimit and umask policies if your site requires specific defaults.

- produce a variant for MPI (multi-node) or for PyTorch/Deep Learning (multi-GPU) with recommended srun/mpirun flags,
- or produce a tested one-line minimal version for quick debugging. Which one would you like?

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,

results.prompt: Explain queue priority using fairshare, Fair Tree usage, and configured priority weights
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Slurm uses the multifactor priority plugin (PriorityType=priority/multifactor) to compute a single numeric job priority as a weighted sum of independent factors. Three of the most important pieces that control queue ordering are: the fairshare factor (how much a user/account has recently consumed), the Fair Tree algorithm (how fairshare is computed across accounts/users), and the configured PriorityWeight* values (how strongly each factor influences ordering).

How job priority is computed (conceptual)
- Job_priority = site_factor
  + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor
  + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
  + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
  + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
  + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
  + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor
  + SUM(TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X)
  - nice_factor
- Each factor is a floating value (roughly 0.0–1.0). The PriorityWeight* entries are unsigned integers; together they scale each factor’s contribution before the total is converted to the final integer priority (0 .. 4294967295).

Fairshare factor — what it means and how it behaves
- Fairshare reduces priority for users/accounts that have used more of the cluster recently; it raises priority for users/accounts that have used less.
- Fairshare values are derived from historical usage per association/account/user and are normalized into a factor used in the multifactor formula.
- Two key configuration knobs:
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife: controls how quickly past usage “decays” (short half-life forgets history quickly; long half-life keeps historical usage influential). A value of 0 disables decay (must then use PriorityUsageResetPeriod).
  - PriorityUsageResetPeriod: optionally reset usage counters on a schedule (useful for enforcing quotas or fixed-period fairness).
- Tools to inspect fairshare: sshare (shows effective shares and usage) and sprio (shows factor contributions for pending jobs).

Fair Tree (the modern fairshare algorithm)
- Since Slurm 19.05 the Fair Tree algorithm is the default method used to convert historical usage into fairshare factors.
- Fair Tree is hierarchical: if two sibling accounts A and B are ordered by fairshare, then all children of A rank above all children of B. This preserves account-level ordering and avoids precision/tie problems seen in the older Classic algorithm.
- Benefits: stable ordering across account hierarchies, predictable behavior when account coordinators adjust shares, and reduced numerical tie/precision issues.
- If you need the older "classic" behavior you can still configure that explicitly, but Fair Tree is typically preferred.

Priority weights — how to make a factor matter (or not)
- PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, and per-TRES weights determine how strongly each factor affects final priority.
- If a weight is set to zero the corresponding factor contributes nothing.
- Typical default pattern: make PriorityWeightFairshare large relative to others so fairshare has strong influence (examples in docs use PriorityWeightFairshare=10000, others 1000).
- Example effects:
  - If PriorityWeightFairshare >> PriorityWeightAge, then users’ historical usage dominates scheduling (new jobs from under-used users jump ahead of old heavy users).
  - If PriorityWeightAge is high, long-waiting jobs will eventually win even if a user has been heavy.
- TRES weights allow bias by resource type (e.g., make GPU usage count differently than CPU usage in the fairshare calculations).

Practical tuning and debugging tips
- Decide policy first: do you want strict account-level fairness, or to allow aging to override recent usage?
- Typical levers:
  - Increase PriorityWeightFairshare to favor historical fairness.
  - Decrease PriorityDecayHalfLife to forget older usage sooner (helps new users recover).
  - Use PriorityUsageResetPeriod for hard periodic resets (monthly allocations, semester quotas).
  - Tune TRES weights to reflect relative cost/importance of GPUs vs CPUs.
- Inspect what Slurm is doing:
  - sshare — view current fairshare/usage for accounts and users.
  - sprio [--all] — show the numeric priority and per-factor contributions for pending jobs.
  - scontrol show config — see configured PriorityWeight* and decay/reset settings.
- When debugging why a particular job is low in the queue, run sprio (or scontrol show job) to see the fairshare_factor and all other factor contributions.

Short examples
- Two accounts A and B, equal job size mix, but A has consumed 4× more resources in the past week:
  - With PriorityWeightFairshare high, jobs from B will be scheduled ahead of A until usage evens out.
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife is short (e.g., 1 day), A’s advantage/penalty fades quickly and A’s jobs recover sooner.
- If PriorityWeightAge is large, even a user with poor fairshare will eventually have jobs win after waiting long enough.

Bottom line
- Fairshare (via Fair Tree) determines how recent historical consumption penalizes or boosts users/accounts.
- Priority weights control how much that fairshare (and other factors like age, job size, QOS, TRES) influence final queue ordering.
- Use sshare and sprio to inspect current effective shares and factor contributions; tune PriorityWeight* and PriorityDecayHalfLife/PriorityUsageResetPeriod to match your site’s fairness vs responsiveness goals.

If you want, I can:
- Show the current configured PriorityWeight* and fairshare settings from your cluster (scontrol show config and sshare/sprio).

results.prompt: Explain queue priority using fairshare, Fair Tree usage, and configured priority weights
results.agent_response:
Summary — how Slurm orders the queue
- Slurm’s default is the multifactor priority plugin (PriorityType=priority/multifactor). A job’s priority is a weighted sum of multiple factors (age, fairshare, job size, partition, QOS, TRES, site, nice, …). The larger the resulting integer, the higher the job is ordered in the queue and the sooner it is eligible to run.

High-level formula (concept)
- Job_priority = site_factor
  + PriorityWeightAge  * age_factor
  + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
  + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
  + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
  + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
  + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor
  + SUM( TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X )
  - nice_factor
- Each factor produces a floating value roughly in [0.0, 1.0] (implementation-dependent). The configured PriorityWeight* values scale each factor’s contribution; weights are integers and the final priority is an integer (0 .. 2^32-1).

Fairshare (what it does)
- Purpose: prevent users/accounts that consumed many resources recently from always winning the scheduler. Fairshare reduces priority for heavy recent users and increases it for under-used users.
- It is driven by historical usage tracked per association (user/account), decayed over time by PriorityDecayHalfLife so older usage matters less.
- Key config knobs:
  - PriorityWeightFairshare: how strongly fairshare influences final priority (higher = more influence).
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife: how quickly historical usage decays (e.g., 7-0 is 7 days). Smaller half-life → recent use matters more.
  - PriorityUsageResetPeriod: optional periodic reset of usage counters (useful if you want hard resets).
- You can inspect fairshare-related usage with sshare (reports effective shares/usage).

Fair Tree (Fair-share algorithm starting ~19.05)
- Fair Tree is the modern fairshare algorithm used by the multifactor plugin by default.
- Behavior:
  - Hierarchical: it respects account/user/account-group hierarchies so that if parent account A ranks ahead of sibling B, then all children of A rank ahead of all children of B. That prevents accidental local re-ordering inside an account that would hurt cross-account fairness.
  - Produces stable, rank-based fairshare factors and avoids precision issues and undesirable inversions that could occur in the older Classic algorithm.
  - Tie-handling is explicit and deterministic (but ties are permitted).
- Use when you have hierarchical accounting (accounts with subaccounts) and want consistent inter-account ordering.

Configured priority weights (how they change behavior)
- Weights are the administrator’s control knobs; they scale each factor’s effect on final priority:
  - PriorityWeightFairshare (commonly big, e.g., 10000): strong influence of fairshare.
  - PriorityWeightAge (e.g., 1000): lets jobs that waited a long time climb the queue (prevents starvation).
  - PriorityWeightJobSize (e.g., 1000): can favor smaller or larger jobs depending on how job_size_factor is defined.
  - PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS etc.: let you prefer jobs in particular partitions or QOS classes.
  - TRES weights (TRESWeight) let CPU, GPU, memory costs change priority (e.g., deprioritize GPU-heavy jobs).
- Example numeric intuition:
  - If PriorityWeightFairshare = 10000 and fairshare_factor for alice = 0.8, that contributes ≈ 8000 points.
  - If PriorityWeightAge = 1000 and age_factor = 0.5, that contributes ≈ 500 points.
  - Final priority is the sum of all such contributions (site + assoc + fairshare + …) minus nice_factor.
- Practical tuning guidance:
  - If fairness matters most, make PriorityWeightFairshare large relative to other weights.
  - If you want long-waiting jobs to eventually run despite fairshare, increase PriorityWeightAge.
  - If small jobs should be favored to improve throughput, tune PriorityWeightJobSize or PriorityFavorSmall.
  - Use PriorityDecayHalfLife to define how much history you want (short half-life = recent use matters; long half-life = long-term quotas).
  - Avoid making all weights zero or heavily skewing one factor unless intentional.

Diagnostics and inspection
- sprio: shows per-job priority and breakdown by factor (useful to see which factors contribute most).
- sshare: shows usage and effective shares for accounts/users (helps understand fairshare state).
- scontrol show config: view the Priority* settings in slurm.conf.
- sdiag and scheduler logs: for deeper scheduler behavior and backfill diagnostics.

Common interactions and gotchas
- Fairshare vs Age: a very large fairshare weight can cause a new or low-usage user’s job to jump ahead of long-waiting jobs unless you also raise PriorityWeightAge.
- TRES weights: assigning large positive weights to a TRES increases priority for jobs consuming that TRES (or the inverse, depending on factor setup); be careful when combining TRES weights with fairshare.
- QOS and partition factors can override account-level fairness for special classes (e.g., interactive or emergency QOS).
- PriorityDecayHalfLife = 0 disables decay (usage never decays) so the usage counters must be reset periodically with PriorityUsageResetPeriod or manually.
- Priority calculations use integers and limited precision; extremely large or tiny weights can lead to unintuitive ordering—test changes in a staging environment.

If you want, I can:
- show example slurm.conf snippets with recommended starting weights, or
- explain how to interpret sprio output for one or more real jobs, or
- suggest a tuning recipe for a cluster profile (research, bursty GPU, or throughput-focused). Which would you like?

results.prompt: Explain queue priority using fairshare, Fair Tree usage, and configured priority weights
results.agent_response:
Summary first
- Slurm’s queue ordering (when PriorityType=priority/multifactor) is a weighted sum of independent priority “factors” (age, fair‑share, job size, QOS, partition, TRES, site, nice, etc.). Each factor is normalized (roughly 0.0–1.0) and multiplied by a configured integer weight in slurm.conf; those products are summed to produce the final job priority score. Larger score → higher queue position.
- Fairshare is the factor that biases scheduling to favor accounts/users that are under‑served historically. The Fair Tree algorithm is the modern fairshare computation that uses the account hierarchy to produce consistent, hierarchical priorities.
- You tune behavior by changing the PriorityWeight* settings and fairshare parameters (PriorityDecayHalfLife, PriorityUsageResetPeriod, PriorityCalcPeriod) and by choosing/keeping Fair Tree.

How the multifactor priority formula works
- Concept: Job_priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS * QOS_factor + SUM(TRES_weight_x * TRES_factor_x) - nice_factor
- Each factor is a floating point value (0.0–1.0). Each PriorityWeight* and TRES_weight_* is an unsigned integer set in slurm.conf. The final job priority is an integer (0 … 4294967295).
- Changing a weight changes the relative importance of that factor compared with the others. E.g., increasing PriorityWeightFairshare will make historical usage (fairshare) more dominant when ordering jobs.

Fairshare — the idea and behavior
- Purpose: prevent a few users/accounts from monopolizing resources by lowering priority for accounts that have already consumed more than their fair share, while boosting priority for under‑served accounts.
- It does not impose hard caps; it only changes ordering. Over‑consuming accounts can still run if nothing else is eligible.
- Fairshare requires the Slurm accounting DB to compute historical usage.
- The fairshare factor is computed from account/user “composite usage” vs. their configured shares/weights; a larger fairshare factor means the account/user is more under‑served (so its jobs get higher priority).
- Historical usage is decayed over time according to PriorityDecayHalfLife (so old usage matters less). PriorityUsageResetPeriod can periodically reset tracked usage if desired.

Fair Tree (the modern fairshare algorithm)
- Introduced in Slurm 19.05 and the default fairshare algorithm.
- Works over the account hierarchy (tree): if account A and account B are siblings and A ranks higher than B, then all children of A will rank higher than all children of B. This preserves hierarchical ordering and prevents strange inversions.
- Benefits:
  - Hierarchical consistency: parent/child relations behave intuitively.
  - Stable ordering: reduces precision errors and odd tie behaviors that could happen with the older “classic” algorithm.
  - Account coordinators can’t accidentally make some users in their account get lower effective priority relative to other accounts’ users by reassigning weights inside the account tree.
- You can still choose the older Classic algorithm if desired, but Fair Tree is generally recommended.

TRES/TRES weights and other factors
- TRES (Trackable RESources) weights let you give extra priority to jobs requesting particular resources (CPU, energy, GRES/GPU, etc.). Example: set TRES_weight_gpu higher to give GPU jobs relatively more priority.
- QOS and partition factors: PriorityWeightQOS and PriorityWeightPartition let QOS and partition membership influence priority.
- Age factor: PriorityWeightAge increases scheduling priority over time so long‑waiting jobs eventually win.

Practical tuning recommendations
- Inspect current behavior with:
  - sprio -l (shows per‑job factor contributions) — useful to see which factors dominate.
  - sshare (shows account shares/consumption).
  - scontrol show config (to view the PriorityWeight* settings and decay parameters).
- Start with moderate weights; don’t make one weight orders of magnitude larger than the others unless you want it to dominate completely.
- If fairness feels “stuck” on old usage, reduce PriorityDecayHalfLife to make recent usage matter more, or reset usage with PriorityUsageResetPeriod.
- Use TRES weights to reflect site policy: e.g., if GPU time is scarce and should be rationed differently, bump TRES_weight_gpu.
- Combine fairshare with Age weight so the system balances fairness with waiting time (avoids starvation of small/over‑used accounts).
- Monitor results (sprio, sdiag) and iterate.

Quick numeric example (illustrative)
- Suppose: PriorityWeightFairshare=1000, PriorityWeightAge=100, fairshare_factor=0.8 (under‑served), age_factor=0.2 (short wait).
  - Contribution from fairshare = 1000 * 0.8 = 800
  - Contribution from age = 100 * 0.2 = 20
  - Total (plus any other factors) → fairshare dominates ordering here.
- If you reduce PriorityWeightFairshare to 100, then age and other factors can more easily change ordering.

Useful Slurm commands for inspection
- sprio -l — show factor values and weighted contributions per queued job.
- sshare — show account share usage and entitlement.
- scontrol show config — view PriorityWeight* and PriorityDecayHalfLife settings.
- lookup docs: priority_multifactor(see Slurm docs) and fair_tree pages (for algorithm details).

If you want, I can:
- Show how your cluster’s priority factors are currently configured (scontrol show config) and show sprio -l for specific queued jobs to explain exactly why those jobs are ordered as they are. (This is a read-only request; tell me which job IDs or if you want the global view.)
