```text
AuthAltParameters=jwks=/local/path/to/jwks.json,userclaimfield=preferred_username
```
Option 2 : Change the identity service to use a different field. In
KeyCloak 25.0, for example, you should find this option under Clients ->
Client details -> Dedicated scopes -> Mapper details . Change the username
mapping to use the `sun` field.

results.prompt: Explain ReqNodeNotAvail and common node availability reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- ReqNodeNotAvail means the scheduler could not find nodes that satisfy the job’s node/feature/GRES/TRES/placement requirements. In other words: “required node(s) not available” — not enough suitable idle nodes right now.

Why that happens (common node-availability causes)
1. Nodes are down/drained/failed/being rebooted
   - Nodes in DOWN, DRAIN, FAIL, or FAILING state are not usable for jobs.
2. Nodes are already allocated to other jobs
   - Idle node count is zero or there’s no set of nodes free that match the request.
3. Resource fragmentation / packing constraints
   - The request needs multiple nodes, contiguous nodes, or specific per-node TRES (e.g., 4 GPUs per node) and the remaining idle nodes can’t satisfy that exact packing.
4. Requested node names or node list (NodeList/ReqNode) don’t exist or are offline
   - A user requested specific hostnames that aren’t present or are not in a usable state.
5. Feature/constraint mismatch
   - The job requested a node feature or constraint (e.g., --constraint=avx512, or a GRES label) and no idle node exposes that feature.
6. GPUs or other GRES aren’t free
   - Nodes may be up but their GPUs/GPUs per node are fully allocated (allocated/mixed), so no node has the required free GPUs.
7. Administrative reservation or maintenance reservation
   - A reservation (or maintenance window) can reserve nodes so they’re not available for normal scheduling.
8. Partition or QOS limits or per-account/per-user limits
   - While those often show other reason codes, they can interact so the scheduler cannot place the job on any available node set.
9. Exclusive or shared mode conflicts
   - An exclusive allocation may prevent scheduling another job onto the same node even if some resources look free.
10. “Future” or scheduled state
   - Nodes marked FUTURE or otherwise scheduled for later use aren’t available now.

How to diagnose (quick commands to run)
- See the scheduler’s pending reason: squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %R"
  - The reason string visible in squeue often shows “ReqNodeNotAvail”.
- Inspect the job’s requirements: scontrol show job <jobid>
  - Look for ReqNodes/ReqTRES/NodeList/NumNodes/Features/Constraints.
- See node and partition states: sinfo
  - Use sinfo_reasons (sinfo -R) or scontrol show node <nodename> to get down/drain reasons.
- Check reservations: scontrol show reservation or squeue --reservation=<name>
- For GPU details, list node GRES/availability: sinfo -o or scontrol show node <node> (look for Gres, AllocTRES).

How to fix or mitigate
- If nodes are down/draining: ask admins to investigate (sinfo_reasons shows the reason).
- If fragmentation is the issue: relax constraints (fewer GPUs per node, allow different nodes, remove exact NodeList or set --ntasks-per-node differently).
- If a feature/constraint mismatch: remove or change the constraint or request a node with that feature.
- If reservation blocks nodes: either wait for reservation to end or request nodes in a different partition/reservation.
- If GPUs are allocated: either wait, request fewer GPUs, or target different nodes/partition.
- If you requested specific nodes that are offline: remove NodeList or pick other nodes.

Notes
- The squeue reason text is what the scheduler encountered for that scheduling pass; multiple deeper causes can exist (e.g., a reservation + lack of matching features). For a single-job deep inspection use scontrol show job and scontrol show node on candidate nodes.
- The canonical Slurm job reason codes and their explanations are in the Slurm docs (job_reason_codes).

If you want, tell me a job ID and I can show the squeue reason and the job’s requested node/TRES details and suggest specific changes.

results.prompt: Explain ReqNodeNotAvail and common node availability reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- ReqNodeNotAvail is a Slurm pending reason that means: the scheduler could not find nodes that satisfy the job's node-related requirements (count, names, features/constraints, GRES, topology, exclusivity, etc.). In plain terms: the nodes you asked for (or nodes with the resources you requested) aren’t available right now.

What ReqNodeNotAvail commonly covers
- Nodes already allocated: the matching nodes are currently used by other jobs (allocated), so they’re not free.
- Nodes drained/maintenance: nodes are DRAINED for admin maintenance or set DRAIN with a reason.
- Nodes down / hardware failure: nodes are DOWN (failed boot, NIC, disk, health check).
- Reservations: nodes are reserved for a reservation, so they’re not available to normal jobs.
- GRES (GPU) exhaustion: requested GPUs (count, type) are already in use or not present on idle nodes.
- Feature/constraint mismatch: job constraints (e.g., --constraint=skylake, --nodelist, CPU model, node features) don’t match any idle node.
- Memory/CPU shortage: no node has the per-node memory/CPU available to satisfy the request.
- Exclusive / topology requirements: the job needs exclusive nodes, particular multi-node topology (interconnect), or colocated resources that aren’t simultaneously free.
- Licensing or managed resource limits: required software license or managed resource (BurstBuffer, special device) is exhausted.
- Power/boot state or provisioning delays: nodes are powering up, provisioning, or in a suspended/power-saving state and not yet usable.
- Admin set states or manual hold: nodes explicitly set to DRAIN/DOWN/MAINT by admins (often with a reason string).

How it differs from similar reasons
- ReqNodeNotAvail focuses on "requested nodes or node attributes cannot be satisfied." Other reasons like Priority, Dependency, or QOS/AccountNotAllowed are unrelated to node physical availability.

How to investigate (quick checklist)
- Check the job’s pending reason: squeue -j <jobid> (reason column) or scontrol show job <jobid> for more detail.
- Check partition/node summary: sinfo -Nel (shows per-node state and features) and sinfo (partition view).
- See why nodes are marked down/drain: sinfo -R (reasons) or scontrol show node <nodename>.
- Inspect GRES/licenses: scontrol show node <node> (shows Gres/AllocTRES), and scontrol_license (for license counts).
- Check reservations: scontrol show reservation (or scontrol_reservation_show).
- If multi-node topology matters, verify available nodes satisfy -N/--ntasks-per-node/affinity and interconnect requirements.
- Ask admin/logs: if nodes are down/drained for hardware/health reasons, admins will have the node reason string and logs.

Remediation ideas
- Loosen or remove strict constraints (drop --nodelist, relax --constraint or GRES requirements).
- Request fewer resources (smaller per-node memory/CPU/GPU).
- Use a different partition or node feature.
- Wait for nodes to become free, or ask the admin to clear a defective reservation or bring nodes back from DRAIN/DOWN.
- If you believe nodes should be available, provide job ID and the output of squeue -j <jobid> and sinfo -Nel to the admin so they can diagnose.

If you want, tell me a job ID and I can show the pending reason and recommended next checks.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html)
Executing squeue sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to squeue to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html)
Print the jobs scheduled in the debug partition and in the COMPLETED state in the format with six right justified digits for the job id followed by the priority with an arbitrary fields size:
```text
$ squeue -p debug -t COMPLETED -o "%.6i %p" JOBID PRIORITY 65543 99993 65544 99992 65545 99991
```
Print the job steps in the debug partition sorted by user:
```text
$ squeue -s -p debug -S u STEPID NAME PARTITION USER TIME NODELIST 65552.1 test1 debug alice 0:23 dev[1-4] 65562.2 big_run debug bob 0:18 dev22 65550.1 param1 debug candice 1:43:21 dev[6-12]
```
Print information only about jobs 12345, 12346 and 12348:
```text
$ squeue --jobs 12345,12346,12348 JOBID PARTITION NAME USER ST TIME NODES NODELIST(REASON) 12345 debug job1 dave R 0:21 4 dev[9-12] 12346 debug job2 dave PD 0:00 8 (Resources) 12348 debug job3 ed PD 0:00 4 (Priority)
```

Use of the scontrol show job option shows two new fields related to
job array support.
The JobID is a unique identifier for the job.
The ArrayJobID is the JobID of the first element of the job
array.
The ArrayTaskID is the array index of this particular entry, either a
single number of an expression identifying the entries represented by this
job record (e.g. "5-1024").
Neither field is displayed if the job is not part of a job array.
The optional job ID specified with the scontrol show job or
scontrol show step commands can identify job array elements by
specifying ArrayJobId and ArrayTaskId with an underscore between
them (e.g. <ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskId>).

## Node Features[#nodefeatures](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the
node is powered down). When the node is powered down, the those features
become available but not active. Any feature not defined by
NodeFeaturesPlugins are always active.
Example:
```text
slurm.conf: NodeFeaturesPlugins=node_features/helpers NodeName=cloud[1-5] ... State=CLOUD Feature=f1,f2,l1 NodeName=cloud[6-10] ... State=...
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the
node is powered down). When the node is powered down, the those features
become available but not active. Any feature not defined by

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

# Slurm Workload Manager
Slurm is an open-source workload manager designed for Linux clusters of
all sizes.
It provides three key functions.
First it allocates exclusive and/or non-exclusive access to resources
(computer nodes) to users for some duration of time so they can perform work.
Second, it provides a framework for starting, executing, and monitoring work
(typically a parallel job) on a set of allocated nodes.
Finally, it arbitrates contention for resources by managing a queue of
pending work.
Slurm's design is very modular with dozens of optional plugins.
In its simplest configuration, it can be installed and configured in a
couple of minutes (see [Caos NSA and Perceus: All-in-one Cluster Software Stack](http://www.linux-mag.com/id/7239/1/)
by Jeffrey B. Layton).

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Node Features[#nodefeatures](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the
node is powered down). When the node is powered down, the those features
become available but not active. Any feature not defined by
NodeFeaturesPlugins are always active.

```text
slurm.conf: NodeFeaturesPlugins=node_features/helpers NodeName=cloud[1-5] ... State=CLOUD Feature=f1,f2,l1 NodeName=cloud[6-10] ... State=...
```

All job allocation commands ( salloc , sbatch and srun )
accept the -S or --core-spec option with a core count value
argument (e.g. "-S 1" or "--core-spec=2").
The count identifies the number of cores to be reserved for system overhead on
each allocated compute node. Note that the --core-spec option will be
ignored if AllowSpecResourcesUsage is not enabled in your slurm.conf.
Each job's core specialization count can be viewed using the scontrol ,
sview or squeue command.
Specification of a core specialization count for a job step is ignored

salloc or sbatch command).

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
Summary — what node features are
- A node feature is a short string tag assigned to a compute node (examples: gpu, v100, ssd, nvme, infiniband, ib, highmem). Features describe hardware, software, or site-specific capabilities that the scheduler can match against job requests.
- Features are visible in two forms:
  - AvailableFeatures: features the node is capable of (from slurm.conf or a NodeFeaturesPlugin).
  - ActiveFeatures: features currently active on that node (what the scheduler actually uses for matching).
- Features can be static (defined in slurm.conf) or dynamic via a NodeFeaturesPlugin/helpers (used for power-saving/cloud nodes or other runtime state changes). Features defined by a NodeFeaturesPlugin may be “available but not active” until the node is prepared for the job.

How features are used for placement
- Filtering candidate nodes: When you request a feature the scheduler only considers nodes that match that feature expression (usually ActiveFeatures). In effect a feature request narrows the pool of candidate nodes before the normal resource-selection/allocation logic runs.
- Example effect: --constraint=gpu limits placement to nodes tagged with the gpu feature. Combined constraints (see next section) further narrow choices, which can increase wait time if matching nodes are scarce.
- Dynamic activation: If a feature is defined as available but not active (e.g., powered-down cloud nodes), and a job requests that feature, Slurm can allocate and activate that node (power it on / enable the feature) at allocation time. Features not managed by NodeFeaturesPlugins are always active.
- Interaction with other resources: Features are one of several filters the scheduler uses (along with partition, QOS, TRES/GRES, CPU/memory requests, topology, affinity). A node may match a feature but still be unsuitable (insufficient CPUs, memory, or GRES), so jobs can still remain pending even when nodes with the feature exist.
- Fragmentation and scheduling behavior: Rare/unique features reduce packing flexibility. If you request many specific features you may force the scheduler to leave small unusable islands of capacity or increase job wait times. Conversely tagging similar nodes with a common feature can make placement more predictable.

Feature expressions / syntax (common usage)
- Request a single feature:
  - sbatch --constraint=gpu
- Logical combinations (supported operators): & (AND), | (OR), ^ (XOR), ! (NOT), parentheses for grouping.
  - sbatch --constraint="gpu&ssd"   (nodes that have both gpu AND ssd)
  - sbatch --constraint="v100|a100" (nodes with v100 OR a100)
  - sbatch --constraint="gpu&!v100" (gpu nodes that are NOT v100)
  - sbatch --constraint="(a100|v100)&nvme" (A100 or V100 nodes that also have nvme)
- Tip: use explicit operators and parentheses to avoid ambiguity.

Commands to inspect and change features
- See a node’s current features:
  - scontrol show node=<nodename>  → look for ActiveFeatures= and AvailableFeatures=
  - sinfo --Node or sinfo -Nel also shows features in the node list output
- Change a node’s ActiveFeatures (requires admin privileges):
  - scontrol update NodeName=<node> ActiveFeatures=<comma-separated-features>
  - scontrol update NodeName=<node> AvailableFeatures=<...>
- If your cluster uses NodeFeaturesPlugins, the plugin/helper controls activation for dynamic features (power on/off, reboot, etc.).

Practical guidance / best practices
- Prefer GRES (e.g., --gres=gpu:1 or --gres=gpu:a100:1) for requesting GPUs when you want specific GPU resources; use features to tag GPU type or other capabilities that aren’t tracked as GRES.
- Avoid over-constraining unless you truly require specific hardware/software — more constraints increase wait time and reduce backfill opportunities.
- For heterogeneous jobs (different components need different node types), use per-step constraints or heterogeneous allocation features (declare components with different constraints).
- If you’re unsure whether a feature is active or available, inspect scontrol show node and consult your cluster admins about any NodeFeaturesPlugin behavior (powering up nodes, reboot requirements).
- Admin note: use features to represent machine capabilities that are meaningful for scheduling decisions (hardware, software stacks, license availability if you map license presence to features, etc.). Use NodeFeaturesPlugins for cloud/power-managed nodes where features may be available but not active until allocation.

If you want, I can:
- Show the current features on a specific node (I’ll need the node name), or
- List all nodes and their Active/Available features (I can call sinfo / scontrol_show_node). Which would you like?

A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:

```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```

```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```

salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

Trackable RESources (TRES) are used in many QOS or Association limits
(GrpTRES* / MaxTRES*). When setting limits, one or more comma-separated
"TRES=value" assignments can be specified.
Each TRES can be one of the Slurm defaults (e.g., cpu , mem ,
node ), or any defined generic resource. You can see the list of available
resources by running sacctmgr show tres .

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.

partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
To summarize the above, the QOSs and their associated limits are
defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The
QOS will only influence job scheduling priority when the multi-factor
priority plugin is loaded and a non-zero "PriorityWeightQOS" has been
defined in the slurm.conf file. The QOS will only determine job
preemption when the "PreemptType" is defined as "preempt/qos" in the
slurm.conf file. Limits defined for a QOS (and described above) will

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html)
Executing squeue sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to squeue to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

When a job array is submitted to Slurm, only one job record is created.
Additional job records will only be created when the state of a task in the
job array changes, typically when a task is allocated resources or its state
is modified using the scontrol command.

Snippet:
## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html)
Executing squeue sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to squeue to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

the [REST API](https://slurm.schedmd.com/rest_quickstart.html), both the base state and current

### Shared File System[#shared](https://slurm.schedmd.com/hdf5_profile_user_guide.html)
The HDF5 Profile Plugin requires a common shared file system on all
the compute nodes. While a job is running, the plugin writes a
file into this file system for each step of the job on each node. When
the job ends, the merge process is launched and the node-step files
are combined into one HDF5 file for the job.
The root of the directory structure is declared in the ProfileHDF5Dir
option in the acct_gather.conf file. The directory will be created by
Slurm if it doesn't exist. Each user will have
their own directory created in the ProfileHDF5Dir which contains
the HDF5 files. All the directories and files are created by the

When a job array is submitted to Slurm, only one job record is created.
Additional job records will only be created when the state of a task in the

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html)
Executing squeue sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to squeue to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html)
Executing squeue sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to squeue to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

### Shared File System[#shared](https://slurm.schedmd.com/hdf5_profile_user_guide.html)
The HDF5 Profile Plugin requires a common shared file system on all
the compute nodes. While a job is running, the plugin writes a
file into this file system for each step of the job on each node. When
the job ends, the merge process is launched and the node-step files
are combined into one HDF5 file for the job.
The root of the directory structure is declared in the ProfileHDF5Dir

the HDF5 files. All the directories and files are created by the

## Squeue Command Use[#squeue](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
When a job array is submitted to Slurm, only one job record is created.
Additional job records will only be created when the state of a task in the
job array changes, typically when a task is allocated resources or its state
is modified using the scontrol command.
By default, the squeue command will report all of the tasks associated with
a single job record on one line and use a regular expression to indicate the
"array_task_id" values as shown below.
```text
$ squeue JOBID PARTITION NAME USER ST TIME NODES NODELIST(REASON) 1080_[5-1024] debug tmp mac PD 0:00 1 (Resources) 1080_1 debug tmp mac R 0:17 1 tux0 1080_2 debug tmp mac R 0:16 1 tux1 1080_3 debug tmp mac R 0:03 1 tux2 1080_4 debug tmp mac R 0:03 1 tux3
```
An option of "--array" or "-r" has also been added to the squeue command
to print one job array element per line as shown below.

## QOS examples[#examples](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
QOS manipulation examples. All QOS operations are done using
the sacctmgr command. The default output of 'sacctmgr show qos' is
very long given the large number of limits and options available
so it is best to use the format option which filters the display.
By default when a cluster is added to the database a default
qos named normal is created.
```text
$ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0
```
Add a new QOS

```text
$ sacctmgr add qos zebra Adding QOS(s) zebra Settings Description = QOS Name $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 0
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html)
Executing squeue sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to squeue to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/squeue.html)
Executing squeue sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run squeue or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to squeue to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

### Shared File System[#shared](https://slurm.schedmd.com/hdf5_profile_user_guide.html)
The HDF5 Profile Plugin requires a common shared file system on all
the compute nodes. While a job is running, the plugin writes a
file into this file system for each step of the job on each node. When
the job ends, the merge process is launched and the node-step files
are combined into one HDF5 file for the job.

results.prompt: Explain sinfo node states such as idle, alloc, drain, and down
results.agent_response:
Good question — sinfo reports a compact node-state code that tells you whether a node can accept new work, is servicing jobs, or needs admin attention. Brief definitions and notes:

- idle
  - Meaning: Node is up and available for scheduling; no jobs are currently allocated.
  - Effect: Jobs may be placed on this node.

- alloc (or allocated / ALLOCATED)
  - Meaning: One or more jobs have been allocated the node.
  - Effect: The node will not be used for other jobs until the allocation(s) end. You may also see ALLOCATED+ when the node is allocated and additional jobs are in the process of being started there.

- drain (DRAINING / DRAINED)
  - Meaning: Administrator-requested state to remove the node from normal scheduling.
    - DRAINING: node is marked to drain; running jobs continue to run but no new jobs will be started.
    - DRAINED (or drain): node has finished running jobs and is now not accepting new jobs.
  - Typical use: planned maintenance, retire node, or to prevent new jobs while current jobs finish.
  - Effect: Scheduler will not place new allocations on the node; running jobs are allowed to finish.

- down
  - Meaning: Node is not responding or has been marked unreachable/unusable by Slurm.
  - Effect: Node will not be allocated; requires admin intervention (investigate network/OS/munge/slurmd).
  - Note: If a non-responsive node remains, it is usually shown as DOWN (vs temporary NOT_RESPONDING suffixes).

Common additional states/flags you may encounter:
- mixed — some CPUs/GPUs on the node are allocated while others are free (common with multi-job packing).
- fail / failing — node has reported hardware/software failure or was administratively marked failed.
- reserved — node held for a reservation (you’ll see “reservation” context).
- POWER_ states (~, %, !, etc.) — node powering up/down or powered off.
- Suffix flags: a short character after the state can indicate special conditions (e.g., ~ = not responding / powered off, $ = in maintenance/reservation, @ = pending reboot, ^ = reboot issued, - = planned by backfill).

How to get more detail
- For the per-node reason field: scontrol show node=<nodename> (shows Reason, State, etc.).
- To list nodes in drain/down states or see reason summaries: sinfo -R or sinfo --states=drained (or your cluster’s sinfo_reasons view).

If you tell me a node name or paste a sinfo line you’re seeing, I can explain that specific state and any suffix flags.

A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the

place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator

The DownNodes= parameter permits you to mark certain nodes as in a
DOWN , DRAIN , FAIL , FAILING or FUTURE state
without altering the permanent configuration information listed under a
NodeName= specification.
DownNodes [#OPT_DownNodes](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) Any node name, or list of node names, from the NodeName= specifications.
Reason [#OPT_Reason_1](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) Identifies the reason for a node being in state DOWN , DRAIN ,
FAIL , FAILING or FUTURE .

A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```
`scontrol update` command actions/states of interest:

Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
reached.

- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with

## Manual Power Saving[#manual](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```
`scontrol update` command actions/states of interest:
POWER_DOWN [#POWER_DOWN](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
reached.
POWER_DOWN_ASAP [#POWER_DOWN_ASAP](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs
will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the
node.

A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```
`scontrol update` command actions/states of interest:
POWER_DOWN [#POWER_DOWN](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
reached.
POWER_DOWN_ASAP [#POWER_DOWN_ASAP](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs
will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with

- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol notify: Root, SlurmUser, or direct owner

The configuration of nodes (or machines) to be managed by Slurm is
also specified in /etc/slurm.conf .
Changes in node configuration (e.g. adding nodes, changing their
processor count, etc.) require restarting or reconfiguring all slurmctld
and slurmd daemons.
All slurmd daemons must know each node in the system to forward
messages in support of hierarchical communications.
Only the NodeName must be supplied in the configuration file.
All other node configuration information is optional.
It is advisable to establish baseline node configurations,
especially if the cluster is heterogeneous.

results.prompt: Explain what scontrol reconfigure does and when it should be used
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- scontrol reconfigure tells the Slurm controller (slurmctld) to reread its configuration and ask the Slurm daemons (slurmd, sackd, etc.) to reload config without doing a full process restart. It is the supported way to apply many configuration changes on a running cluster with minimal disruption.

What it does (technical summary)
- Sends an RPC to slurmctld asking it to reload slurm.conf and other configuration files (cgroup.conf, burst_buffer.conf, mpi.conf, plugin configs, etc.) and to propagate the new configuration to slurmd/sackd where possible.
- Daemons may re-read files or be signalled (equivalent to a SIGHUP in many cases) so settings that are reconfigurable take effect immediately.
- Reconfig behavior is controlled by ReconfigFlags (for example KeepPowerSaveSettings affects how power‑save state is preserved across a reconfigure).
- It is not a code upgrade — it does not replace running binaries or change options that were set on daemon command lines.

When to use scontrol reconfigure
- After editing slurm.conf or one of the Slurm config files when the change is supported by dynamic reconfigure and you want to avoid a full daemon restart.
- To update scheduling, partition, qos, plugin configuration, cgroup settings, burst-buffer settings, or many runtime parameters that Slurm documents as reconfigurable.
- When you want to roll out configuration changes without interrupting running jobs (for supported parameters).

When a full restart is still required (common examples / gotchas)
- Some changes cannot be applied dynamically and require restarting the daemons. Examples include (but are not limited to):
  - Changing daemon command-line options (ports, daemon-level --conf-server/--authinfo, a different Munge socket location).
  - Major node identity changes (renaming nodes / very large topology changes) — check docs; node definition changes sometimes require restarting/reconfiguring all slurmd and slurmctld.
  - Changes to binaries (upgrades) — you must restart to run new executables.
  - Certain plugin/init behaviors or configuration parameters that the docs explicitly mark as “restart required.”
- If you are unsure whether a particular parameter can be reconfigured, check the documentation for that parameter or confirm with a staged test.

Practical guidance / safe workflow
1. Check the docs for the files/parameters you changed (the slurm.conf, cgroup.conf, burst_buffer.conf pages indicate whether scontrol reconfigure applies).
2. Make the change on the controller (and on nodes if needed).
3. Optionally run scontrol show config (and inspect logs) to confirm current settings.
4. Run scontrol reconfigure on the controller to apply the change.
5. Watch slurmctld and slurmd logs for errors and verify cluster state (sinfo, squeue) after the reconfigure.
6. Schedule reconfigures during low load if possible; avoid scripting frequent/infinite scontrol calls (it’s an RPC and can overload slurmctld).

Warnings and tips
- scontrol reconfigure is an RPC to slurmctld — many repeated calls can degrade the controller. Don’t call it in tight loops.
- Some cluster features have ReconfigFlags that change how reconfigure behaves (for example preserving power-save state). Review those flags if you use power-save or other delicate features.
- When in doubt, test on a small subset or in a staging environment; if a setting really requires a restart, plan a maintenance window.

If you want, tell me which file/parameter you changed and I can check the docs for that specific setting and say whether scontrol reconfigure should be sufficient or if a restart is required.

restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")

configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling

## NOTES[#SECTION_NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurmd.html)
It may be useful to experiment with different slurmd specific
configuration parameters using a distinct configuration file
(e.g. timeouts). However, this special configuration file will not be
used by the slurmctld daemon or the Slurm programs, unless you
specifically tell each of them to use it. If you desire changing
communication ports, the location of the temporary file system, or
other parameters used by other Slurm components, change the common
configuration file, slurm.conf .
If you are using configless mode with a login node that runs a lot of client
commands, you may consider running slurmd on that machine so it can
manage a cached version of the configuration files. Otherwise, each client
command will use the DNS record to contact the controller and get the
configuration information, which could place additional load on the controller.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Executing scontrol sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from scontrol or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run scontrol or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to scontrol to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sdiag.html)
Executing sdiag sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sdiag to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

## Backfill Scheduling [#backfill](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.
Backfill scheduling will start lower priority jobs if doing so does not delay
the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.
Since the expected start time of pending jobs depends upon the expected
completion time of running jobs, reasonably accurate time limits are important
for backfill scheduling to work well.
Slurm's backfill scheduler takes into consideration every running job.
It then considers pending jobs in priority order, determining when and where
each will start, taking into consideration the possibility of

## Preemption Design and Operation [#operation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html)
The SelectType plugin will identify resources where a pending job can
begin execution. When PreemptMode is configured to CANCEL ,
SUSPEND or REQUEUE , the select plugin will also preempt running
jobs as needed to initiate the pending job. When
PreemptMode=SUSPEND,GANG the select plugin will initiate the pending
job and rely upon the gang scheduling logic to perform job suspend and resume,
as described below.
The select plugin is passed an ordered list of preemptable jobs to consider for
each pending job which is a candidate to start.
This list is sorted by either:
- QOS priority,
- Partition priority and job size (to favor preempting smaller jobs), or
- Job start time (with PreemptParameters=youngest_first ).

## Limitations [#limitations](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The backfill scheduler has limitations in how it tracks usage of CPUs and
memory in the future.
This typically requires the backfill scheduler be able to allocate each
component of a heterogeneous job on a different node in order to begin its
resource allocation, even if multiple components of the job do actually get
allocated resources on the same node.
In a federation of clusters, a heterogeneous job will execute entirely on
the cluster from which the job is submitted. The heterogeneous job will not
be eligible to migrate between clusters or to have different components of
the job execute on different clusters in the federation.

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
Slurm is designed to perform a quick and simple scheduling attempt at
events such as job submission or completion and configuration changes.
During these event-triggered scheduling events, default_queue_depth
(default is 100) number of jobs will be considered.
At less frequent intervals, defined by sched_interval , the main
scheduling loop will run, considering all jobs while still honoring the
partition_job_depth limit.
In both cases, jobs are evaluated in a strict priority order and once any
job or job array task in a partition is left pending, no other jobs in that
partition will be scheduled to avoid taking resources from the higher-priority
pending job.

The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.

the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.

in a denial of service.

that programs limit calls to sdiag to the minimum necessary for the

results.prompt: Explain sacctmgr archive, dump, and load workflows
results.agent_response:
Short overview — two related but different sacctmgr file workflows

- sacctmgr dump / load (flat-file dump/load)
  - Purpose: export and import accounting associations (Cluster, Account, User, Parent, QOS) — essentially the accounting configuration.
  - Typical use cases: copy association setup from one cluster to another, back up account/QOS/user associations, rebuild associations after DB restore.
  - Command family: sacctmgr dump ... and sacctmgr load file=<file>
  - File format: human-readable flat file where each line begins with one of the titles (Cluster, Account, User, Parent, QOS) followed by entity and colon-separated specs. Comments allowed with #. (QOS included beginning v25.05.)
  - Important notes:
    - Must be run as Slurm administrator/root.
    - When loading, records are reconciled with existing ones (load will not blindly duplicate). There is a clean option (clean=...) to remove existing cluster/associations/account/qos/user entries before import if you want to start fresh.
    - Order matters conceptually: clusters should exist before accounts, and accounts before users; sacctmgr load reconciles but you should still prepare files or use clean appropriately.
    - If no file argument to dump, a filename defaulting to <clustername>.cfg is generated.

- sacctmgr archive dump / archive load (accounting archive)
  - Purpose: export historical accounting data (jobs, events) to archive files and optionally remove (purge) those records from the slurmdbd DB; and later re-import archived accounting data.
  - Typical use cases: offload old job/event rows to archive files to shrink the active DB, transfer archived history to another slurmdbd, or temporarily purge old records.
  - Command family: sacctmgr archive dump <options> and sacctmgr archive load file=<file>
  - Key options (common/important):
    - Directory= — where to write/read archive files (must be accessible on the slurmdbd host).
    - Jobs=, Events= — which data types to include in the archive.
    - Purge-related options: archive dump will only remove rows if a corresponding purge option is specified (or configured via slurmdbd.conf PurgeJobAfter/PurgeEventAfter). Be careful: the dump+purge operation cannot be rolled back.
    - File parameter to point to a specific archive file for load.
    - Archive files from current or prior Slurm releases may be loaded.
  - Important notes:
    - The archive file must be present on the slurmdbd host (not necessarily your local shell).
    - archive load will refuse to load records that already exist in the DB (it does not silently duplicate). If you try to load the same archive twice you’ll get errors for duplicate records.
    - slurmdbd can be configured to create archive files automatically; manual sacctmgr archive dump should be used only when you understand the purge consequences.
    - archive dump is irreversible once purged — keep backups of archive files.

Suggested workflows and examples

1) Back up / move associations (dump → transfer → load)
- On source cluster (admin/root):
  - sacctmgr dump cluster=<clustername> file=/tmp/cluster-assoc.cfg
- Transfer the file to the destination slurmdbd host.
- On destination cluster (admin/root):
  - Option A — merge into existing DB:
    - sacctmgr load file=/path/cluster-assoc.cfg
  - Option B — replace cluster associations for a named cluster:
    - sacctmgr load file=/path/cluster-assoc.cfg clean=cluster
    - Or to remove accounts/qos/users as well: clean=cluster,account,qos,user
- Verify with sacctmgr list or sacctmgr show commands.

2) Archive old accounting data (archive dump), with optional purge
- Decide retention and archive directory configured or passed.
- Manual archive-only (no purge):
  - sacctmgr archive dump Directory=/archive/path Jobs=Yes Events=No
  - This writes archive files but does not remove DB rows unless purge options or slurmdbd.conf purge settings are used.
- Archive + purge (destructive):
  - sacctmgr archive dump Directory=/archive/path Jobs=Yes PurgeJobAfter=now-365days
  - Or rely on slurmdbd.conf PurgeJobAfter/PurgeEventAfter settings (check them first).
  - IMPORTANT: this can’t be rolled back after purging; ensure archive files are safely copied off the slurmdbd host before or immediately after.
- Confirm produced files in the Directory and check their timestamps/content.

3) Restore archived accounting (archive load)
- Make sure the archive file is on the slurmdbd host and accessible.
- sacctmgr archive load File=/archive/path/archivefile
- If records already exist the load will not insert duplicates and will report errors for duplicates — load is intended to restore data not to re-ingest the same history repeatedly.

Practical tips, checks, and safety
- Always run these commands as a Slurm admin/root.
- Check slurmdbd.conf for ArchiveDir, PurgeJobAfter, PurgeEventAfter before running archive dump; automated purging may already be configured.
- For any destructive purge, copy/archive the generated archive files to a safe backup location first.
- Test loads on a staging DB if you must validate import behavior (especially when migrating clusters).
- Use sacctmgr dump/load for configuration (associations) and sacctmgr archive dump/load for historical accounting records — don’t confuse the two.
- Read the sacctmgr man page or the sacctmgr archive and dump/load sections before running in production; there are additional options (Insert, clean, etc.) that affect behavior and recovery.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact sacctmgr subcommand syntax for your current Slurm docs (I can fetch the relevant man snippets), or
- prepare a safe step-by-step runbook for an archive+purge operation tailored to your slurmdbd.conf settings (I’d first read your slurmdbd.conf ArchiveDir/Purge settings).

loaded if the records already exist in the database - therefore, trying to load

directory ArchiveDir, a new archive file will be created (see ArchiveDir in the

will have duplicate records.

through archive load .

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .

$ scontrol update job=101 ... $ scontrol update job=101_1 ...

## System Administration [#administration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A new configuration parameter has been added to control the maximum
job array size: MaxArraySize . The smallest index that can be specified
by a user is zero and the maximum index is MaxArraySize minus one.
The default value of MaxArraySize is 1001.
The maximum MaxArraySize supported in Slurm is 4000001.
Be mindful about the value of MaxArraySize as job arrays offer an easy way
for users to submit large numbers of jobs very quickly.
The sched/backfill plugin has been modified to improve performance with
job arrays. Once one element of a job array is discovered to not be runnable
or impact the scheduling of pending jobs, the remaining elements of that job

sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

```text
function read_str_field(req, desc, field)
local value = ""
if desc ~= nil and desc[field] ~= nil then

end
if req ~= nil and req[field] ~= nil then
value = req[field]
end
```

Slurm accounting is mainly focused on parallel computing. For this reason it

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote

in a denial of service.

procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## NODE CONFIGURATION[#SECTION_NODE-CONFIGURATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
The configuration of nodes (or machines) to be managed by Slurm is
also specified in /etc/slurm.conf .
Changes in node configuration (e.g. adding nodes, changing their
processor count, etc.) require restarting or reconfiguring all slurmctld
and slurmd daemons.
All slurmd daemons must know each node in the system to forward
messages in support of hierarchical communications.
Only the NodeName must be supplied in the configuration file.
All other node configuration information is optional.
It is advisable to establish baseline node configurations,
especially if the cluster is heterogeneous.
Nodes which register to the system with less than the configured resources
(e.g. too little memory), will be placed in the "DOWN" state to

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

Slurm controller and assigned a Slurm job ID. The batch script is not

Snippet:
## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Snippet:
## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

also specified in /etc/slurm.conf .
Changes in node configuration (e.g. adding nodes, changing their
processor count, etc.) require restarting or reconfiguring all slurmctld
and slurmd daemons.
All slurmd daemons must know each node in the system to forward
messages in support of hierarchical communications.

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
