# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will
allow them to start and finish quick...

results.prompt: Explain QOS priority and possible preemption policy
results.agent_response:
Summary — what QOS priority is
- QOS (Quality of Service) is a database-configured entity you can assign to jobs (and also attach limits to partitions). A QOS carries a numeric priority and many limits (GrpTRES, MaxJobs, MaxWall, etc.).
- The QOS priority is one factor in Slurm’s multifactor scheduling priority. It only affects scheduling priority when the multifactor priority plugin is enabled and PriorityWeightQOS in slurm.conf is non‑zero. Higher numeric QOS.priority -> higher contribution to job priority.
- QOS assigned to a job (job QOS) is what gives a job the QOS priority and preemption behavior. A Partition QOS only supplies limits to the partition; it does not by itself change a job’s scheduling priority unless you configure Flags=OverPartQOS or the job explicitly requests that QOS.

How to set QOS priority (example)
- Create/modify with sacctmgr, e.g.:
  - sacctmgr add qos high
  - sacctmgr modify qos high set priority=100
(That numeric value becomes part of the multifactor priority calculation when enabled.)

Preemption — concepts and configurable pieces
- Preemption = allowing a higher-priority queued job to stop one or more running lower-priority jobs so the queued job can run.
- Decision points are split across:
  1. PreemptType (which attribute(s) determine who can preempt whom — common is preempt/qos so job QOS relationships are used).
  2. PreemptMode (what to do to preempted jobs: CANCEL, REQUEUE, SUSPEND, or SUSPEND,GANG).
  3. Select/placement logic and PreemptParameters (how candidate preemptable jobs are ordered for preemption, e.g., youngest_first).
  4. Partition PriorityTier and QOS configuration (which QOSs are allowed to preempt which others).

Key configuration knobs (common values)
- PreemptType=preempt/qos
  - Use the job’s QOS and QOS preemption lists to determine eligibility. QOS objects can be given an allow-list of other QOSs they may preempt (configured via sacctmgr).
- PreemptMode=...
  - CANCEL — preempted jobs are killed.
  - REQUEUE — preempted jobs are requeued (so they will run again later).
  - SUSPEND — preempted jobs are suspended; they can resume after the preemptor finishes.
  - SUSPEND,GANG — used with the gang scheduler to timeslice/schedule competing jobs on the same resources.
- PreemptParameters=youngest_first (optional)
  - Controls ordering of candidates (e.g., prefer preempting the youngest running jobs).
- PriorityWeightQOS (in slurm.conf)
  - Must be >0 for QOS.priority to count in the multifactor priority calculation.

How Slurm chooses which jobs to preempt
- The select plugin is given an ordered list of preemptable running jobs for a pending preemptor. That order can be by:
  - QOS priority,
  - partition priority + job size (to prefer preempting smaller jobs), or
  - job start time (youngest_first),
  depending on PreemptType/parameters.
- If resources need to be freed, Slurm will preempt enough jobs (following the ordering/rules) to start the pending job.

Effects, tradeoffs, and operational notes
- CANCEL — simplest but loses in-progress work.
- REQUEUE — preserves job for a later attempt, but restart may still cost time and data; job state is dropped from the node.
- SUSPEND — preserves working memory/state and lets the job resume, but suspended jobs continue to occupy memory (can cause overcommit/swap). Requires appropriate SelectType/SelectTypeParameters and system/kernel support for suspension.
- SUSPEND,GANG — enables gang scheduling/timeslicing where multiple jobs share nodes by alternating active periods; more complex to configure but can improve responsiveness.
- Backfill and whole-node reservations: the backfill scheduler reserves whole nodes, so preemption during backfill can reserve more nodes than the preemptor requested (limits on partial-node preemption).
- Resource accounting: when using suspend or timeslicing, configure SelectTypeParameter to track memory (e.g., CR_Memory or CR_Core_Memory) to avoid swapping and incorrect overcommit.
- Test your chosen mode: preemption semantics are disruptive; pick the mode that matches your policy (e.g., SLAs favor CANCEL for strict isolation, SUSPEND/GANG for interactive responsiveness, REQUEUE for checkpointable batch jobs).

Practical example snippets
- Enable QOS priority in slurm.conf:
  - PriorityWeightQOS=100
- Make QOS preempt others (job-side preemption based on QOS), set slurm.conf:
  - PreemptType=preempt/qos
  - PreemptMode=REQUEUE   (or CANCEL, SUSPEND, SUSPEND,GANG)
  - (optionally) PreemptParameters=youngest_first
- Configure which QOS can preempt which (sacctmgr):
  - sacctmgr modify qos high set preempt=normal,low
  - sacctmgr modify qos high set priority=200

When to use which preemption policy
- CANCEL: when you cannot tolerate suspended/queued state or checkpointing is not widely used and you prefer resource predictability.
- REQUEUE: when jobs can be restarted safely and you want to avoid losing job records.
- SUSPEND / SUSPEND,GANG: when preserving job execution state is needed and you have the memory/OS/kernel support and SelectType configured to handle suspended memory.

References and next steps
- Slurm docs: “Quality of Service (QOS)” and “Preemption” pages describe all options and examples (see sacctmgr examples, PreemptType, PreemptMode, PriorityWeightQOS). If you want, I can quote exact scontrol/sacctmgr commands or show example slurm.conf excerpts for the combination you plan to use (e.g., high-priority interactive QOS that suspends, or a job QOS that can cancel lower QOS jobs). Which policy do you want to design for your cluster?

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.

and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

results.prompt: Explain partition constraints and availability for gpu
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise, practical explanation of how Slurm partitions, constraints, and GPU availability interact — what they mean, how Slurm counts “available” GPUs, common ways to request GPUs, and checks you can run.

Key concepts
- Partition: a named queue of nodes (e.g., "gpu"). Jobs use --partition= to pick which set of nodes to run on. Partitions may be restricted by accounts/QOS and can contain mixed node types.
- GRES (Generic RESources): Slurm’s mechanism for GPUs. Nodes are configured with gres=gpu:<count> in slurm.conf (and optionally detailed in gres.conf). Use --gres=gpu:N (or with a type: --gres=gpu:tesla:2) to request GPUs.
- Node features/constraints: Nodes can have feature strings (e.g., "a100", "rtx6000"). Use --constraint="feature" to restrict scheduling to nodes with that feature.
- Availability = idle GPUs on idle nodes (not allocated, mixed, drained or down). Slurm schedules only against GPUs actually free on nodes.

How Slurm reports availability
- sinfo partition summary shows NODES in the format A/I/D (per-site note: A = allocated, I = idle, D = down/drain). The middle number (I) is the count of idle nodes in that partition — for GPU submissions you need idle nodes with idle GPUs.
- A node with some GPUs already allocated (or marked mixed) is not fully “available” for a new request unless enough free GPUs remain for the job’s request and Slurm is configured to allow partial-node allocations.
- squeue shows running allocations that consume GPUs; scontrol show node <node> or scontrol show hostname will show the node’s total GRES and what’s currently assigned.

How to request GPUs (common examples)
- Request N GPUs on one node:
  --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:2 --nodes=1
- Request GPUs of a specific type (when types are configured):
  --gres=gpu:a100:1
- Use constraint to require nodes with a feature:
  --constraint="a100|rtx"  (OR/AND syntax depends on cluster config)
- Control exclusivity:
  --exclusive (take whole node even if you requested fewer GPUs)
- For MIG devices, Slurm may expose them as separate GRES types; request them by the configured GRES name.

Practical checks to determine GPU availability
- sinfo -p gpu  (or sinfo -N -p gpu -o \"%20N %10Gres %8State\") — shows partition/node availability and configured GRES.
  - Look at NODES(A/I/D); I (idle) > 0 means there are idle nodes in that partition.
- squeue --partition=gpu or squeue -o to see which jobs are using GPUs and which nodes are allocated.
- scontrol show node <node> — shows Gres and AllocTRES to see how many GPUs are free on a particular node.

Important caveats and behavior
- “Idle node” vs “idle GPU”: A node can be idle (I) or partially allocated (mixed). For conditional submissions that require free GPU nodes, only nodes with sufficient idle GPUs count as eligible.
- Mixed/allocated/drained/down nodes are not treated as available for new GPU submissions unless they have free GPUs that satisfy the job and cluster config supports partial allocation.
- Scheduling and backfill: extra constraints (features) can reduce the scheduler’s ability to backfill, potentially increasing wait time.
- Sharing GPUs: some clusters allow multiple jobs/tasks on the same GPU (shared GRES) — check site policy. Otherwise expect exclusive GPU allocation per task by default.
- Configuration matters: whether GPUs are exposed as types, whether MIG instances are enumerated, and whether GPUs can be shared or oversubscribed is determined by slurm.conf/gres.conf and site policy.

Quick example sbatch header
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
(optional) #SBATCH --constraint=a100

If you want, I can check the live GPU partition state on your cluster (sinfo + squeue) or show exact node-level GPU counts. Would you like me to run that check?

results.agent_response:
Here's a concise explanation of how partition constraints and GPU availability work in Slurm, what to request, and how to interpret availability when targeting a GPU partition.

1) Partitions — what they are and how they affect GPU jobs
- A partition is a logical queue grouping nodes. Partitions can differ in allowed users, time limits, QOS, limits (MaxNodes, MaxCPUsPerNode, etc.), and which nodes they include.
- Jobs are allocated entirely within a single partition. If you submit to partition "gpu" your job will only be scheduled onto nodes that are members of that partition.
- Partition configuration can also set defaults (time limit, features) and restrict who may use it.

2) How to request GPUs and node features
- --gpus=N (modern): request N GPUs total for the job (or per task when combined with task options). Preferred when supported by your cluster.
- --gres=gpu:N (older/common): request N GPUs; can include model e.g. --gres=gpu:V100:2 or --gres=gpu:2 to request specific devices.
- --constraint="feature" or --constraint="a100|v100": require nodes with a node feature (often used to pick GPU model or NIC). Multiple constraints can be combined with boolean expressions if enabled.
- Combine CPU/memory and GPU requests carefully: e.g., sbatch --partition=gpu --gpus=2 --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=64G
- If you want GPUs per task: use --gpus-per-task or --gres per task with appropriate ntasks settings.

3) How Slurm accounts and exposes GPU availability
- GRES (Generic RESources) tracks GPUs: node Gres= shows total GPUs; AllocTRES and TRES show allocated resources. scontrol show node gives detailed AllocTRES/Gres assignments.
- sinfo shows partition/node counts and resource totals; sinfo -Nel (or sinfo --Node) can show GPUs per node and states.
- In sinfo partition summaries the node counts appear as NODES(A/I/D) meaning Allocated / Idle / Down (the middle number is idle). For a new GPU job to be considered eligible in a conditional check, the idle count must be > 0.
- A GPU is considered available only when it is not already allocated to another job (or reserved). Allocated, mixed, down, or drained nodes do not count as available for a new GPU allocation.

4) Interpreting why GPU jobs are pending or not starting
- Common pending reasons: "Resources", "Priority", "ReqNodeNotAvail", "PartitionTimeLimit", "QOSMaxSubmit" — use squeue to see the pending reason. For more detail on a specific job, scontrol show job <jobid> or scontrol show node <nodename> helps.
- If the pending reason says resources, it usually means no node in the requested partition currently has the free GPUs/memory/CPUs you requested.
- If you requested a specific GPU model or used a constraint and no idle node matches, the scheduler will wait until such a node becomes free.

5) Node states that affect GPU availability
- IDLE: node has no allocated jobs (GPUs free).
- ALLOCATED/MIXED: node has at least one allocation; may still have some free GPUs depending on configuration and sharing policy.
- DRAINED/DOWN/MAINT: node is not eligible; GPUs there are not available.
- Some clusters configure exclusive node allocation for GPUs (one job per node) — then a node is either fully free or not.

6) Best practices
- Use --gpus if available (simpler and common in recent Slurm versions); fall back to --gres if needed.
- Check sinfo -Nel and squeue before submitting to understand current idle GPU nodes and pending jobs.
- If you need a particular GPU model, use both --constraint and/or --gres with model name to avoid mismatches.
- Request GPUs per task explicitly when using multi-task parallel workloads (e.g., --gpus-per-task=1 with mpirun or srun).
- If jobs remain pending, inspect the squeue reason and scontrol show node / scontrol show job for allocations and node features.
- When using extra node attributes (extra_constraints), be aware backfill accuracy can be affected and scheduler planning may be less precise.

7) Quick example requests
- Request 2 GPUs in the gpu partition (job-level): sbatch --partition=gpu --gpus=2 myscript.sh
- Request 1 GPU per MPI task, 4 tasks: sbatch --partition=gpu --ntasks=4 --gpus-per-task=1 my_mpi_job.sh
- Request specific model: sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:A100:1 --constraint="a100" myscript.sh

If you want, I can:
- show current GPU availability in your cluster (sinfo) and which nodes are idle, or
- inspect a specific pending GPU job to explain why it’s not starting (need the job ID).
Which would you like?

results.prompt: Explain partition constraints and availability for gpu
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise explanation of how partition constraints and availability work for GPU jobs in Slurm, what affects whether GPUs are usable, and what to check when you need GPU capacity.

1) Partition basics
- A partition is a named queue: it groups nodes and sets defaults/limits (time, max nodes, allowed users/accounts/QOS, etc.). Jobs are allocated within one partition.
- Nodes can belong to more than one partition; each partition may have different policies (e.g., one partition for short GPU jobs, another for long runs).

2) How GPUs are modeled and requested
- GPUs are exposed as consumable resources (GRES) and TRES (e.g., gres/gpu or gres:gpu). Common request forms:
  - Older syntax: --gres=gpu:2 (request 2 GPUs on the same node)
  - Newer shorthand: --gpus=2 or --gpus-per-node=1 (depends on Slurm version)
- You can also request specific GPU types or features using constraints and GRES names (for example --constraint="v100" or --gres=gpu:tesla_v100:2 if configured).
- By default Slurm will try to satisfy the GPU count on a single node unless you also request multiple nodes.

3) Partition constraints that affect GPU availability
- Partition membership: only nodes assigned to the GPU partition(s) are considered for jobs submitted to that partition.
- QOS / account / user limits: QOS or account associations can limit how many GPUs a user/account can consume concurrently.
- Time/size limits: partition max-time or max-nodes can prevent large GPU jobs.
- OverSubscribe / sharing: partition OverSubscribe or node config controls whether multiple jobs can share a node’s GPUs or whether GPUs are exclusive. If oversubscribe is disabled, GPUs are exclusive.
- Reservations: active reservations for a partition or specific nodes can make GPUs temporarily unavailable.
- Node features / constraints: node features (set in slurm.conf) let you constrain nodes by hardware or software (e.g., GPU model). If you use --constraint, only nodes matching those features are considered.

4) What “available” GPUs mean in practice
- For a new GPU allocation, Slurm needs idle GPUs on nodes that match your partition and constraints.
- Idle GPUs = nodes shown as idle in sinfo (not allocated, not drained, not down, not reserved for others). Allocated, mixed, drained, or down nodes are not eligible.
- If a node is in “mixed” state it has some resources allocated and some free; whether it can serve your request depends on the requested shape and the node’s remaining free GPUs (but for conditional checks many admins treat mixed as not fully free).
- Nodes in multiple partitions: even if a node is in another partition as well, availability is determined by whether it’s idle for the partition you submit to and by partition policies.

5) How the scheduler decides
- Slurm considers partition, node features/constraints, GRES inventory (gpu counts/types), per-user/account/QOS limits, reservations, and node states when placing a job.
- Backfill works only when the scheduler can predict future allocations; complex per-node extra constraints can reduce backfill accuracy.

6) Quick checks and useful commands to inspect availability
- sinfo (partition and node summary) — shows node states (idle/alloc/drain) and partition membership. Look at the idle count; NODES(A/I/D) middle number > 0 means there are idle nodes in that partition.
- squeue — shows current jobs using GPUs (who’s holding resources).
- scontrol show node <node> — shows node’s GRES inventory and current allocations.
- scontrol show reservation — shows reservations that may block nodes.
- scontrol show config / scontrol show config | grep Gres — view GRES config.

7) Common pitfalls and troubleshooting
- You request more GPUs than any single node has (Slurm will wait unless you request multiple nodes explicitly).
- You request a specific GPU model/constraint but no idle node matches that feature.
- GPUs are held by other users/accounts or blocked by a reservation or QOS cap.
- Node is drained/down for maintenance or because of a driver/hardware issue — check sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons for reasons.
- Mismatch between gres.conf and slurm.conf (Slurm must be configured with correct GRES and types).

8) Practical submission examples
- Request 2 GPUs (same node): sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:2 ...
- Request specific model (if configured as a feature): sbatch --partition=gpu --constraint=v100 --gres=gpu:2 ...
- Request 1 GPU per node across 4 nodes (newer Slurm): sbatch --partition=gpu --nodes=4 --gpus-per-node=1 ...
(Exact flags available depend on your Slurm version; check local docs.)

If you want, I can:
- Check current GPU partition availability on your cluster (I’ll run sinfo for the gpu partition), or
- Explain the exact sbatch options supported by your Slurm version (I can consult local Slurm docs for syntax).

Which would you like me to do next?

results.prompt: Explain partition constraints and availability for cpu
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise explanation of how Slurm treats partitions, constraints, and CPU availability — what to look at and how to request CPUs.

1) Partition basics
- A partition is a named queue of nodes (e.g., "cpu", "gpu", "batch"). Use --partition or -p to target one when you sbatch/salloc/srun.
- Partition availability (AVAIL) can be up, down, drain, or inact. If a partition is not "up" your jobs won’t start there.

2) Checking availability and capacity
- sinfo gives a partition/node summary. Useful fields:
  - PARTITION / AVAIL: partition name and availability (up/down/drain/inact).
  - NODES(A/I/O/T) or a similar form: counts of Allocated / Idle / Other (e.g., drained/down/doing maintenance) / Total nodes in that partition.
  - CPUS: number of CPUs per node (for the shown node set) or, with format %C, CPU(A/I/O/T) showing allocated/idle/other/total CPUs across nodes.
- Interpretation: “idle” nodes or idle CPUs are the resources eligible for new jobs. Allocated, drained, down, or reserved nodes/CPUs are not available.

3) CPU resource accounting in Slurm
- Slurm counts CPU as a TRES (Trackable RESource) named "cpu". Allocation is based on requested cpus-per-task, ntasks, tasks-per-node, and nodes.
  - Example: sbatch --partition=cpu --cpus-per-task=4 --ntasks=8 requests 8 tasks × 4 cpus/task = 32 cpu TRES.
- Key options when requesting CPU resources:
  - --cpus-per-task (or -c): threads/cores to give each task (affects CPU TRES).
  - --ntasks (or -n): number of tasks (MPI ranks).
  - --nodes: number of distinct nodes to allocate.
  - --ntasks-per-node: tasks on each node.
  - --exclusive: allocate whole node(s), preventing sharing.
- If you want a whole node, use --nodes=1 --exclusive (or request enough cpus to exceed node capacity under a restrictive policy).

4) Constraints (node selection filters)
- --constraint lets you request node features defined in slurm.conf (Feature=...) or via helpers/extra. Constraints filter which nodes can be allocated.
- Boolean operators accepted (site may differ slightly): & and comma (,) act as AND, | acts as OR. Parentheses can group expressions when supported.
  - Examples:
    - --constraint="skylake"  (nodes with feature skylake)
    - --constraint="skylake&avx512" or --constraint="skylake,avx512" (nodes must have both)
    - --constraint="skylake|haswell" (either feature)
- There is also --extra (SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints must be enabled) for JSON-style extra attributes and richer comparisons.

5) Practical checks before submitting
- Use sinfo -s or sinfo -o to see partition/node counts and CPUs:
  - sinfo -s shows partition with NODES(A/I/O/T) and quick state.
  - sinfo -o "%P %a %D %C" shows partition, availability, node count, and CPU(A/I/O/T).
- Use squeue to see current jobs consuming CPUs (per-user/partition filters).
- If you need a conditional action (e.g., submit only if idle nodes exist), first inspect sinfo (or sinfo + squeue) to confirm idle nodes/CPUs.

6) Scheduling and access caveats
- QOS, accounts, reservations, and limits can make a partition appear usable but still block your job (job held or backfilled by policy). If a partition is up and shows idle CPUs, your job still may be pending because of QOS/account limits or a reservation.
- Some systems use select/cons_tres for TRES-based allocation; that controls how CPUs/GRES are assigned.

7) Quick example requests
- Single multi-threaded task needing 8 CPU cores on cpu partition:
  sbatch --partition=cpu --cpus-per-task=8 --ntasks=1 myscript.sh
- MPI job with 16 ranks, 2 CPUs per rank:
  sbatch -p cpu --ntasks=16 --cpus-per-task=2 my_mpi_job.sh
- Force nodes with feature "highmem":
  sbatch -p cpu --constraint=highmem --cpus-per-task=4 myjob.sh

If you want, I can show the current "cpu" partition availability and CPU counts on your cluster (sinfo) or list running jobs using CPU resources (squeue). Which would you like me to check?

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Dynamic Node Communications [#communications](https://slurm.schedmd.com/dynamic_nodes.html)
For regular, non-dynamically created nodes, Slurm knows how to communicate with
nodes by reading in the slurm.conf. This is why it is important for a
non-dynamic setup that the slurm.conf is synchronized across the cluster. For
dynamically created nodes, The controller automatically grabs the node's
NodeAddr and NodeHostname for dynamic slurmd registrations. The
controller then passes the node addresses to the clients so that they
communicate, and even fanout, to other nodes.

results.prompt: Explain partition constraints and availability for debug
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise explanation of what “partition constraints” and “availability” mean for the debug partition, how they affect job scheduling, and the quick checks you can run.

What a partition (e.g., "debug") can constrain
- Timelimit (TIMELIMIT): max walltime a job may request in that partition (debug often very short, e.g., 30m). Jobs requesting longer than this will be refused or placed in a different partition.
- Job size limits: max/min nodes, tasks, CPUs or memory per job that the partition allows.
- Access controls: which accounts, users, groups, or QOS can submit to the partition (AllowAccounts/AllowGroups/Default/RootOnly).
- Node membership: which nodes are in the partition (Nodes or NodeSet). Nodes may be shared across partitions but with different limits.
- Features/GRES expectations: the partition may be intended for nodes with specific features (e.g., gpu, fastnet). Jobs that use --constraint or --gres must match available node attributes.
- QOS/priority limits: a partition may be associated with particular QOS that impose MaxJobs, MaxWall, or other limits taking effect before user/account limits.
- Reservation and maintenance flags: reservations may reserve debug nodes for a time window; nodes can be drained/down for maintenance and removed from availability.

What “availability” (as shown by sinfo) means and how to read it
- Use sinfo to inspect partition state:
  - sinfo -s or sinfo --partition=debug --long
- Key columns you’ll see:
  - AVAIL / State: whether the partition is administratively up/down and usable.
  - TIMELIMIT: the partition walltime limit.
  - NODES(A/I/O/T) or NODES column: summary of nodes and states. NODES(A/I/O/T) typically shown as Allocated/Idle/Other/Total.
    - Allocated (A): nodes currently running jobs for that partition.
    - Idle (I): nodes free for immediate allocation — these are the nodes eligible for new jobs.
    - Other (O): nodes in other states (drain, down, reserved, etc.).
    - Total (T): total nodes assigned to the partition.
- Example sinfo summary and interpretation:
  - debug up 30:00 0/8/0/8 dev[0-7]
    - TIMELIMIT 30:00, 8 total nodes, 0 allocated, 8 idle → 8 nodes available for new jobs.
  - debug up 30:00 0/0/8/8 dev[0-7]
    - 0 idle, 8 in "other" (likely drained/down/reserved) → no nodes currently available to schedule jobs.

Common reasons debug jobs don’t start (check in this order)
1. Walltime or size exceeds partition limits (request shorter time or smaller node count).
2. Job’s constraints/features do not match any idle node (job used --constraint, --gres, or requested a feature not present).
3. No idle nodes (allocated or reserved) — check NODES(A/I/O/T) in sinfo.
4. Reservation holds the nodes (check scontrol show reservation / squeue --reservation=<name>).
5. User/account/QoS limits or association caps prevent scheduling (check sacctmgr or QOS).
6. Nodes are in DRAIN/DOWN for maintenance (sinfo --states=drain,down or sinfo -N).
7. Pending reasons from the queue (use squeue -p debug to see pending reason strings; for a single job use scontrol show job <jobid> to get the detailed reason).

Quick commands to inspect the debug partition and a job
- Partition/node status:
  - sinfo -s                  # short summary for all partitions
  - sinfo --partition=debug --long
  - sinfo -N --partition=debug   # one line per node
  - sinfo --states=drained,down --partition=debug
- Queue and pending reasons:
  - squeue -p debug
  - squeue -p debug -o "%.18i %.9P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10l %.6D %R"  # custom format including REASON
  - scontrol show job <jobid>   # detailed job info & pending reason
- Reservations and access:
  - scontrol show reservation
  - scontrol show partition debug   # if available on your system for partition details
  - sacctmgr list associations or sacctmgr show user <user>  # for account / association limits

Practical tips
- Debug partitions are typically configured to favor very short, small runs: ask for the lowest necessary walltime and node count.
- If you need longer or larger runs, submit to a non-debug partition.
- If your job requests GPUs or specific features, run sinfo -N -o "%N %f %G" (or equivalent) to confirm nodes in debug actually have that feature/GRES.
- When in doubt, check squeue for the job’s pending reason; it’s usually explicit (Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOSMaxJobs, etc.).

If you want, I can:
- Check the current cluster’s debug partition status now (sinfo) and show how many idle nodes are available; or
- Inspect a specific job in the debug partition (provide job ID) and report why it’s pending.

Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order

flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None

- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS

results.prompt: Explain how license availability affects a future sbatch submission
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- When you request a software license in sbatch, Slurm treats that license like a shared cluster resource. If the requested license count isn't available at scheduling time, your job will remain PENDING until enough licenses are free — it will not start even if compute nodes are idle.
- Licenses are allocated at job start and released when the job (or job step) ends.

How you request a license
- Command-line: sbatch -L license_name:count script.sh
  - Example: sbatch -L ansys:2 myjob.sh
- Or request via TRES: --tres-per-task=license/<name>=N (requires that the license tres is listed in AccountingStorageTRES in slurm.conf).

Where licenses are configured
- Local licenses: configured in slurm.conf (Licenses=...). View with scontrol show lic.
- Remote/dynamic licenses: configured in the accounting DB via sacctmgr and can be periodically updated (LastConsumed/LastDeficit) so Slurm knows how many are effectively available.

How availability affects scheduling (key points)
- Scheduling requirement: Both compute resources (nodes/CPUs/GPUs) AND the requested license(s) must be available for a job to be started. If either is missing, the job stays PENDING.
- Pending reasons: A job waiting for licenses will remain PD and the squeue pending-reason will reflect resource/license constraints (check squeue for the specific reason).
- If you ask for more licenses than exist (or more than the cluster can ever provide), the job will never be satisfied and will remain pending indefinitely unless changed.
- Remote license deficits and reservations: sacctmgr/remote updates can set aside licenses (Reserved/LastDeficit/LastConsumed). Even if Total looks large, Reserved/LastDeficit can reduce Free, causing jobs to wait.

How to inspect and troubleshoot
- Check available counts: scontrol show lic (or scontrol show lic LicenseName=<name>)
  - Output has Total, Used, Free, Reserved, Remote, LastConsumed/LastDeficit for remote licenses.
- See why a specific job is pending: squeue (shows PD and a reason). For more detail, scontrol show job <jobid>.
- If jobs are stuck waiting for licenses while nodes are free, check the license counts (scontrol show lic) and talk to admins to sync with the license server (dynamic license updates via sacctmgr may be needed).

Best practices
- Request only the number of licenses actually needed.
- Prefer TRES-based license accounting if you want per-task granularity — ensure AccountingStorageTRES is configured.
- If using remote license servers, run a periodic sync/update so LastConsumed/LastDeficit reflect reality.
- If a workflow needs guaranteed access, coordinate via reservations or talk to admins to carve out license capacity.

If you want, I can show the current license counts on your cluster (scontrol show lic) or explain the exact pending reason for a specific pending job — which would require running scontrol/squeue.

results.prompt: Explain how license availability affects a future sbatch submission
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Slurm treats software licenses as cluster-wide consumable resources (TRES). If a job requests a license (sbatch -L name:N or via --tres-per-task), the scheduler will not start the job until that many licenses are available. If they are not available, the job stays PENDING.

What happens when you sbatch with a license request
- Request syntax:
  - sbatch -L <license_name>:<count> script.sh
  - or request it via a TRES (e.g., --tres-per-task=license/<name>=<count>) if your cluster uses AccountingStorageTRES.
- Scheduling effect:
  - The requested license is treated like any other scarce resource (CPUs, GPUs). The job will remain pending until Free >= requested count.
  - Slurm shows license totals as Total, Used, Free (scontrol show lic).
  - While pending, the job blocks other jobs that also request the same license if not enough free licenses remain.
- Visibility:
  - Pending reason columns in squeue may indicate license/resource shortage (you may see a resources/license-related pending reason).
  - Use scontrol show lic or sacctmgr show resource to inspect counts for a specific license (example license name: ansys).
- Reservation/consumption timing:
  - Slurm reserves/allocates license counts as part of scheduling. The cluster reports Used/Free so administrators and the scheduler know how many are reserved/consumed. (Administrators can configure dynamic/remote license updates; see next point.)
- Dynamic/remote licenses:
  - If your cluster integrates with an external license server, Slurm can be updated with the external usage (LastConsumed/LastDeficit), and Slurm will account for those values when deciding availability. Administrators update these with sacctmgr scripts or tools.

Operational notes / pitfalls
- If you request more licenses than exist (or than are currently free), the job will remain pending until licenses are freed or admin updates counts.
- If your site uses --tres-per-task for licenses, the license must be present in AccountingStorageTRES and sacctmgr-managed resources.
- Administrators can check and debug license contention with scontrol show lic, sacctmgr show resource, and by reading squeue pending reasons.

Example
- Submit: sbatch -L ansys:2 job.sh
- Inspect: scontrol show lic  (shows LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=2 Free=98)
- If Free < 2, the job will stay PENDING until at least 2 become free.

If you want, I can show the current license counts on your cluster (scontrol show lic / functions.scontrol_license). Would you like me to check?

results.agent_response:
Short answer: Slurm treats software licenses as cluster-wide allocatable resources. If your sbatch requests a license that isn’t free at schedule time, the job will stay PENDING until enough of that license becomes available.

Details — what happens and what to check
- How to request: use sbatch -L name:count (also written --licenses=name:count), or request a license via TRES (e.g., --tres-per-task=license/foo) if the license is configured in AccountingStorageTRES.

- Remote/dynamic licenses: if admins sync LastConsumed (from an external license server) into the DB, Slurm may account for deficits (LastDeficit) and withhold allocations until the deficit is resolved — this can make jobs stay pending even when the configured Total looks sufficient.
- Failure modes to watch for: requesting more licenses than Total (job will not start until changed); requesting via --tres-per-task without the AccountingStorageTRES mapping (the request may be ignored or misrouted).
- Useful commands (ask your admin or run if you have permissions): scontrol show lic (shows Total/Used/Free), sacctmgr show resource (for remote license config), and squeue / scontrol show job to see pending reason and job license request details.

results.prompt: Explain how license availability affects a future sbatch submission
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- If a job requests a software license when you run sbatch (for example sbatch -L ansys:2), the scheduler treats that license as a cluster resource (a TRES). The job may be accepted but will remain PENDING until the requested license count is available. Slurm will not start the job unless it can allocate the requested licenses.

What happens end-to-end
1. Admin config
   - Licenses are configured either in slurm.conf (local licenses) or in the accounting DB via sacctmgr (remote/dynamic licenses). Each license has a Total count; Slurm tracks Used and Free counts.
   - If you use license requests via TRES (--tres-per-task or --tres), the license name must also appear in AccountingStorageTRES so usage is recorded.

2. How users request licenses
   - Short form: sbatch -L license_name:count script.sh
   - TRES form: sbatch --tres-per-task=license/license_name=count (or --tres=...) depending on your site
   - Either method declares the job’s license needs to the scheduler.

3. Scheduling and start-time behavior
   - The scheduler checks license availability when considering a job for allocation. If the Free count for that license is less than the job’s request, the job stays PENDING.
   - Jobs do not consume license counts until they are allocated/started; Used counts update when the allocation is made (you can see this with scontrol show lic).
   - Backfill/priority still respects license counts: a lower-priority job can only start if enough licenses are free at the time it would start.

4. Local vs remote/dynamic licenses
   - Local licenses (configured in slurm.conf) are static counts maintained by slurmctld.
   - Remote/dynamic licenses can be updated from an external license server (via sacctmgr updates). Slurm uses LastConsumed/LastDeficit info to avoid oversubscription; administrators can push dynamic counts into Slurm so scheduling reflects real license availability.

5. Effects on users and common outcomes
   - Submission is usually accepted; the job becomes PENDING with a reason related to resources/licenses until licenses free up.
   - Jobs do not fail just because licenses are unavailable at submit time; they wait.
   - If you over-request licenses (request more than Total), the job will never start until the request or the license counts are changed.

How to check and troubleshoot
- Check configured and current counts: scontrol show lic  (or scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys)
- See why a job is pending: squeue -j <jobid> (look at the REASON column) and for more detail scontrol show job <jobid>
- Admins can inspect/adjust license resources with sacctmgr (add/update resource) and push dynamic counts if integrated with a license server.

Example
- Cluster has Licenses=ansys:10, 8 are used → Free=2.
- sbatch -L ansys:3 script.sh → job accepted but stays PENDING until at least 3 licenses are free (e.g., when other jobs release them).

If you want, I can show current license counts on this cluster (scontrol show lic) or explain how to convert an sbatch -L request into a --tres request for your site.

results.prompt: Explain how license availability affects a future sbatch submission
results.agent_response:
Summary — how licenses affect an sbatch submission

- What a "license" is in Slurm
  - A license in Slurm is a cluster-wide shared resource (not tied to a specific node). Examples: license=ansys, fluent, etc.
  - Licenses are configured either in slurm.conf (local licenses) or in the SlurmDB (remote/dynamic licenses).

- How you request licenses when submitting
  - sbatch -L <name>:<count> (short) or sbatch --licenses=<name>:<count>.
    Example: sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh
  - Alternatively you can request a license as a TRES: --tres-per-task=license/ansys=1 (requires the license be listed in AccountingStorageTRES).

- Scheduling behavior
  - The scheduler treats licenses like any other scarce shared resource. A job that requests N of a license will not be eligible to start until at least N free licenses exist.
  - If the requested license count is not available at submit/schedule time, the job remains PENDING and will be released when enough licenses become free.
  - When a job is allocated, Slurm decrements the license “Free” count and increments “Used”; when the job completes the count is returned.

- Dynamic and remote license effects
  - For remote/dynamic licenses, administrators can update the LastConsumed value (e.g., via sacctmgr) from an external license server. Slurm uses LastConsumed and computes LastDeficit to avoid overcommitting licenses that appear missing.
  - If LastDeficit indicates licenses are missing, the scheduler will reserve (set aside) those licenses and may keep jobs pending even if the total configured count looks sufficient.

- Practical consequences you should expect
  - If you submit with -L and licenses are currently in use, your job will queue and wait for licenses rather than fail.
  - If you forget to request a license that your job’s software actually needs, the job may start but later fail when the software cannot check out a license (that check is external to Slurm). Requesting the license via Slurm is the way to make scheduling respect that dependency.
  - Use --tres-per-task when you want per-task accounting of licenses; ensure the license TRES is configured in AccountingStorageTRES.

- How to check license status (admin/user commands)
  - scontrol show lic (or the scontrol_license view) shows LicenseName, Total, Used, Free.
  - Administrators use sacctmgr to add/update resources and to adjust LastConsumed for dynamic setups.

If you want, I can show the current license list/free counts on your cluster (scontrol show lic). Would you like me to check that?

results.prompt: Explain safe steps for maintenance reservations without changing state
results.agent_response:
Below are concise, safe, read-only steps and best practices for planning and using Slurm maintenance reservations while avoiding node state changes (drain/down) until you are explicitly ready to modify nodes.

1) Plan the window and scope
- Choose nodes (or partitions) and a maintenance window (start time + duration). Prefer low-usage windows.
- Decide whether you need to take nodes completely offline at the maintenance start (this would be a state change later) or just prevent new long-running jobs from starting.

2) Verify current and near-future usage (read-only checks you should run)
- Check current queue and running jobs: squeue (filter by nodes/partition or user).

- Confirm no critical jobs are running on the targets (sacct / job owners).

results.prompt: Explain safe steps for maintenance reservations without changing state
results.agent_response:
Below are safe, read-only steps and checks you can follow to plan and create maintenance reservations without changing cluster state. I include the recommended Slurm queries to inspect current state, guidance for choosing parameters/flags, and a short verification & rollback checklist. Do these preparatory reads first; only create or modify reservations when you’re ready and have operator approval.

1) Define the maintenance window and scope
- Choose concrete StartTime (ISO or relative like "now+2hours") and Duration.
- Decide nodes vs. partition vs. node count. Prefer a specific node list when taking nodes fully offline for maintenance.
- Decide access controls (Users, Accounts, QOS) and whether the reservation should be visible/attractive to jobs (magnetic) or marked for accounting as maintenance (flags=maint).

2) Inspect cluster state (read-only checks to run)
- Inventory partitions/nodes and per-node availability:
  - sinfo (optionally sinfo -N -l) — find idle vs allocated nodes, per-partition context.
  - sinfo_reasons — list nodes already DRAIN/ DOWN and reasons.
  - sinfo_node (partition=..., state=...) if you need node-level detail.
- Check current and pending jobs that could overlap your window:
  - squeue (filter by partition or node) — show running and pending jobs and TIME limits.
  - squeue --reservation=<name> (after a reservation exists) to see reservation queue entries.
- Find long-running or critical jobs historically:
  - sacct (e.g., sacct -S now-30days -u <user>) — identify recurring long jobs or jobs that may run into your window.
- Check existing reservations and avoid conflicts:
  - scontrol show reservation (or scontrol_reservation_show) — list current/future reservations.
- Check scheduler/backfill/fairshare effects that might impact start:
  - sdiag and sprio or sshare (if you need to understand backfill behavior and priorities).

3) Choose safe reservation flags and parameters
- flags=maint — marks it as a maintenance reservation for accounting and policy clarity.
- Avoid flags that forcibly terminate running jobs unless absolutely necessary:
  - flags=ignore_jobs will allow creation even if jobs are running, but you must manually handle or cancel those jobs later — use with caution.
  - flags=replace can cause Slurm to replace allocated nodes; use only if you understand the replacement behavior and consequences.
- For minimal disruption, prefer:
  - StartTime in the near future (gives users notice) and Duration just long enough plus buffer.
  - Not using ignore_jobs or replace unless you have a plan to cancel or migrate running jobs.
  - Optionally restrict Users/Accounts so only maintenance staff can use it.

4) Test with a small/dry approach (no state change)
- Plan a small test reservation on one non-critical node with StartTime far enough in future; verify with scontrol show reservation to see how it will be applied. There’s no true “dry-run” flag in Slurm, so creating a future reservation is the safe way to preview behavior without immediate effect.
- Verify that jobs that would start within your window are either blocked or will finish before StartTime by checking squeue elapsed/time limits and expected end times.

5) Verification right before the window (read-only)
- Re-run sinfo and squeue shortly before the StartTime to confirm nothing changed.
- Check scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name> to confirm nodes, StartTime, Duration, and flags are correct.
- Use squeue --starttime or examine TIME left on running jobs to ensure none will overrun — if uncertain, communicate or coordinate with users.

6) Communication and coordination
- Notify affected users well in advance with the window and the exact nodes/partitions that will be impacted.
- Publish contact/rollback plan and how users can checkpoint or migrate jobs.
- Consider creating a short “maintenance reservation” announcement with ReservationName and StartTime so users can plan.

7) Execution considerations (mutating actions — operator steps, do not run yourself here)
- Typical sequence after reservation becomes active:
  - Optionally drain nodes (scontrol_node drain) if you must prevent new jobs from starting on those nodes.
  - Cancel or requeue jobs that will interfere (scancel / scontrol requeue) only after notification and approval.
  - Perform maintenance, then resume nodes (scontrol_node resume) and/or delete reservation (scontrol delete reservation <name>).
- Note: these are state-changing operations; follow your site’s change-control and call the operator / run them from an authorized admin environment.

8) Rollback and clean-up plan (prepare before making changes)
- How to abort: scontrol delete reservation ReservationName=<name>.
- How to restore service: clear node drains/resumes, verify with sinfo and a small smoke test, and notify users.
- Keep logs of actions and times for post-maintenance accounting.

9) Quick example (informational only — does not execute)
- Example create command you would run when ready:
  - scontrol create reservation ReservationName=maint_win1 StartTime=2026-05-05T02:00:00 Duration=02:00 Nodes=node[05-08] Flags=maint Users=maintteam
- Verify:
  - scontrol show reservation ReservationName=maint_win1
  - squeue --reservation=maint_win1

Safety checklist before creating/activating
- [ ] Confirm chosen nodes are healthy (sinfo, sinfo_reasons).
- [ ] Confirm no critical jobs will be interrupted (squeue + sacct history).
- [ ] Notify users and get approvals.
- [ ] Pick conservative StartTime and Duration with buffer.
- [ ] Avoid aggressive flags (ignore_jobs/replace) unless planned.
- [ ] Have rollback steps and contacts ready.

If you want, I can:
- run the read-only checks for the cluster (sinfo, squeue, scontrol_reservation_show, sacct) and provide the exact current state and a recommended reservation window and node list; or
- prepare an exact scontrol create reservation command using concrete StartTime/Duration/Nodes you provide.

Which of those would you like me to do next?

results.agent_response:
Below are concise, safe steps and best practices for creating and using maintenance reservations while avoiding unintended state changes (cancels, drains, or job replacement). This is a prescriptive checklist you can follow — none of these steps change cluster state by themselves.

1) Plan the window and scope
- Decide exact nodes (or partitions), start time, and duration. Prefer reserving whole nodes for maintenance (simpler) rather than per-core reservations.
- Choose a reservation name that encodes purpose/date (e.g., maint-kernel-2026-05-10).

2) Inventory current state (read-only checks)
- Check node/partition availability: sinfo (or sinfo --Node) to list nodes and partitions.
- Check running and queued jobs on target nodes: squeue -w nodeX,nodeY (or squeue --nodes=...).
- Check existing reservations: scontrol show reservation (or scontrol_reservation_show).
- Use sacct if you need historical job/run patterns to pick low-impact times.

3) Create a reservation that does NOT force immediate disruption
- Create an advanced reservation scheduled in the future (StartTime=...) and set Duration=... so it only becomes active when you plan to maintain.
- Use Flags=MAINT to mark it as a maintenance reservation (good for accounting and planning).
- Critically: do NOT set Flags=REPLACE or Flags=IGNORE_JOBS unless you explicitly want running jobs to be replaced or ignored. Leaving those out ensures Slurm will not forcibly evict running allocations.
- Example form (adapt to your cluster’s time format and node list):
  scontrol create reservation ReservationName=maint-2026-05-10 StartTime=2026-05-10T01:00:00 Duration=120 Nodes=node[01-04] Flags=MAINT Description="kernel update"
  (This is an example—adjust fields to your environment.)

4) Use floating reservations if you want a sliding maintenance window without immediate node state changes
- TIME_FLOAT reservations can be used to create a floating maintenance window relative to now (they are treated differently in scheduling and prevent new long-running jobs).
- This is useful when you want the reservation to “float” but still block starts that would overlap the intended maintenance.

5) How reservations affect job starts (important safety behavior)
- When a reservation exists for a future period, Slurm will generally prevent new jobs from starting if they cannot complete before the reservation’s start time. This reduces the chance you’ll need to cancel running jobs.
- Creating a MAINT reservation does not, by itself, cancel or requeue currently running jobs unless you used IGNORE_JOBS or REPLACE.

6) Notify users and monitor as the window approaches
- Announce the planned maintenance window and affected nodes/users well in advance.
- Monitor squeue for jobs that will still be running as the start time approaches; follow local policy (wait, ask users to checkpoint, or cancel individual jobs).
- If you must remove running jobs, do so explicitly and with communication (scancel), do not rely on reservation flags that implicitly evict jobs unless you intended that behavior.

7) When ready to start maintenance (this is when you change state)
- If you need nodes pulled out of service immediately, change node state (for example, put nodes into DRAIN with a reason) and then stop or requeue running jobs as required. Note: these are explicit state changes and should be done only when ready.
- After maintenance, clear DRAIN and/or delete the reservation:
  scontrol delete reservation ReservationName=...

8) Clean up and accounting
- Remove the reservation when maintenance is complete (scontrol delete reservation=...).
- Confirm nodes returned to normal with sinfo and check for any blocked jobs.
- Document the maintenance (start/end times) — MAINT reservations are recorded in reports as PlannedDown.

Safety checklist (quick)
- Reserve in the future; do not set IGNORE_JOBS or REPLACE unless you understand and want eviction.
- Verify squeue for overlapping jobs before the reservation starts.
- Communicate to users and give them time to finish or checkpoint.
- Use MAINT flag for accounting; use TIME_FLOAT if you want a floating window.
- Delete reservation and clear drains after work is done.

References / notes
- MAINT reservations are intended for system maintenance and are reported as maintenance/planned down in accounting.
- Flags that will forcibly affect running jobs: IGNORE_JOBS (creates reservation even if jobs running), REPLACE (replace allocated nodes). Use these only with explicit intent.

If you want, I can:
- Show current reservations and any jobs on a specific node set (read-only checks), or
- Draft an example scontrol command for your exact nodes/start time/duration. Which nodes/start time should I use?

## Maintenance Reservations [#maint](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
For ease of system maintenance, you can create a reservation with the
MAINT flag that overlaps existing reservations. This is equivalent to the
OVERLAP flag but with the following distinctions:
- Reserved nodes will be shown in maint state
- Reserved nodes will not be available as replacements in other reservations
- Cluster usage reports will show this time as PlannedDown

for some nodes daily from noon until 1PM. If there is a maintenance reservation
for all nodes starting at 12:30PM, the only jobs they may start in their
reservation would have to be completed by 12:30PM, when the maintenance
reservation begins.

Good — below are safe, read-only / non-mutating steps and best practices for creating maintenance reservations in Slurm (so you can schedule maintenance without immediately changing node state). I include the key flags/behaviors you should know and example commands you can run when ready.

High-level approach
- Inspect cluster state and job activity to pick nodes and a safe time window.
- Create an advanced reservation (StartTime in the future or TIME_FLOAT) with the MAINT flag so it’s treated as maintenance and does not immediately evict running jobs.
- Verify the reservation and communicate it to users.
- When the window arrives, perform the node-state changes (drain/down) as a separate, explicit step.

Recommended safe checklist (read-only until you decide to act)
1) Identify candidate nodes and check current usage
- Use sinfo and sinfo_reasons to view partition/node counts and any nodes already down/drained.
- Use squeue to see running/pending jobs and which nodes they occupy; check job end times or runtimes to choose a window when nodes will be free.

2) Pick a start time and duration that gives running jobs time to finish
- Prefer a future StartTime with a buffer (e.g., several hours) so you don’t need to cancel running work.
- If you want the reservation to “float” a fixed time into the future (so it always stays a set period ahead), use the TIME_FLOAT flag with StartTime=now and a Duration.

3) Create a reservation (non-destructive example)
- Key flags:
  - Flags=MAINT marks it as maintenance for accounting/behavior.
  - TIME_FLOAT makes the reservation float relative to now (optional).
  - Users= / Account= / QOS= can limit who may use the reservation.
  - REPLACE / IGNORE_JOBS / OVERLAP have strong effects — avoid IGNORE_JOBS unless you intend to forcibly cancel running jobs.
- Example (safe: schedules a future maint reservation; does not change node state now):
  scontrol create reservation ReservationName=maint_window StartTime=2026-05-10T02:00:00 Duration=120 Nodes=node[01-04] Flags=MAINT Users=admin
- Example (TIME_FLOAT floating reservation that won’t immediately block running jobs):
  scontrol create reservation ReservationName=float_maint StartTime=now Duration=120 Nodes=node[05-06] Flags=MAINT,TIME_FLOAT Users=admin

Notes on dangerous flags
- IGNORE_JOBS: if used, allows creating the reservation even when nodes have running jobs and implies you will cancel or otherwise handle them. Do not use unless you intend to mutate running jobs.
- REPLACE: can cause Slurm to move reservation allocations; use only with full understanding of behavior.
- OVERLAP vs MAINT: MAINT is specialized for maintenance and will show the reserved nodes in maint state while the reservation is active.

4) Verify the reservation (read-only)
- scontrol show reservation ReservationName=maint_window
- squeue --reservation=maint_window
These let you inspect reservation details and any jobs bound to it before doing node actions.

5) Communicate and prepare
- Notify affected users, post the reservation name, start time, duration, and impacted nodes.
- Consider creating a small test reservation on a single node first.

6) When ready to take nodes out of service (this is a separate, state-changing step)
- At the reservation start time you can change node state (scontrol update NodeName=... State=DRAIN Reason="maintenance").
- Only perform node drains/down when you have confirmed no important running jobs remain or you have permission to cancel them.

Other best practices
- Use short durations and do repeated short reservations for recurring maintenance rather than long disruptive windows.
- Restrict reservation usage to admin accounts/users when the reservation is for exclusive maintenance.
- Test the flow on a small set of nodes first.
- Clean up afterwards with scontrol delete reservation ReservationName=... if you want to remove the reservation.

Quick summary of commands you’ll use (read-only verification + reservation creation)
- Inspect: sinfo; sinfo -R; squeue; squeue --start; sacct (history)
- Create reservation: scontrol create reservation ReservationName=... StartTime=... Duration=... Nodes=... Flags=MAINT[,TIME_FLOAT] Users=...
- Verify: scontrol show reservation ReservationName=... ; squeue --reservation=ReservationName
- Delete: scontrol delete reservation ReservationName=...

results.prompt: Explain safe steps for maintenance reservations without changing state
results.agent_response:
Below are safe, non‑mutating steps (planning, validation, and examples) you can follow when preparing maintenance reservations. All examples are read‑only checks or command templates — do not run any scontrol create/drain commands unless you intend to change cluster state.

1) Inventory current cluster state and reservations
- Check node/partition availability and states (allocated/idle/drain/down):
  - sinfo  (or sinfo -Nel for per‑node rows)
  - sinfo_node --partition=<partition> --state=ALL
  What to look for: idle node counts in the partition you plan to use, nodes already DRAIN/MAINT/DOWN.
- List existing reservations (to avoid collisions):
  - scontrol_reservation_show
  What to look for: overlapping reservation names/times, partitions/nodes already reserved.

2) Identify jobs that would be affected
- See running and pending jobs (global or by partition/node/user):
  - squeue --states=RUNNING,PENDING --format="%.18i %.20P %.20j %.8u %.8T %.10M %.20R %.20N"
  - squeue --partition=<partition> or squeue --nodelist=<node>
  What to look for: running jobs on target nodes, pending jobs bound to a reservation or partition, pending reasons.
- For any specific running job you might impact, get details:
  - sstat --jobid=<jobid> (running job resource usage)
  - scontrol_show entity=job id=<jobid> (detailed job limits, start time, steps)
- Check historical job durations to pick a safe StartTime/Duration:
  - sacct --user=<user> --starttime=now-30days --format=JobID,JobName,Elapsed,MaxRSS
  What to look for: common job durations so you choose a StartTime that lets most running jobs finish.

3) Choose reservation parameters and flags (planning only)
- Required fields: ReservationName, StartTime (or StartTime=now / TIME_FLOAT), Duration or EndTime, Nodes/NodeCnt, and at least one access control (Users/Accounts/QOS/AllowedPartitions).
- Typical flags and their meaning (use in planning and in your command template):
  - Flags=MAINT  — marks the reservation as maintenance: nodes show in maint state during reservation; usage reporting shows PlannedDown.
  - Flags=IGNORE_JOBS — allows creating a reservation even if jobs are running (you will need to cancel them at start time if you want them gone).
  - Flags=REPLACE or REPLACE_DOWN — controls replacement behavior for down/drained/allocated nodes (careful: REPLACE can move reservations).
  - Flags=TIME_FLOAT — floating reservation that keeps a fixed period in the future (useful for a recurring window without occupying nodes now).
  - Flags=MAGNETIC — attracts matching jobs without them specifying the reservation.
- Access control: restrict who can use the reservation (Users=, Accounts=, QOS=) so production jobs are not unintentionally scheduled.

4) Validate conflict and impact (read-only checks)
- Verify if new reservation would overlap active reservations or nodes:
  - scontrol_reservation_show  (scan times and node lists)
- Find running jobs that will not complete before your planned StartTime:
  - Use squeue elapsed and the typical job walltime (from sacct) to estimate whether they will finish before StartTime.
  - If uncertain, inspect individual jobs with scontrol_show job id=<jobid>.
- If planning a full‑node maintenance, prefer a StartTime far enough in the future to allow currently running jobs to complete; otherwise plan to coordinate cancellation.

5) Communication & policies (non‑Slurm steps)
- Announce maintenance window and reservation name, start/end time, and affected partitions/nodes to all users well ahead of time.
- Provide instructions for users to checkpoint or stop jobs, and give a deadline.
- Offer a fallback contact and expected impact (job cancellations, delayed start).

6) Test on a small scope (recommended)
- Create a short test reservation on one or two nodes (off‑peak) to verify the behavior you expect (reservation visibility, how jobs are prevented from starting there).
  - Use the same Flags you plan to use for the real maintenance to validate effects.
- Review squeue and scontrol_reservation_show after the test to confirm semantics are as you expect.

7) Example command templates (do not run unless ready)
- Template for a planned maintenance reservation (creates the reservation):
  - scontrol create reservation ReservationName=<name> StartTime="YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS" Duration=<minutes> Nodes=<node-list> Users=<admin-user> Flags=MAINT
- If you want to allow the reservation to be created even if jobs are present (you will handle cancellations separately):
  - scontrol create reservation ReservationName=<name> StartTime=<time> Duration=<min> Nodes=<nodes> Users=<user> Flags=MAINT,IGNORE_JOBS
- Floating reservation template:
  - scontrol create reservation ReservationName=<name> StartTime=now+<offset> Duration=<min> NodeCnt=<n> Flags=TIME_FLOAT,MAINT

8) When you are ready to perform the maintenance (procedural sequence; changes cluster state)
- Recommended execution sequence (for the operator to run when ready):
  1. Create reservation with Flags=MAINT and the chosen StartTime/Duration.
  2. Monitor running jobs; at StartTime, either allow running jobs that can finish by EndTime to complete, or cancel them if you used IGNORE_JOBS.
  3. Optionally set nodes to DRAIN (scontrol update NodeName=<node> State=DRAIN Reason="maintenance") to prevent new starts while you work.
  4. Perform maintenance.
  5. Resume nodes (scontrol update NodeName=<node> State=RESUME) and remove/delete the reservation (scontrol delete reservation ReservationName=<name>).
- Note: creating a MAINT reservation itself will mark nodes in maintenance during the reservation window in reporting; draining is optional depending on your workflow.

9) Caveats and gotchas
- By default Slurm will not create a reservation that would evict running jobs unless you use IGNORE_JOBS or later force cancels — plan communications accordingly.
- Flags that replace allocated resources (REPLACE) can change which nodes are in the reservation; only use if you understand the replacement semantics.
- Magnetic reservations can attract jobs unexpectedly; prefer explicit access control for maintenance.
- TIME_FLOAT is useful for “floating” windows but does not itself put nodes in DRAIN — it prevents long jobs from being started.

If you want, I can:
- Run the read‑only checks for your planned node set/partition and a proposed StartTime (sinfo, squeue, scontrol_reservation_show, sacct) and report which running jobs would be impacted and whether idle nodes are available — or
- Produce the exact scontrol create reservation command line filled in from your inputs (ReservationName, Nodes or NodeCnt, StartTime/Duration, Users/Account, Flags) so an operator can run it when ready.

Which would you like me to do next?

  - sacctmgr show users
  - sacctmgr show accounts
  - sacctmgr show qos
- Validate recent job accounting records if specific jobs are missing/wrong
  - squeue (for active jobs)
  - sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,User,Account,State,Start,End,Elapsed,ExitCode
- Check time sync (timestamp issues cause apparent mis-attribution)
  - timedatectl status or chronyc sourcestats / ntpq -p on controller and compute nodes
- Verify backups and maintenance
  - Confirm scheduled DB backups exist and test a restore periodically

Likely problems and concise remediation actions
1) slurmdbd down / DB unreachable
   - Symptom: new jobs not recorded, slurmdbd errors in journal.
   - Remediation: examine slurmdbd journal/logs, fix DB connectivity (network/credentials), free DB disk space, then restart slurmdbd. If DB schema/permissions broken, restore from most recent backup.

2) Database full or corrupt
   - Symptom: write errors in slurmdbd logs, sacct/sacctmgr calls failing.
   - Remediation: free space or grow storage, repair/restore DB from backup. If corruption suspected, stop slurmdbd and take DB snapshot before repair.

3) Missing or incorrect user/account/association mappings
   - Symptom: usage not charged to expected account or jobs show "Unknown" account.
   - Remediation: create/modify associations with sacctmgr (e.g., sacctmgr create user name=alice account=acct), review and fix account limits or QOS as needed.

4) QOS/account limits rejecting or throttling jobs
   - Symptom: users report job rejections or severely throttled submissions; accounting shows unexpected usage patterns.
   - Remediation: inspect sacctmgr limits/QOS and adjust (sacctmgr modify account/qos ...), or increase quotas. Check fairshare if entitlement complaints appear.

5) Time synchronization issues
   - Symptom: job start/end timestamps inconsistent across nodes / negative or huge elapsed times.
   - Remediation: enable/fix NTP/chrony on all nodes and controller, then re-evaluate affected records.

6) Backup/restore gaps
   - Symptom: inability to restore or missing historical accounting data after failure.
   - Remediation: implement/verify regular DB backups, document restore procedure, test restores periodically.

What I can do next
- If you want, I can run any of the checks above and return the outputs (slurmdbd status/log tail, sacctmgr show associations, sacct for specific jobs, etc.). Tell me which check(s) to run.
- If you have a concrete problem (missing job records, counts mismatching, specific users affected), give me job IDs, user/account names, or the time window and I’ll inspect those records.

If you want me to proceed with any state-changing remediation (restart slurmdbd, modify associations, restore DB), note that those are mutating actions and I’ll transfer to the operator per policy — tell me which action to perform and provide explicit targets/parameters.

results.prompt: Audit accounting problem reports and explain likely remediation
results.agent_response:
I checked accounting problem reports for you.

Summary
- I ran sacctmgr show problems and found: No accounting problems found.

What that means
- The accounting DB and Slurm accounting configuration report no current consistency or configuration errors detectable by sacctmgr.
- No immediate remediation actions are required based on that check.

If you want a proactive audit or to investigate potential accounting symptoms (missing jobs, unexpected usage totals, negative balances, slow queries), here are the common accounting problem categories, how to detect them, and likely remediation steps.

1) slurmdbd unreachable / authentication / connectivity failures
- Symptoms: sacct / sacctmgr slow or empty, periodic “failed to connect” errors in logs, new jobs not appearing in accounting.
- Diagnostics to run (read-only): check slurmdbd responsiveness, slurmctld logs, and DB process:
  - systemctl status slurmdbd && journalctl -u slurmdbd
  - scontrol ping (checks slurmctld responsiveness)
  - Check slurmdbd log for DB connection/auth errors.
- Likely remediation:
  - Restart slurmdbd after resolving underlying DB connectivity or credentials issues.
  - Verify AccountingStorageType/AccountingStorageHost and DB credentials in slurm.conf and slurmdbd.conf.
  - Ensure network/firewall allows DB traffic; check DB server health and credentials.
  - If DB is down, start DB and ensure replication or backups are intact.

2) Database corruption / schema mismatch / version incompatibility
- Symptoms: sacctmgr shows schema errors, errors referencing missing tables/columns, or weird accounting totals.
- Diagnostics: inspect slurmdbd logs and DB error logs, compare slurmdbd and slurmctld versions vs DB schema expected.
- Likely remediation:
  - If schema mismatch (after upgrade), apply the Slurm DB schema upgrade procedure (use slurmdbd tools documented by SchedMD).
  - If corruption, restore from recent DB backup and re-ingest job records if needed.
  - Coordinate version upgrades: ensure slurmctld/slurmdbd and DB schema versions are compatible.

3) Job completion logging missing (JobComp plugin misconfiguration)
- Symptoms: recent jobs exist in squeue/sacct system but sacct shows missing or incomplete job records.
- Diagnostics:
  - Check JobCompType and JobAcctGatherType in slurm.conf and slurmdbd.conf.
  - Review slurmctld and slurmdbd logs for JobComp/JobAcctGather errors.
- Remediation:
  - Fix misconfigured JobComp/JobAcctGather plugin settings, restart the daemons if configuration changed.
  - Re-run accounting ingestion only after confirming stable configuration (do not re-ingest blindly).

4) Incorrect user/account/association data (wrong allocations, unexpected usage)
- Symptoms: users see unexpected usage or limits; QOS/account associations look wrong.
- Diagnostics:
  - sacctmgr show associations, sacctmgr show users, and sacctmgr show accounts
  - sshare -l for fairshare/effective shares
- Remediation:
  - Correct associations with sacctmgr (create/modify associations, set correct QOS/account).
  - Recompute shares or adjust limits; document changes.
  - For bulk errors, consider scripting safe, auditable sacctmgr changes and testing on a small set first.

5) Incorrect or missing job charging (TRES/count mismatch, GPU accounting)
- Symptoms: GPU-hours or TRES usage not matching expectation.
- Diagnostics:
  - Inspect job records with sacct -j <jobid> -o JobID,JobName,AllocTRES,Elapsed
  - Verify node TRES config in gres.conf and slurm.conf
- Remediation:
  - Fix gres.conf / slurm.conf TRES/gres definitions and restart daemons if necessary.
  - For retrospective correction, you may need to update accounting records carefully (usually via sacctmgr or DB edits) — treat as a destructive operation and plan backups.

6) Performance problems with accounting queries (slow sacct/sacctmgr)
- Symptoms: sacct or sacctmgr queries are slow or time out.
- Diagnostics:
  - Check DB server load, slow query logs, slurmdbd and MySQL/Postgres performance metrics.
- Remediation:
  - Tune DB (indexes, query plans), add resources or replica depending on load, and archive old records (use sacct or sreport with Start= to limit queries).
  - Consider purging/archiving very old accounting rows if growth is excessive (after backups).

7) Time skew / NTP issues
- Symptoms: job times inconsistent, negative elapsed times, unusual accounting windows.
- Diagnostics:
  - Check time sync (ntp/chrony) on slurmctld, slurmdbd, compute nodes.
- Remediation:
  - Fix NTP/chrony configuration and resync clocks; address any nodes with persistent skew.

8) Permission / RBAC problems for sacctmgr users
- Symptoms: operators cannot run sacctmgr or see expected rows.
- Diagnostics:
  - Check sacctmgr user permissions and authentication method.
- Remediation:
  - Update sacctmgr user roles/permissions, verify authentication backend (LDAP/munge), and rotate credentials if needed.

Suggested prioritized audit checklist (what I’d run next if you want a deeper audit)
- sacctmgr show problems (done) — returns no problems.
- scontrol ping and scontrol show config — verify controller responsiveness and accounting config.
- systemctl status & journalctl -u slurmdbd (on slurmdbd host) — check DB connectivity and errors.
- sacctmgr show associations; sacctmgr show users; sacctmgr show accounts — confirm associations and limits.
- sacct -S now-7days -u <user> -j <jobid> to inspect specific job accounting.
- sshare -l and sreport for usage summaries.
- Check DB health (mysql/postgres status, slow query log).

Preventive measures
- Regularly run sacctmgr show problems on a schedule and alert on non-empty output.
- Backup slurmdbd DB daily and test restores.
- Monitor slurmdbd and DB health (CPU, I/O, connection errors).
- Keep slurm versions aligned between slurmctld and slurmdbd; follow upgrade docs for database migrations.
- Enforce time sync on all cluster hosts.

- Investigate a specific symptom (missing jobs, wrong usage for a user, slow sacct queries).
